Above is a big cloudy sky, red buoys and a snorkeler in an orange vest floating face-down. The bold white title 'Snorkeling in Cozumel 🤿🇲🇽' sits in the upper-middle. It answers 'where/what' instantly with a destination name plus two emoji. Then at 1.33s it cuts on an audio hit (1.37) from the surface straight under water into a swarm of striped fish around snorkelers. That surface-to-underwater plunge is the scroll-stopper. A 'Thank you' sound plays at 0.91s, part of the music/audio bed.

beats.what: Waterline split shot: turquoise water, clouds, buoys, snorkeler floating; title 'Snorkeling in Cozumel 🤿🇲🇽'.
Plunge under water: snorkelers above, a school of striped sergeant major fish, a blue fin in the foreground; the title stays on.
Fish over the sandy bottom; caption 'Photographers brought fish food to attract them and capture photos' (insider tip on how the tour works).
Same shot: a photographer in an orange shirt with a camera is mobbed by fish; caption changes to 'Dozens of fish of all types came to eat, not scared of us at all'.
Looking down at the sandy bottom with a red hand-drawn arrow pointing at a camouflaged stingray; a finger points at it; caption 'Even a Stingray came to join us!'.
The guide free-dives to the bottom to the stingray; the creator's fins in the foreground; caption 'Our guide dove down to say hello'.
The orange-shirt feeder swims with a cloud of fish trailing him, other snorkelers in the background blue; caption 'The fish eventually figured out who to follow for food'.
Closest shots: fish swim right into the lens (a fish face fills frame ~24s); caption 'Being able to get so close to these beautiful animals and capture it on camera was a breathtaking experience!'
Ends mid-shot on fish and legs with no CTA; the cut back to the waterline opening makes a soft loop.

study.action_shots: All handheld wide-angle underwater camera at normal speed. 1.33-3.07s (1.73s): follow/among shot of snorkelers kicking with fish. 3.07-8.93s (5.87s): close medium of the feeder and the photographer with fish swirling; steady motion around 30-38. 12.7-16.73s (4.03s): overhead/following view of the guide diving down and finning along the bottom, with the creator's blue fin crossing frame at ~14.9 and ~16.1s. 16.73-22.2s (5.47s): tracking alongside the swimmer as fish follow him. 22.2-28.5s (6.33s): POV with fish darting into the lens; the biggest motion spike (61.3) is at ~24.0s when a fish face fills the frame. Cuts at 1.33, 8.93, 12.7 and 16.73 sit within ~0.05s of audio hits (1.37, 8.93, 12.75, 16.72), so each new chapter lands on a beat. The action inside shots is not otherwise synced.
study.views: There are no drone or sunset views. The 'view' is the water itself. 0-1.33s is the only above-water wide: a waterline split showing sky, buoys and the turquoise surface, held 1.33s. The reveal is the cut to under water at 1.33s, which shows the depth, the blue and the fish school. The bluest, deepest open-water views come at 16.73-22.2s, with snorkelers silhouetted against the blue and surface light in the background. Camera movement is handheld swimming drift, with no push-ins or pans planned. The biggest visual payoff (fish right in the lens) is saved for the last 6.33s shot.
study.how_place_is_shown: Almost entirely mediums and close-ups from inside the action, on a wide-angle action-cam/phone-in-case at a shallow depth. People are always in frame: the orange-shirt photographer/feeder, the guide in a green rash guard, other snorkelers and the creator's own blue fins. That makes it read as 'this could be you'. It was shot in midday sun, so the water glows cyan and the sand looks almost white. The details used are the fish faces, the striped bodies, the camouflaged stingray (made legible with an arrow) and the fins, which prove the creator is there. No food, room or amenity shots.
study.info_and_value: Light but useful. The location 'Cozumel 🇲🇽' and activity 'snorkeling' are in the title. One insider tip: the photographers bring fish food to attract fish, which is why the fish swarm. Wildlife you can expect: dozens of fish types and a stingray. The guide dives down to show you wildlife. All of it comes as on-screen text, with no prices, tour name or booking info. That absence drives 'which tour?' comments. The save value is 'add this to my Cozumel excursion list'.
study.pacing: Seven shots in 28.5s, 2.1 cuts per 10s, median shot 4.03s. Fast open: 1.33s then 1.73s, so the first two shots are done in 3.07s. Then it settles into long holds of 5.87, 3.77, 4.03, 5.47 and 6.33s, timed so each caption can be read. Each cut is a new story chapter with a new caption. Major cuts land on audio hits (1.33/1.37, 8.93/8.93, 12.7/12.75, 16.73/16.72). Overall rhythm is a quick hook, then a calm, readable stroll. The longest shot comes last.
study.speed: none apparent. Everything plays at roughly real-time swimming speed. The stingray shot (8.93-12.7s) has the lowest motion (about 18-22) because the camera hovers still over the bottom, not because of slow motion.
study.on_screen_text: Two styles. (1) Title 'Snorkeling in Cozumel' plus the emoji 🤿🇲🇽 on a second line: bold white sans-serif, sentence case, thin black outline/shadow, centered in the upper third. Shown 0-3.07s across the first 2 shots. (2) Narrative captions in white regular-weight sans-serif with a soft shadow and no box, mostly left-aligned at mid-lower frame, 2-4 lines and 7-24 words each. They switch at every cut: 'Photographers brought fish food to attract them and capture photos' (3.07-~5.6s); 'Dozens of fish of all types came to eat, not scared of us at all' (~5.6-8.93s); 'Even a Stingray came to join us!' (8.93-12.7s, centered upper-middle, bolder); 'Our guide dove down to say hello' (12.7-16.73s); 'The fish eventually figured out who to follow for food' (16.73-22.2s, centered); 'Being able to get so close to these beautiful animals and capture it on camera was a breathtaking experience!' (22.2-end). Emoji appear only in the title.
study.captions: none. The only speech, 'Thank you' at 0.91-1.61s, is uncaptioned and part of the audio bed. All text is narration overlay, not speech captions.
study.audio: A music/audio track with no narration. The only words are 'Thank you' at 0.91s, likely a sample or lyric. Strong hits at 1.37, 8.93, 12.75 and 16.72s line up with the chapter cuts. A cluster of hits at 21.25-26.55s energizes the final close-up section. No obvious natural underwater sound is featured.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. At 8.93s the red arrow is already visible on the last frame of the previous shot, so the graphic was placed a frame early. That is a sloppy but invisible edit, not a designed transition. The 1.33s cut works as a surface-to-underwater 'plunge' even though it is a straight cut.
study.effects: One graphic: a red hand-drawn curved arrow pointing at the stingray, middle-right of frame, roughly 8.93-12.4s. It turns a hard-to-see animal into a 'spot it' moment. Color is strong, saturated cyan/turquoise, either native to the action cam underwater or pushed. There are no zooms, freeze frames, light leaks or split screens.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, about 2.8 Mbps h264. Soft by modern standards, with compression smearing on the busy sand texture and handheld swim-shake throughout. But the bright midday light and the saturated turquoise make it look like paradise anyway. The wide-angle lens with fish inches from it gives an immersive, authentic 'I was there' feel that polished footage would not.
study.ending: No CTA. The last shot (22.2-28.5s) is the most intimate footage, with fish swimming into the lens, plus the emotional summary caption. It simply ends on fish and legs. Looping back to the bright waterline title shot is a soft restart that encourages a rewatch.
study.why_viral: 1) An instant location-plus-activity title with flag emoji, combined with a surface-to-underwater plunge in the first 1.33s, tells excursion planners 'this is for you' and gives a visual jolt. 2) Fish swarming inches from the lens is a wildlife-closeness payoff people want to experience and send to their travel partner. 3) The caption storytelling turns raw GoPro clips into a mini-narrative with an insider tip (the fish food) and a surprise (the stingray, with an arrow), which keeps people watching to the end. 4) Relatable, unpolished traveler footage makes it feel bookable and real, and no tour name prompts comments asking which operator.
lessons: Open with the destination plus activity as a bold 3-4 word title and a flag/activity emoji in the upper third, and keep it on for the first 2 shots (~3s).
If you have water footage, cut from an above-water or waterline shot to under water within the first 1.5s, ideally on a beat, as the hook.
Give every clip one caption sentence that advances the story (tip, then surprise, then person, then feeling), and change captions only on cuts or clear beat points.
Hold each captioned shot at least 3.5-6s so captions of 10-20 words are readable; save the quick 1.3-1.8s cuts for the opening only.
When the subject is hard to see (camouflaged stingray, distant whale), add a bright red hand-drawn arrow for the whole shot, and make sure it doesn't leak onto the previous clip.

Include one insider/practical fact (e.g. 'photographers bring fish food') to give viewers a reason to save, and consider adding the tour name or price, since leaving it out trades bookings for comments.
Put the closest, most intimate wildlife shot last and make it the longest shot (~6s), paired with an emotional summary caption.
Snap chapter cuts to audio hits within ±0.05s; here 4 of 6 cuts land on hits, which makes the simple edit feel deliberate.
Keep people and the filmer's own fins/hands in frame so viewers project themselves into the experience.

study.format: 'Everything I ate on [ship]' food list / cruise dining montage. A titled establishing shot of the ship is followed by 7 dishes, each one shot (1.6-3.6s) with its name burned on screen. There is no voiceover, no ranking and no prices. It is pure food-porn sequencing set to music.
study.place: Carnival Horizon, a Carnival Cruise Line ship, seen docked at a sunny concrete cruise pier with turquoise-blue water, a second ship and puffy clouds. The trip is a mainstream Caribbean-style cruise. What makes it look special is the onboard food. There are upscale steakhouse-style plates (melting chocolate sphere with poured sauce, filet mignon and lobster tail, lobster bisque poured tableside) next to the ship's casual named venues (Guy's Burger, wood-fired pizza, shrimp tempura with fried rice, banana split). The message is that the food range runs from fine dining to fast food, all on one ship.
study.audience: Cruisers and would-be cruisers, especially people booked on or considering Carnival Horizon or Carnival in general, plus foodies. It reads as a regular traveler/creator sharing their trip, not the cruise line. It makes people save it as a 'what to eat onboard' checklist, tag their cruise partner ('we're getting the chocolate sphere'), and comment asking which restaurant or whether it costs extra.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0-2.47s) is a handheld walk down a sunny pier toward the docked Carnival Horizon, panning across to blue water. A two-tier title sits dead centre: small white 'Everything I Ate On' over a huge bubbly red-and-white 'Carnival Horizon'. Music starts with an audio hit at 0.05s. It stops the scroll because the ship name is a search/identity trigger for anyone sailing her, and the 'everything I ate' promise tells viewers a food payoff is coming in seconds. That payoff lands on cut one at 2.47s, a chocolate pour right on the 2.52s audio hit.

beats.what: Handheld walk along cruise pier, pan from docked Carnival Horizon across blue water. Title 'Everything I Ate On / Carnival Horizon'.
Ship, second ship, clouds and deep-blue harbour water. The only scenery shot in the video.
Melting Chocolate Sphere: hot chocolate sauce poured from a white jug collapses the dome in real time. Longest shot, 3.6s.
Lowercase 'so satisfying' text pops in lower-left as the sphere caves in.
Wood Fired Pizza: crew member rolls a pizza cutter through fresh pizzas at the counter, ocean deck visible behind.
Surf & Turf, Filet Mignon & Lobster Tail: starts on an extreme close-up of seared filet and grilled lemon, then pulls back to the full plate with butter cup.
Guy's Burger: close on a cheeseburger and seasoned fries on branded paper, pulls back to reveal the whole tray.
Banana Split: close on sprinkles and chocolate drizzle, pulls back to the full boat on a plate with spoon.
Lobster Bisque: empty bowl with garnish, then the bisque is poured tableside and fills the bowl.
Shrimp Tempura: close on tempura shrimp and dipping sauce, pulls up to a top-down full plate with fried rice. Motion settles to near-still and the video ends at 19.3s.

study.action_shots: There are no people or adventure action; the 'action' is all food movement, handheld. 2.47-6.07 (3.6s): chocolate sauce pour melting the sphere, close top-down medium, real-time. Its start lands on the 2.52s audio hit, and the low motion of 9-10 lets the slow melt read. 6.07-8.47 (2.4s): pizza cutter rolling across pizzas, eye-level medium through the counter, real-time (motion 13-30). The audio hit at 8.29 sits just before the cut out. 14.43-16.73 (2.3s): lobster bisque tableside pour, medium, real-time, the cut in synced to the 14.38s hit. 0-2.47: creator's POV walk down the pier (motion 20-25), the only human-movement shot.
study.views: Only one view: 0-2.47s, a handheld POV walk/pan along the pier from the bow area of Carnival Horizon swinging left across the deep-blue harbour toward a second ship. Bright midday light, white clouds, held 2.47s under the title. It's revealed by a pan, not a drone or door reveal. The biggest (and only) view lands first and serves as context; the rest of the video is food.
study.how_place_is_shown: Almost entirely close-ups and medium plate shots. Food shots typically open on a tight, slightly soft macro and pull back or tilt to the full plate (surf & turf, burger, banana split, tempura). This gives every dish a mini reveal. The only people are hands: a server pouring sauce and bisque, and a crew member cutting pizza. The creator never appears. Everything is phone-handheld POV with no gimbal or drone. Light varies: bright daylight on the pier and the casual pizza/burger venues, dim warm dining-room light for the steakhouse dishes (filet, sphere, bisque, banana split), and white plates under cool light for the tempura. The details are chosen for crave value: dripping chocolate, melted cheese, butter cup, sprinkles, garlic clove on filet. The branded Guy's Burger paper and the crew uniform quietly prove it's really onboard.
study.info_and_value: Only names, given as on-screen text: the ship (Carnival Horizon) and 7 dish names, including venue-identifying ones ('Guy's Burger', 'Wood Fired Pizza', 'Surf & Turf, Filet Mignon & Lobster Tail', 'Lobster Bisque'). There are no prices, venue names for the specialty dishes, included-vs-extra info or tips. That gap drives comments ('was that the steakhouse?', 'is it included?'). The dish list itself works as a save-worthy 'order this' checklist for people sailing that ship.
study.pacing: 19.3s, 8 shots, 3.62 cuts per 10s, median shot 2.35s (range 1.63-3.6). The hook holds 2.47s. The chocolate sphere gets the longest hold (3.6s) because the melt needs time. After that the shots tighten to 2.4 / 2.07 / 1.63 / 2.27 / 2.3, with the 1.63s burger as the quickest. The last shot runs 2.58s and slows to a still. Cuts that land on audio hits: 2.47 (hit 2.52), 14.43 (hit 14.38), 16.73 (hits 16.63/16.95), and 8.47 near 8.29. The cuts at 6.07, 10.53 and 12.17 sit between hits. The rhythm is steady and calm: one dish, one shot, roughly every 2 seconds.
study.speed: none — all footage appears to play at real time; pours and the melt are shown at natural speed.
study.on_screen_text: Title (0-2.47s), centred mid-frame: line 1 'Everything I Ate On' in small white sans with a thin black outline; line 2 'Carnival Horizon' in a huge bold rounded bubble font, white-to-red fill with a thick white and red outline (sticker/3D look), 2 lines. Then one dish label per shot, fixed in the upper third (~25% from top) and centred, shown for the whole shot and replaced on each cut, in a different colour each time. 'Melting Chocolate Sphere' is red with a white outline. 'Wood Fired Pizza' is yellow with a dark outline. 'Surf & Turf / Filet Mignon & Lobster Tail' is two lines, coral-red with a white outline. 'Guy's Burger' is yellow with a black outline. 'Banana Split' is cream/white with a black outline. 'Lobster Bisque' is orange with a white outline. 'Shrimp Tempura' is orange with a black outline. All labels are title case, 2-6 words, with no emoji. Plus a reaction text, 'so satisfying', in lowercase white with a black outline, lower-left, from ~5.0s to 6.07s.
study.audio: There is no voiceover or speech. A music track (likely a trending sound) runs throughout, with hits at 0.05, 1.71, 2.2, 2.52, 2.84, 4.12, 4.77, 5.08, 5.41, 6.68, 7.62, 8.29, 8.93-10.21 (a run of hits ~0.32s apart), 11.64, 14.38, 16.63, 16.95 and 17.9. No natural sound is evident. The first food reveal (2.47) and the bisque pour (14.43) are cut onto beats. The 'so satisfying' text appears around the 5.08 hit.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only (2.47, 6.07, 8.47, 10.53, 12.17, 14.43, 16.73). Text labels swap instantly with each cut.
study.effects: none — no added zooms, grade, glow or graphics. The 'push/pull' feel comes from the handheld camera pulling back from macro to full plate. Colour is the phone's natural look: warm in the dining room, bright blue water on the pier.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, ~1157 kbps h264. This is a compressed phone-snapshot level, not cinematic. Daylight shots (pier, pizza) are clean and saturated. The dim dining-room shots (sphere, bisque) are noisy and soft. Several shots open blurry because the camera starts too close (surf & turf, burger, banana split, tempura) before focus settles. The handheld wobble is mild. It reads as 'real guest footage', and that authenticity helps credibility more than polish would. The crave factor carries it, not the image quality.
study.ending: It ends on the 7th dish, shrimp tempura, settling into a near-still top-down plate (motion drops 8.9 → 6.1 → 3.0 in the last 1.5s), ~2.5s after the last cut. There is no CTA, summary or final view. It just stops, and the short length and abrupt end encourage a replay or loop back to the ship title.
study.why_viral: 1) The ship name is huge in the title: anyone sailing or considering Carnival Horizon stops, saves and shares it with their travel group. 2) It opens with a 'satisfying' pour (chocolate sphere collapsing on the beat at 2.5s) and repeats the pour later with the bisque, the classic food-porn trigger. 3) The high-low mix (filet and lobster tail next to Guy's Burger and a banana split) answers the cruiser's real question, 'is the food good and varied?', in under 20 seconds. 4) It's short and quiet, with one dish per ~2s and a label on every shot, so it's easy to watch twice and to screenshot as an 'order this' list.
lessons: Put the destination/ship/resort name in the first frame at the biggest text size on screen (here 2 lines filling ~40% of width at centre). People search and share by property name.
Spend at most ~2.5s on the scenic establishing shot, then hit the first 'payoff' shot on a music beat (cut at 2.47 vs hit at 2.52).
Lead with your most satisfying motion clip (a pour, melt, sizzle or reveal) and give it the longest hold, ~3.5s, so it plays through. Keep the other items around 1.6-2.4s.
Label every item with a short name (2-6 words) in a fixed upper-third position so viewers can screenshot a checklist. Changing the label colour per item makes each one feel new without extra effects.

For still subjects like plates, start the shot tight on a texture (cheese, drizzle, sear) and pull back to the full plate in the first ~1s. It turns a static shot into a mini reveal, but wait for focus before you start the clip.
Mix luxury with familiar comfort items and alternate them (dessert → pizza → steak & lobster → burger → sundae → bisque → tempura) to show range and keep the contrast high.
Use one small reaction text ('so satisfying') on the best moment rather than captions everywhere. It tells the viewer how to feel at the peak.
If adding info, put price, venue name and 'included vs extra' on each label. It's the top comment question and would raise saves further.

study.format: Activity/excursion POV montage: a no-talk snorkel clip built as surface → dive → reef → surface. One persistent title card names the activity, resort and location for the whole runtime. There is no list, no choice and no voiceover. The story is just the swim: start at the water's surface, go under, glide over the reef with fish, then come back up to the surface.
study.place: Moon Palace Resort, Ocho Rios, Jamaica (all-inclusive beach resort). The video shows its house reef right off the resort shoreline: glassy clear green-turquoise water with a hilly green coastline behind it, the resort's pier/pilings at the edge of frame, sun glitter on the surface, rippled sand, and rocky reef with schools of small yellow/striped fish, sea urchins and a big silver baitfish school. The special part is that this reef is reachable straight from the resort, no boat trip needed.
study.audience: People planning a Jamaica or all-inclusive trip, especially couples and families who want a 'what can you actually do at this resort' check. It is made to be saved for trip planning and shared or tagged to a travel partner ('we're doing this'). It reads as a traveler/creator or travel-agent style resort content (name plus location pin), not an official brand ad: the footage is raw action-cam with a foot visible at the end.
study.hook: 0.0s: an at-surface POV over crystal-clear green water with sun sparkle, the green Jamaican hillside on the left and a dramatic cloudy sky. A three-line title is already on screen: 'Snorkeling at Jamaica's' (small white), 'Moon Palace Resort' (large gold serif), '📍Ocho Rios, Jamaica📍'. Music hits immediately (audio hits at 0.19, 0.59, 0.76s). The camera floats at the waterline toward the pilings, so the viewer feels about to dip under. Clear water plus a named resort answers 'where is this' instantly, and the half-in-water angle promises an underwater reveal within 2 seconds.

beats.what: Surface POV at the waterline: clear green water, sun glitter, hills and pier pilings, with the resort title card on screen.
Cut to underwater: the camera glides over bright rippled sand with sun caustics. This is the 'we're in' moment.
First reef shot: rocky coral rubble with small yellow and striped fish swimming through. Lands on an audio hit at 3.15s.
Closer push along rocks: a school of small translucent fish and dark algae tufts.
Glide beside the pier piling: yellow-tailed fish (snapper/grunts) circle the rocks. Cut lands on the 8.4s audio hit.
Big moment: a huge silver baitfish school shimmering over the sand/rock boundary in bright blue light.
Fast tilted glide low over the rocks with a striped fish. Highest motion section (about 55-60).
Sunlit rocks with dancing light caustics, then a slow push over rocks with black damselfish.
Wider reef glide revealing sea urchins and green algae, with fish in the background.
Back to the surface: sun glitter, a kayaker on the horizon, a foot in frame and the coastline. The camera bobs at the waterline into the final frame.

study.action_shots: Everything is a first-person snorkel glide on a handheld action cam (POV). 1.67-3.13s (1.47s): the descent glide over sand, cut on the 1.75s hit. 3.13-8.4s: two slow forward drifts over the reef (2.8s and 2.47s), motion about 30-40. 10.13-12.53s: the fastest stretch, with motion peaking at 51-64 around 6.5-8s inside the reef shots and again about 55-60 around 14.5-15s. The 11.27s shot is a tilted, quick skim over rocks with a striped fish. The surface bob at 18.13-20.4s (2.27s) has motion falling to about 16-23. All of it plays at normal speed. Cuts land on or very near audio hits at 1.75 (cut 1.67), 3.15 (cut 3.13), 5.89 (cut 5.93), 8.4 (cut 8.4), 11.34 (cut 11.27), 12.63 (cut 12.53) and 15.35 (cut 15.47). The cut rhythm follows the beat, but the action itself is a continuous drift rather than a single drop moment.
study.views: Opening surface wide (0-1.67s, held 1.67s): a waterline-level drift toward the pier, with the coastline and sky giving scale. Biggest underwater view: the silver baitfish school at 10.13-11.27s (1.13s, the shortest shot), revealed by gliding forward into bright open water, the brightest and most blue frame of the reef section. The closing surface wide (18.13-20.4s, 2.27s) shows sun glitter on the water, a kayaker and the coastline, revealed by surfacing. It acts as a bookend that re-establishes the resort setting. There is no drone, no room view and no sunset. All views are reached by swimming forward or by the camera breaking the surface.
study.how_place_is_shown: About 80% underwater mediums and details (rocks, fish, urchins, sand caustics) and about 20% surface wides at the open and close. There are no faces. The only person is the creator implied by POV, with a foot at 18.3s and a distant kayaker. The light is bright daylight under a partly cloudy sky. Sun caustics and glitter carry the 'clear Caribbean water' feel. The camera is a handheld action cam held low, with no gimbal or drone. There is no food, drinks or room. The water clarity and marine life stand in for 'amenities': what's right off the beach.
study.info_and_value: Facts given: the activity (snorkeling), the resort name (Moon Palace Resort) and the location (Ocho Rios, Jamaica), all as one on-screen text card that stays for the full video. There is no price, no booking info and no voiceover. The value is proof: the resort has a snorkel-worthy reef with real fish right at its pier. That makes it a save for anyone comparing Jamaica resorts, and a share to a travel partner.
study.pacing: 10 shots in 20.4s, 4.41 cuts per 10s, median 2.0s per shot. The shortest is 1.13s (the baitfish school) and the longest is 2.93s (rocks/damselfish, 12.53-15.47s). The first two shots are quick (1.67s, 1.47s) to get underwater fast. The middle alternates 2.5-3s reef drifts with 1.1-1.7s punchy shots at 10.13-12.53s. It ends on a 2.27s calm surface hold. Almost every cut sits within 0.1s of an audio hit. The overall feel is relaxed but never still, with median motion of 30.9.
study.on_screen_text: One static three-line title block, top-center (about 13-23% from the top), visible 0-20.4s without changing. Line 1: 'Snorkeling at Jamaica's' in a white medium-weight sans-serif with a soft shadow. Line 2: 'Moon Palace Resort' in a large bold gold/yellow serif with a dark outline/shadow (the dominant line). Line 3: '📍Ocho Rios, Jamaica📍' in a small white sans with red pin emoji on both sides. That's 8 words total, with no animation.
study.audio: There is no speech. A music track drives the edit, with dense hits early (0.19, 0.59, 0.76, 0.99, 1.37, 1.75, 1.94, 2.34, 2.94, 3.15s) and then spaced accents at 5.21, 5.53, 5.89, 8.4, 11.14, 11.34, 11.88, 12.63, 15.35s. A cluster at 18.5-20.28s closes the track. Cuts are placed on these hits (8.4s exactly). No natural underwater sound is evident from the data.
study.transitions: hard cuts only. The 1.67s cut (surface to underwater) and the 18.13s cut (underwater to surface) work as cut-on-motion 'dive' and 'surface' moments without effects.
study.effects: No graphics beyond the title. The colour shows a light lift and saturation on the green-turquoise water and bright highlights on the sun glitter. Underwater shots are hazy and slightly washed toward cyan/white, with no heavy red-correction. There are no zooms, shakes or freeze frames.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps and 2433 kbps h264, low-to-mid resolution. Underwater footage is soft and hazy, with backscatter and some blown highlights in the caustics. Handheld action-cam movement is visible. It looks like an authentic phone/action-cam snapshot rather than a cinematic production, which reads as a real guest's experience. The water clarity at the surface shots does the 'dream trip' work.
study.ending: It ends on the surfacing shot (18.13-20.4s): sun glitter on clear water, the coastline and a kayaker, held 2.27s, cut right after the final audio hit at 20.28s. The surface water frame at the end closely matches the opening frame, so it loops almost seamlessly. There is no spoken or text CTA.
study.why_viral: 1) The resort name and location are on screen from frame 1, so it works as instant search/save content for anyone booking Jamaica all-inclusives. 2) It shows an unexpected perk: real reef fish and a huge baitfish school right off a resort pier, which makes people want to go. 3) The surface-dive-reef-surface arc plus beat-synced cuts make 20s feel like a complete mini-experience, and the matching first and last frames encourage rewatch loops. 4) The authentic POV footage feels trustworthy and achievable.
lessons: Put the place name and location (with 📍 pins) on screen from 0.0s to the end. Keep it to 3 lines and about 8 words, top 25% of the frame, with the resort name largest and in an accent colour like gold with an outline.
Open on a waterline/surface shot and cut underwater within 1.5-2s. The 'about to dive' frame is the hook for any water activity.
Bookend the clip: start and end on near-identical surface wides (1.5-2.5s each) so it loops and re-anchors the setting.
Cut on music hits: place cuts within ±0.1s of the track's transients, using 2.5-3s for slow reef drifts and 1.1-1.5s for the single most striking shot (fish school, big reveal).
Give the most visually unique moment (e.g. a fish school) its own short, bright shot about halfway through (around 50% of the runtime) as a mid-video payoff.
Keep the total around 20s with about 10 shots (median about 2s) for activity POV content. No voiceover needed when the visuals plus title tell the story.
Lightly boost saturation and brightness on turquoise water and sun glitter, but don't over-sharpen hazy underwater footage. Authenticity outweighs polish for 'real guest' resort content.
Include one small human cue (foot, hand, a kayaker) in the surface shots so viewers read it as an experience they could have, not stock footage.

study.format: Destination montage / quick-hit landmark list: 8 handheld clips (7 locations) from a Spain trip. Each location gets a two-line name label and a matching AI-style voiceover line that names it. The structure is hook title → Valencia landmark → Barcelona landmarks → a humor beat (Dunkin') → viewpoint → food market finale. There are no numbers, rankings or choices; it is a 'come see Spain with us' sampler.
study.place: Spain, multi-city sightseeing trip (city/culture travel, not resort). The opening is an unlabeled river with a white-water weir below a hillside town. Then L'Umbracle area at Valencia's City of Arts and Sciences: futuristic white Calatrava architecture over a turquoise pool with water bikes. Then inside La Sagrada Familia: stained glass throwing blue/green and orange light onto tree-like columns. Then a Dunkin' on a Barcelona street. Then a hilltop city panorama labeled 'Olympic Village in Barcelona' (statues, a busker, blue sky). Last is Mercado de La Boqueria: towering fruit pyramids and hanging jamón with euro price tags. What makes it special is the variety, from modern architecture to Gaudí light to market color, packed into 15 seconds.
study.audience: Made for people who daydream about Europe/Spain trips, especially group-travel shoppers. 'Take a trip to Spain with us' reads as a travel agency or group-tour host inviting followers along, not a solo creator diary. It aims for saves ('places to see in Spain'), shares to a travel buddy, and inquiries about joining the trip. The Dunkin' line adds a relatable, comment-bait American-tourist moment.
study.hook: Frame 1 is a wide landscape of churning white water over a river weir, with a green hillside and stone buildings under a dramatic cloudy sky. Centered on it is a stacked title: 'Take a Trip To' (white), a large 'SPAIN' in red serif with a yellow outline, and 'With Us!' (white). The voiceover starts at 0.00s: 'Take a trip to Spain with us.' Moving water gives instant motion (~36 on the motion graph). The bold red-yellow flag-colored 'SPAIN' names the destination in under a second, and 'with us' frames it as an invitation rather than someone else's vacation.

beats.what: River weir with white rapids and a hillside town, handheld pan left-to-right along the river; title 'Take a Trip To SPAIN With Us!'; VO 'Take a trip to Spain with us.'

L'Umbracle, Valencia: Calatrava's white arched bridge and domed building over a turquoise pool with people on water bikes; camera pans right along the white ribbed architecture; label 'L'Umbracle in Valencia'; VO 'La Braco in Valencia.'
Inside La Sagrada Familia: blue stained glass and carved stone, camera tilting up past a crowd looking up; label 'La Sagrada Familia Church in Barcelona'.
Second Sagrada Familia shot: the nave's tree-like columns glowing orange/yellow from stained glass, people holding up phones; VO finishes 'Church in Barcelona.'
Humor/relatability beat: a Dunkin' storefront on a Barcelona street, a passerby walks through frame; label 'Of course, they have a Dunkin''; VO 'Of course they have a Duncan.'
Hilltop panorama over Barcelona from steps with statues and a busker playing guitar, blue sky; slow pan right revealing the palace towers and plaza below; label 'Olympic Village in Barcelona'.
Mercado de La Boqueria: walking pan across towering, saturated fruit displays (oranges, dragon fruit, papaya, dates); label 'Mercado de La Boqueria in the heart of Barcelona'.
Boqueria jamón stall: hanging Iberian hams and cured meats in red light with euro price tags (e.g. '9'50 €Und.'), shoppers at the counter; video ends mid-pan at 15.6s.

study.action_shots: There are no action-sport shots. All the movement comes from handheld walking pans and people moving through frame. The water bikes and paddlers in the Valencia pool (2.0–3.93s, wide, normal speed) are the closest thing to activity. A pedestrian crosses the Dunkin' frame at ~8.1s. Shoppers and phone-holding tourists appear at Sagrada Familia (3.93–7.17s) and Boqueria (11.47–15.6s). The motion graph peaks at 55–67 during 11.0–13.0s, the fast pan across the Boqueria fruit, so the busiest movement sits in the final third. None of it is timed to a specific drop.
study.views: 1) 0–2.0s: river weir and hillside town, wide, held 2.0s, handheld pan right revealing the town on the cliff. 2) 2.0–3.93s: Valencia's white Calatrava structures over the turquoise pool, wide, 1.93s, pan right along the ribbed museum facade. 3) 3.93–7.17s: Sagrada Familia interior across two shots (1.33s + 1.9s), tilting up and panning to reveal the glowing stained-glass nave; the warmest, most 'wow' visual. 4) 8.93–11.47s: Barcelona city panorama from the hilltop steps, the longest shot at 2.53s, slow pan right that moves from statues to the full city and plaza below. This is the biggest landscape view, placed just past the midpoint. Everything is ground-level phone footage; there are no drone shots, sunsets or reveals through doors or curtains.
study.how_place_is_shown: Mostly wides and mediums of landmarks, finishing on dense medium/close detail of market food. Strangers appear for scale and authenticity (crowds looking up at Sagrada, a busker, shoppers); the creator never appears on camera, only the 'us' in the voiceover. Everything is filmed handheld on a phone with smooth walking pans, all eye-level POV of a visitor. The light is mostly overcast daylight (river, Valencia, Dunkin'), the blue sky with sun at the panorama, and warm colored interior light at Sagrada Familia and the Boqueria. Food details (fruit pyramids, hanging ham, price tags) close the video because they are the most color-saturated, sensory images.
study.info_and_value: Names and cities only, given twice: as on-screen labels and as voiceover. L'Umbracle in Valencia; La Sagrada Familia Church in Barcelona; Dunkin' (joke); 'Olympic Village in Barcelona' (the footage is actually a Montjuïc hilltop view); Mercado de La Boqueria 'in the heart of Barcelona'. Visible jamón price tags (e.g. 9.50 €) give incidental price info. There are no tips, no trip price and no booking info. Save value comes from it working as a quick Spain bucket list; the 'with us' framing hints at a bookable group trip but never spells it out.
study.pacing: 8 shots in 15.6s, 4.49 cuts per 10s. Shot lengths: 2.0, 1.93, 1.33, 1.9, 1.77, 2.53, 2.0, 2.14s, median 1.96s, tightly uniform between 1.33 and 2.53s. Each location gets one voiceover sentence, and cuts land at or just after the sentence ends (VO lines end 1.72, 3.54, 6.62, 8.60, 11.00, 14.90; cuts at 2.0, 3.93, 7.17, 8.93, 11.47). The music bed hits roughly every 0.5s (0.35, 0.85, 1.35, 2.35…), and several cuts sit on hits: 2.0≈1.97, 3.93≈3.98, 7.17≈7.1, 8.93≈8.85, 13.47≈13.35. Sagrada Familia is split into two shots (3.93–7.17) under one label so the most beautiful place gets 3.24s total. The longest single hold (2.53s) goes to the panorama. Motion rises in the back half (median 37.8 overall, 55–67 at 11–13s), so the end feels busier than the start.
study.on_screen_text: Hook (0–2.0s): three stacked centered lines in the upper third. 'Take a Trip To' and 'With Us!' are in white bold sans with a black outline. 'SPAIN' is about 3× larger, red serif caps with a yellow outline/glow (Spanish flag colors). Location labels (2.0s onward) are white sans, sentence case, thin black stroke, two centered lines in the upper third (~25–30% from top): 'L'Umbracle / in Valencia', 'La Sagrada Familia Church / in Barcelona', 'Of course, they have / a Dunkin'', 'Olympic Village / in Barcelona', 'Mercado de La Boqueria / in the heart of Barcelona'. Each label pops on at the cut and stays the full length of its location, carrying across the two Sagrada shots and the two Boqueria shots. Each is 3–7 words, with no emoji, boxes or animation.
study.captions: No separate speech captions. The location labels function as captions since they match the voiceover text almost word for word. They are written correctly even where the voice mispronounces ('La Braco' vs 'L'Umbracle', 'Duncan' vs 'Dunkin'').
study.audio: An upbeat music bed with a steady pulse roughly every 0.5s (strong hits at 0.35, 0.85, 1.35… through 15.35). Over it runs a text-to-speech style voiceover that names each place. It starts at 0.00s, so there is no silent intro, and it fills almost every second (36 words, ending at 14.90s). Gaps between lines are short (0.3–0.6s) and sit at the cuts. No natural sound (water, crowd, busker guitar) is noticeably featured. Cuts tend to fall on the music pulse right after each VO sentence ends.
study.transitions: hard cuts only
study.effects: No zooms, graphics or maps added in the edit; the movement is all camera pans. The color appears boosted: the Boqueria fruit and jamón shots look heavily saturated and sharpened (HDR-ish), the Valencia pool water reads very turquoise, and Sagrada's stained-glass oranges and greens are vivid. The only graphic styling is the red/yellow 'SPAIN' title.
study.quality: 576×1024 at 30fps, h264 ~2.8 Mbps: moderate resolution, fine on a phone but a bit soft. It is handheld and fairly smooth, likely phone stabilization. Exposure is uneven: overcast skies are flat and slightly blown in the hook and Valencia shots, while the panorama has a proper blue sky. Sagrada and the Boqueria look the most premium because of the warm colored light and saturation. Overall it reads as an authentic phone travel diary rather than cinematic, which suits the 'trip with us' group-tour tone.
study.ending: Ends on the Boqueria jamón stall mid-pan, about 0.7s after the last voiceover word (14.90s → 15.6s). There is no CTA, no recap and no final title; it simply stops on the richest food shot. The abrupt stop on busy motion makes a soft loop back to the moving water of the opening.
study.why_viral: 1) An instant, clear promise: a bold flag-colored 'SPAIN' plus 'take a trip with us' in the first second, with voiceover starting at 0.0s. 2) High variety at a steady ~2s rhythm (futuristic Valencia, glowing Gaudí interior, city panorama, color-bomb market), so every cut delivers a new 'wow' and viewers watch to the end. 3) The Dunkin' joke breaks the postcard pattern and invites comments (Americans abroad, 'why would you go to Dunkin' in Spain'), and the mispronunciations ('La Braco', 'Duncan') provoke correction comments. 4) Named landmarks make it a saveable mini bucket list.
lessons: Put the destination name on the first frame in huge, colored, outlined type (3× the surrounding text) and say it out loud starting at 0.0s; no silent intros.
Give each location exactly one 1.3–2.5s shot (or two shots under one label for the showpiece), and cut 0.2–0.5s after the voiceover sentence ends, snapped to the nearest music beat.
Label every place with a 2-line, 3–7 word 'Name / in City' caption in the upper third, white with a black stroke, that stays for the whole location and changes on the cut.
Split your most beautiful location into two shots (~1.3s + ~1.9s) under one label so it gets the most screen time (~3.2s) without any single shot dragging.
Insert one off-script, relatable or funny beat (a familiar chain, a local quirk) around the midpoint to break the montage pattern and trigger comments.
Order clips so color and motion build: flatter overcast shots early, warm interiors and saturated food last; end on the most vivid, busiest shot.
Use slow handheld walking pans (not static frames) so every shot carries motion; reserve the longest hold (~2.5s) for the widest panorama.

Spell names correctly on screen even if the TTS voice mispronounces them, and if you want the trip booked, add a clear final 1s CTA (dates, 'link in bio', 'comment SPAIN'), which this video is missing.

study.format: Embarkation-day ship tour / mini day-in-the-life on a cruise. It is built as a chronological voiceover checklist: drive to the terminal, pier, staff welcome, free champagne, ship neighborhoods, cabin, balcony, food, gym, relaxation room, entertainment, and a sunset closer. Each stop gets one short spoken line, matched by a caption, over 1-4 quick clips. There are 13 spoken lines across 24 shots in 36s.
study.place: Royal Caribbean's Wonder of the Seas, an Oasis-class mega cruise ship, as a cruise vacation. It looks special because of its sheer scale. The ship towers over the pier at 1.4-2.47s. You also see Central Park with water slides visible at the end of the open-air neighborhood (8.4-9.9s), the colorful pool deck and slide tower at golden hour (9.9-11.27s), and the Boardwalk/AquaTheater canyon seen from a lounger (11.27-13.33s). Then come a balcony cabin with open ocean, Chops Grille, buffet and bakery, a big gym, a blue-lit relaxation room, the AquaTheater fountain show, the carousel and an atrium bar. It ends on a sunset over the sea.
study.audience: First-time and would-be cruisers, plus families and couples comparing ships. It makes them want to save it as a 'what embarkation day is like' preview, tag a travel partner ('we need to do this'), and look up the ship. It reads as an everyday traveler or creator, a friendly woman in selfie shots toasting champagne. It could be a travel agent's FAM-style content, but it is not branded by the cruise line. The relatable, unpolished phone footage builds trust.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0-1.4s) is a POV through a car windshield driving under 'TERMINAL 1' gantry signs, with the giant white ship already visible on the horizon. A big title is stacked in the upper-middle: small white 'Let's Sail on the' over large italic blue outlined 'WONDER OF THE SEAS®'. A voiceover starts at 0.14s: 'Let's sail on the wonder of the seas.' At 1.4s it cuts on an audio hit to a walking shot at the pier with the ship filling the frame. It stops the scroll because the 'arriving at the ship' moment is instantly understood, the ship name is a searchable promise, and 'Let's sail' invites the viewer along.

beats.what: Windshield POV driving into the cruise terminal, ship on the horizon. Title 'Let's Sail on the WONDER OF THE SEAS®' and VO line.
Walking down the pier with passengers in matching caps. The ship towers on both sides, with a second shot of the bow and dome.
POV walking in. A staff member dances toward camera and the crew cheer and wave in Santa hats. The creator waves back. 'Here's how we were greeted by the staff!'
Waiter offers a flute from a tray, handed to the camera. 'Free Champagne?!'
Selfie toast to camera with the glass. 'Don't mind if I do!'
Central Park walkway looking up the open canyon to the water slides. 'Is that a water slide?'
Golden-hour pool deck, slide tower, pan across a striped cabana.
Feet up on a lounger behind glass, looking down the ship's interior canyon at sunset light. Held 2.07s.
Walk through the cabin door to the bed. 'Here's our cabin!' (VO 'Our cabin').
Sofa, balcony door and pan to the vanity mirror.
Balcony table: sunscreen, neon green sunglasses and a Cruise Compass, ocean behind. 'Views from our balcony!'
Tilt up from the balcony to open blue ocean and horizon.
Purple-lit Chops Grille entrance. 'Can't forget our favorite part...'
Buffet station pans, then bakery case and bread case. 'The FOOD!'
Gym bikes, then weight floor. 'The perfect gym / For when you eat too much'.
Hand pushes the 'Relaxation Room' door open to reveal a blue-lit glass sculpture. 'Plus a relaxation room!'
0.5s flash of the creator lying on heated tile loungers.
AquaTheater show: performers and fountain jets. 'Tons of entertainment'.
Lit-up carousel turning, then the atrium bar from above. '& activities across the ship!'
Orange sunset with the sun on the ocean horizon, held 2.97s. 'Where else can you get this view?'

study.action_shots: 1.4-2.47s (1.07s): follow/POV walk down the pier behind other passengers, normal speed, cut in on the 1.48s audio hit. 2.47-5.0s (2.53s): staff member dancing toward the POV camera while the creator's arm waves into frame, handheld, normal speed. Motion peaks at 47.6 (1.5s) and 41.9 (2.0s). 5.0-7.47s: champagne handed directly into the lens, a POV 'gift' action. 26.4-28.77s: POV hand pushing a door open, a walk-through action. 29.27-30.67s (1.4s): wide from the audience of AquaTheater performers with fountains firing, cut in on the 29.32s audio hit. 30.67-31.8s (1.13s): carousel rotating, wide/medium, cut near the 30.82s hit. Nothing is ramped; cuts follow the voiceover phrasing more than a beat drop.
study.views: Ship exterior: 0-1.4s, approaching through the windshield (forward travel). Then 1.4-2.47s, walking up beside the hull with the ship filling the top of the frame. Central Park canyon: 8.4-9.9s, slow handheld walk with the slides revealed at the far end. Pool deck: 9.9-11.27s, slow pan in golden light. Interior canyon from the lounger: 11.27-13.33s, held 2.07s, near-static with feet in the foreground framing the view. Balcony: 16.53-17.5s, a props shot with ocean behind, then 17.5-18.93s, a tilt/pan up from the railing to the horizon (1.43s). The biggest view lands last: the sunset at 33.0-36.0s, the longest shot at 2.97s, almost static (motion drops to 4-8). It is framed with the balcony glass at the bottom so it reads as 'from our room'.
study.how_place_is_shown: Almost all handheld phone footage, about 50/50 POV and filmed scenes. No drone or gimbal. The mix is mostly mediums and walking wides, with a few details: champagne flute, sunscreen and sunglasses with the Cruise Compass, bread baskets. The creator appears in a selfie toast (7.47s), as feet in the lounger shot, as a hand opening a door, and lying on the heated loungers (28.77s). This makes it a real person's trip rather than an ad. Light moves through the day: bright blue-sky terminal morning, warm golden-hour decks, neutral interiors, purple and blue night lighting (Chops, relaxation room, AquaTheater, carousel), then the sunset. The details are chosen because they are tangible perks (free champagne, food, a balcony with ocean) that viewers imagine themselves using.
study.info_and_value: Facts are given only by voiceover and captions. They cover the ship name (Wonder of the Seas®), free champagne at boarding, a staff welcome, a water slide, a balcony cabin, Chops Grille (named on the sign), the buffet and bakery, the gym, the relaxation room, entertainment (AquaTheater, carousel, bar) and the ocean sunset. There are no prices, cabin category, dates or booking info. The value is a quick 'here's everything you get' checklist that makes people save it as a preview, and a rhetorical CTA question ('Where else can you get this view?') that invites comments and shares.
study.pacing: 36s, 24 shots, 6.39 cuts per 10s, median shot 1.4s, range 0.5-2.97s. Rhythm follows the voiceover: each spoken line gets 1-3 shots, and cuts land just before or at the start of each phrase (2.47 vs 'Here's' at 2.54, 5.0 vs 'Free' at 5.08, 8.4 vs 'Is' at 8.18, 18.93 vs 'Can't' at 18.66, 28.77 vs 'Tons' at 28.98, 33.0 vs 'Where' at 32.86). Several cuts also sit on audio hits (1.4/1.48, 2.47/2.53, 17.5/17.49, 29.27/29.32). Held shots are the arrival moments: the greeting at 2.53s, champagne at 2.47s, the canyon view at 2.07s, the relaxation door reveal at 2.37s and the sunset at 2.97s. The fastest run is the food and gym montage, 20.67-24.73s, with shots of 1.37, 0.83, 0.8 and 1.07s and motion of 40-46. The quickest flash is the lounger at 0.5s. It speeds up in the middle and settles on the end shot.
study.on_screen_text: Opening title only, 0-2.47s, upper-middle centered over the sky. Line 1 'Let's Sail on the' is small white sans with a dark shadow. Below it, 'WONDER OF THE SEAS®' sits on 3 lines in heavy italic blue display type with a white outline and glow. It stays for the first two shots and disappears at the cut to the greeting.
study.captions: Present for every voiceover line from 2.47s to the end. They are white sentence-case sans-serif (TikTok Classic style) with a thin black stroke and shadow, placed in the lower-middle around 65-75% height, sometimes slightly higher. Each line appears whole on its shot and stays until the next line. Long lines are split into two chunks timed to the VO: 'The perfect gym' (23.67s) then 'For when you eat too much' (24.73s), 'Tons of entertainment' then '& activities across the ship!', 'Where else can you' then 'get this view?' (about 34.5s). Wording is lightly punched up versus speech: 'Here's our cabin!', 'Free Champagne?!', 'The FOOD!' in caps for emphasis, and an ellipsis on 'favorite part...' to tease the reveal.
study.audio: A voiceover carries the whole video: 69 words, first word at 0.14s, 13 short upbeat lines with small gaps. It is a light, cheerful, slightly jokey tone ('Don't mind if I do', 'for when you eat too much'). Underneath is an upbeat music bed whose strongest hits (0.22, 1.48, 2.53, 17.49, 29.32, 30.82, 35.49) coincide with several cuts. Natural crowd and cheering are likely under the staff welcome. Sound and picture line up mainly by phrase: each new line triggers a new location.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. Some are motivated by movement: the walk-through door at 13.33s into the cabin and the door push at 26.4s act as in-shot reveals rather than edited wipes.
study.effects: No zooms, shakes, freeze frames or graphics beyond the title. The colour looks like native phone processing with high saturation: punchy blue sky and sea, warm orange at golden hour, saturated purple and blue in night interiors. The sunset is rich orange with no visible extra grade.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, about 2.2 Mbps H.264, so modest resolution with some softness and compression in dark interiors (Chops, relaxation room, AquaTheater). It is handheld and mostly steady enough, with walking bob in POV shots. Bright skies are well exposed with blue retained, and the ocean and sunset look rich. It reads as an authentic phone snapshot trip rather than a cinematic ad. The dream-trip feeling comes from the content (scale, perks, golden hour, sunset), not the technical polish.
study.ending: Ends on the biggest, calmest view: the 2.97s ocean sunset with the rhetorical question 'Where else can you get this view?', finishing at 34.88s with about 1.1s of held sunset after. There is no explicit save or follow CTA. The question works as a soft comment prompt. It does not loop seamlessly (sunset back to the car POV), but the calm-to-busy contrast invites a rewatch.
study.why_viral: 1) A complete 'what boarding day feels like' journey in 36s, from terminal to sunset, a highly searched first-cruise fantasy, and every stop is a relatable perk (free champagne, balcony, food). 2) Warm human moments, a dancing staff welcome and a champagne handed into the lens, put the viewer in the creator's shoes via POV. 3) Fast phrase-driven cuts (median 1.4s) with a clear voiceover and caption keep information dense, so it gets saved as a preview. 4) It saves the best view for last and closes with a question that invites comments and tags.
lessons: Open with a moving POV toward the destination (car, walkway, gangway), with the place's name as a big two-tier title in the first frame, and start the voiceover within 0.2s.
Write the voiceover as a checklist of 8-13 short lines of 2-8 words, and cut to the new location 0-0.3s before each line starts.
Give each stop 1-3 shots of 0.8-2.5s. Hold 'gift' or 'welcome' moments (staff greeting, a drink handed into the lens) for 2.5s, and run food or amenity montages at 0.8-1.4s per shot.
Use POV interactions (hand taking a drink, hand pushing a door open, feet up framing a view) so the viewer feels they are the traveler. Use at least 3 in a 30-40s edit.
Use real doors and walk-throughs as reveals for rooms and spaces instead of edited transitions.
Order the day's light: bright arrival, golden-hour decks, night-lit venues, and end on the single best view (sunset or ocean) as the longest shot, about 3s and nearly static.

Caption every line in white sans with a black stroke in the lower-middle. Split long lines into two timed chunks, and use caps or an ellipsis to tease the next reveal ('The FOOD!', 'favorite part...').
Add one self-aware joke line (e.g., gym 'for when you eat too much') to make amenity shots shareable and personal.
Close with a rhetorical question over the final view to prompt comments and tags in place of a hard sell.

study.format: Multiple choice / 'Choose Your Vacation' destination montage, labelled 'part 1' as a series. It opens with a 3.87s airplane-window takeoff under a title card. Then come 7 rapid one-shot destination options (Bali, The Maldives, Paris, Santorini, Egypt, Rome, Hawaii), each with a one-word name label. There is no voiceover. It is a pure music-cut slideshow of bucket-list postcard shots.
study.place: A global bucket-list mix rather than one trip: Bali (pink-purple sunset over a rock island with a natural arch), the Maldives (drone over a turquoise lagoon with a resort jetty and thatched overwater restaurant), Paris (Eiffel Tower lit gold/pink at night with searchlight beams), Santorini (Oia blue dome above the caldera at dusk), Egypt (Sphinx in front of the Great Pyramid under blue sky), Rome (a woman sitting on a grassy hill facing the Colosseum and cypress trees) and Hawaii (palm-framed golden beach with turquoise surf). Each is the single most iconic, instantly recognisable image of that place, and the mix spans beach, city, history and island.
study.audience: Broad daydreaming travelers, couples and friend groups. It is built to make people comment their pick and tag the person they'd go with. The 'part 1' tag also makes them follow for the next part. It reads as an aggregator/creator travel-inspiration page, not a resort or agent: the footage is clearly compiled from many sources, and only the Rome shot has a person in it.
study.hook: Frame 1 is a POV through a plane window as it rolls down the runway at dawn. The wing sits mid-frame under a soft cloudy sky. The centered title 'Choose Your Vacation' is in white serif with black outline, with a small pink script 'part 1' beneath. The music starts immediately with a ticking build: audio hits at 0.56, 0.91, 1.26, 1.63, 1.95 and so on, about every 0.35s. It stops the scroll because the takeoff POV triggers the 'leaving on a trip' feeling everyone recognises. The title is also a direct game invitation: the viewer knows choices are coming and waits to see the options.

beats.what: Plane window POV, wing on runway at dawn; title 'Choose Your Vacation' + 'part 1' held over a slow takeoff roll while the music builds.
The title itself is the question; it stays on screen the whole 3.87s intro.
Bali: pink-purple sunset, silhouetted rock island with arch, gentle waves on wet sand.
The Maldives: drone shot moving over a turquoise reef lagoon toward a jetty and thatched overwater building.
Paris: Eiffel Tower lit gold/pink at night with blue searchlight beams, low angle.
Santorini: Oia blue dome and white houses above the dusk caldera, boats on the water; a near-still shot.
Egypt: Sphinx in front of the Great Pyramid, bright blue sky.
Rome: woman seated on a grassy hill looking at the Colosseum, sun flaring behind clouds, tall cypresses.
Hawaii: palm fronds framing a golden beach and turquoise surf, saturated blue sky; held longest as the closer.

study.choice_format: The question is the title 'Choose Your Vacation' (part 1). There are 7 options, labelled only by destination name in one-to-two words ('Bali', 'The Maldives', 'Paris', 'Santorini', 'Egypt', 'Rome', 'Hawaii'). There are no numbers, letters or emoji. Labels use white bold monospace/typewriter-style type with a thin black outline, placed in the upper-middle third (about 37-40% from the top), roughly left-centered and changing slightly per shot. Each option gets exactly one shot. On-screen times are 1.0, 0.9, 0.9, 0.87, 0.93 and 0.87s, then 1.69s for the last (Hawaii). Options are separated by hard cuts placed on the music beat (audio hits at 3.78/4.68/5.61/6.55/7.47/8.4/9.32 against cuts at 3.87/4.87/5.77/6.67/7.53/8.47/9.33). The order alternates moods (sunset beach → lagoon → night city → white-and-blue island → desert history → people/ruins → tropical beach) so no two neighbours feel alike. It ends on the brightest, most saturated beach as the 'best last' hold. There is no explicit comment CTA on screen; the 'choose' title implies 'comment your pick'.
study.action_shots: There are no real action shots. The only movement is camera or ambient. The plane takeoff roll runs 0-3.87s as a handheld POV at normal speed, with motion staying low (0.7-2.7) as the runway slides by slowly. The Maldives drone glides forward from 4.87-5.77, with motion rising to about 9.5-13.6, the most active part of the video. Bali waves wash in from 3.87-4.87. Hawaii palm fronds and surf move gently from 9.33-11.03 (motion about 4-4.8). Every shot change lands on the beat, so the beat itself acts as the 'action'.
study.views: Every option is a big view held under 1s. Bali (3.87-4.87) is a locked sunset wide with a slight wave drift. The Maldives (4.87-5.77) is a drone aerial pushing forward over the reef: the most dynamic reveal. Paris (5.77-6.67) is a low-angle night shot looking up at the lit tower. Santorini (6.67-7.53) is an almost perfectly still dusk wide (motion 0.5 at 7.0s). Egypt (7.53-8.47) is a static frontal postcard. Rome (8.47-9.33) is an over-the-shoulder 'person facing the view' wide. Hawaii (9.33-11.03) is framed by foreground palms and held 1.69s, nearly double the others. That makes it where the biggest, most saturated view lands. There are no door, curtain or balcony reveals; the hard cut on the beat is the reveal mechanism.
study.how_place_is_shown: Almost entirely wide establishing shots. There are no mediums or detail shots (no food, drinks or rooms). Only one person appears: a solo woman seen from behind in Rome, an aspirational 'that could be you' frame. The intro is a first-person POV; the rest are filmed or stock-style shots. Light is varied on purpose: dawn (plane), pink sunset (Bali), harsh blue midday (Maldives, Egypt, Hawaii), night lights (Paris), dusk (Santorini). Capture mixes phone handheld (plane, Rome), drone (Maldives) and tripod/stock (Bali, Egypt, Santorini). Each destination is reduced to its single most iconic landmark, so it is identified in a fraction of a second.
study.info_and_value: None beyond the destination names. There are no prices, tips or booking info. The value is the poll itself: people share it to ask friends or partners which one, and comment their pick. 'Part 1' promises more options in a series.
study.pacing: There is one long setup shot, then a strict metronome. The intro is 3.87s (35% of the video). Then 6 options at 0.87-1.0s each (median 0.92s) run at about 6.35 cuts per 10s overall. The final hold is 1.69s. Cuts sit about 0.06-0.12s after each strong audio hit, which are spaced about 0.93s apart, so each destination occupies exactly one beat. Over the Hawaii hold the beat speeds up (hits at 9.77, 10.0, 10.21, 10.43) toward the loop point. The whole thing is 11.03s: short enough to rewatch several times to decide.
study.speed: None. Everything plays at normal speed. Low motion values are from naturally still footage, not slow motion.
study.on_screen_text: Intro (0-3.87s): 'Choose Your Vacation' in a white classic serif, title case, with a thin black outline/shadow, centered at about 37% height. Under it sits 'part 1' in small pink-red italic script with a white outline. Both are on screen the whole intro, 3 words plus 2. Options (3.87-11.03s): one label per shot in a white bold monospace/typewriter-style font with a black stroke, upper-middle third. The words are 'Bali', 'The Maldives', 'Paris', 'Santorini', 'Egypt', 'Rome' and 'Hawaii'. Each appears on the cut and disappears on the next cut, with no animation. There are no emoji.
study.audio: A music track only, with no voiceover and no audible natural sound. Over the intro the hits come every 0.3-0.4s (0.56-3.01), a ticking build under the takeoff. A strong hit at 3.78 drops into the first destination (cut at 3.87). After that the hits arrive about every 0.93s (4.68, 5.61, 6.55, 7.47, 8.4, 9.32), and each cut lands right on one. The end has a rapid run of hits (9.77-10.43) under the final Hawaii hold.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only, all 7 on the beat. The intro-to-Bali cut at 3.87 is the big contrast cut: from a muted grey runway to a saturated pink sunset.
study.effects: Color is pushed on the destination clips. Bali has strong pink/magenta saturation, the Maldives and Hawaii get a turquoise/blue-water boost, and Hawaii's sky and sand are noticeably oversaturated. The plane intro is left natural and muted, which makes the first destination pop. There are no zooms, shakes, light leaks, freeze frames or graphics beyond the text.
study.quality: 576x1024 at about 45fps and 1383 kbps h264: low-resolution and soft, with visible compression in the Bali sky and waves. The sources are mixed (phone, drone, stock), so sharpness varies shot to shot. It still reads as a dream reel because each frame is well composed, brightly exposed and color-boosted. The dreaminess comes from postcard subject choice and saturation, not technical quality.
study.ending: It ends on the Hawaii palm-framed beach, held 1.69s with no CTA card, and cuts off at 11.03s. The cut back to the plane-window intro makes a natural loop ('choose your vacation' again). The short length and lack of an end card encourage rewatches. The implied CTA is 'comment your pick / tag who you'd take', plus 'part 1' promising a part 2.
study.why_viral: 1) A participatory poll with zero effort: the viewer instantly picks a favourite, which drives comments and debates in the replies. 2) The takeoff-window POV opener is a universal wanderlust trigger, and its muted look makes the saturated destinations hit harder. 3) Seven iconic, instantly identifiable landmarks in about 7s, each landing on the beat, feel satisfying and are rewatched to decide. 4) 'Part 1' builds a series that pulls follows, and the share-to-a-friend 'which one?' use case spreads it.
lessons: Open with a 3-4s 'journey starting' shot (plane window, airport, car on a coastal road) under a one-line title question; keep it muted so the first destination pops.
For a pick-one video, give each option exactly one beat (about 0.9-1.0s) and one shot; 6-8 options keeps the total near 10-12s.
Place every cut on or within about 0.1s after a strong music hit; space options to the track's beat interval rather than a fixed duration.
Label options with the place name only, 1-2 words, in bold white with a black stroke in the upper-middle third, so the bottom UI never covers it and the label is read in under 0.5s.
Pick the single most iconic, instantly recognisable frame per destination, and alternate mood and time of day (sunset, aerial, night lights, dusk, midday) so neighbouring options never look alike.
Hold the last option about 1.7x longer than the rest (here 1.69s vs about 0.9s) and make it the brightest, most saturated view.
Boost saturation and blue-water tones on the destination clips, but leave the intro natural for contrast.
Include at least one shot with a person facing the view from behind, so the viewer imagines themselves there.
Add a 'part 1' tag to turn a one-off into a series that earns follows, and end without an end card so it loops.

study.format: 'Choose your vacation' pick-one montage (part 2 of a series). It opens with a 4s airplane-window takeoff, then runs seven destination clips of roughly 1 beat each, every one labelled only with the place name. There is no voiceover or ranking; the viewer picks by commenting.
study.place: Seven international destinations, each shown with its single most iconic image. Cancun (turquoise beach aerial), London (Big Ben street level), Florence (Duomo and Giotto's bell tower drone at dusk), Costa Rica (empty Pacific beach drone), Thailand (night sky lantern festival), Alaska (glacier-fed fjord drone), Istanbul (Galata Tower drone). The mix covers beach, city, culture, festival, nature and history, so every type of traveler sees their vibe.
study.audience: General wanderlust and bucket-list viewers, and couples or friends planning a trip. It asks people to comment their pick, tag the person they'd go with, and follow for the next part. It reads as a travel-aggregator or creator page built from stock or compiled drone footage, not a personal trip.
study.hook: Frame 1 is a POV out of a plane window over the wing during takeoff, with a moody cloudy sky and the ground tilting away. 'CHOOSE YOUR VACATION' sits centered in bold white caps with 'part 2' in pink script below. The music hits at 0.04s and a sung 'You' lands at 1.17s. It stops the scroll because the takeoff feeling triggers trip anticipation, and the text promises an instant, low-effort game.

beats.what: Plane-wing POV during takeoff/climb, 4.0s, with title 'CHOOSE YOUR VACATION / part 2'. Water and islands appear below as the plane banks.
Sung lyric 'You' lands while the question text holds; the music builds over the takeoff.
Cancun: drone over turquoise shallows and a white rocky beach with swimmers, slow drift, 0.93s.
London: wide-angle street-level shot of Big Ben under blue sky with crowds, 0.87s.
Florence: drone orbiting the Duomo and bell tower in soft dusk light, 1.0s.
Costa Rica: near-static drone of an empty beach, deep blue water and white surf, about 0.8s.
Thailand: handheld night shot of hundreds of lit sky lanterns rising over a crowd, about 1.2s.
Alaska: drone rising and panning over a turquoise fjord to snowy peaks and a glacier, 0.9s.
Istanbul: drone orbit of Galata Tower with people on the balcony, held 1.96s to the end.

study.choice_format: Question: 'CHOOSE YOUR VACATION' (part 2). Seven options: Cancun, London, Florence, Costa Rica, Thailand, Alaska, Istanbul. They are labelled by name only, with no numbers or emoji, in white bold sans with a thin black outline and shadow, left of center at roughly mid-height (about 50% down). The label stays in the same spot for every option and appears on the first frame of each clip. Each option gets one shot of about 0.73-1.27s, except the last at 1.96s. Options are separated by hard cuts on the song's beat, about every 0.93s (audio hits at 4.0, 4.91, 5.84, 6.77, 7.69, 8.63, 9.55). The order alternates beach/city/culture/nature for contrast and is not ranked. Istanbul sits last and gets the longest hold. The answer is invited implicitly through the title, so viewers comment their pick and the 'part 2' label pulls them to other parts.
study.action_shots: Few true action shots. The takeoff 0-4.0s is a POV out the window, real-time, with the wing tilting as the plane climbs and banks (motion 12-17). Thailand (about 7.6-8.8s) is handheld with lanterns rising and crowd movement, the highest motion in the video (41.7-48 at 8.0-8.5s), and it lands right on the beat hits. London has pedestrians walking through frame. All play at normal speed.
study.views: Almost every option is a big view. Cancun is an aerial beach with a slow forward drift for 0.93s. Florence is an aerial at dusk with a slow orbit/pan right for 1.0s. Costa Rica is an aerial beach, nearly static (motion 1.9 at 7.0s). Alaska is an aerial fjord with a rising pan that reveals the glacier within 0.9s. Istanbul is an aerial orbit around Galata Tower, slowly pushing closer, held 1.96s. Reveals are cuts plus slow drone movement, with no door or curtain reveals. The plane-wing climb works as a mini pull-back reveal of the coastline in the first 4s. The longest view lands last (Istanbul).
study.how_place_is_shown: Mostly wide drone shots, plus one street-level ultra-wide (London) and one handheld night crowd shot (Thailand). No creator on camera; people appear only as small figures (swimmers, crowds, tower visitors). Light varies by clip: overcast for the plane, bright midday blue for Cancun, London and Costa Rica, golden dusk for Florence, night lantern glow for Thailand, soft overcast for Alaska and Istanbul. No food, drink or amenity details. Each place is reduced to one instantly recognizable postcard image so the decision takes under a second.
study.info_and_value: Only destination names, as text. No prices, tips or booking info. The value is the game itself: people comment their choice, tag a travel partner, and save it as a bucket-list mood board.
study.pacing: One long 4.0s intro, then seven fast beat-locked cuts. Shot lengths are 4.0, 0.93, 0.87, 1.0, 0.73, 1.27, 0.9 and 1.96s, with a median of 0.97s and 6 cuts per 10s. Cuts at 4.0, 4.93, 5.8, 6.8 and 8.8/9.7 sit within about 0.1s of the audio hits at 4.0, 4.91, 5.84, 6.77, 8.63 and 9.55. The slow intro builds anticipation, then the montage clips along at about one destination per beat. The last shot is held about twice as long to resolve.
study.speed: none; all clips appear to play at normal speed (drone footage is naturally smooth/slow-moving)
study.on_screen_text: The title 'CHOOSE YOUR VACATION' is in white bold sans-serif uppercase with a black outline/shadow, centered at about 37% height, with 'part 2' below in pink/magenta italic script with a white outline. Both are on screen 0-4.0s, 3 words plus 2. Destination labels (Cancun, London, Florence, Costa Rica, Thailand, Alaska, Istanbul) are in white bold sans with a thin black outline, title case, left of center at about 50% height. They are 1-2 words each, appear on every cut and stay for the whole clip. No emoji.
study.audio: A trending music track with no voiceover. The only transcribed word is a sung 'You' at 1.17s. A dense run of hits in the first 3.2s (0.04-3.24) drives the takeoff intro. After that, regular beats about 0.93s apart (4.0, 4.91, 5.84, 6.77, 7.69, 8.63, 9.55) and every destination cut lands on one. A cluster of hits at 9.99-10.65 plays under the final Istanbul hold. No natural sound is audible.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only, every one on a music beat.
study.effects: Light color enhancement on the stock drone clips, with saturated turquoise in Cancun and Alaska and deep blue in Costa Rica. The plane shot is left cool and desaturated, which makes the bright destinations pop on the cut at 4.0s. No zooms, graphics or maps beyond the text.
study.quality: 576x1024, 30fps, about 1738 kbps h264, so modest compression. The drone clips are stable and look cinematic (smooth gimbal moves, clean horizons). London is a sharp action-cam ultra-wide, while Thailand is grainier phone night footage. Bright skies are well exposed and the water reads vividly. The dream-trip feel comes from the stability and color of the aerials, not from resolution.
study.ending: Ends on the Istanbul Galata Tower drone orbit, held 1.96s, with no CTA text. The music keeps hitting (9.99-10.65) and it cuts at 11.66s. The short length and abrupt end make it loop straight back to the takeoff, encouraging rewatches to 'decide'.
study.why_viral: The 'choose your vacation' game turns passive viewing into a decision, which drives comments and tags. The takeoff POV hook sparks instant trip-anticipation. Seven iconic postcard images in about 7.7s, each cut on the beat, give fast and satisfying rhythm and high rewatch and loop rates at 11.7s. The 'part 2' series label signals there's more and drives profile visits and follows.
lessons: Open on a 3-4s 'journey starting' shot (plane window, boarding, car on road) with the question text centered. Then switch to fast cuts, so the slow-to-fast contrast hits on the first beat.
Give each option exactly one shot of about 0.9s (one beat at about 128 BPM) and cut every option on a music hit. Keep variance within ±0.3s.
Pick the single most iconic image per destination (landmark or signature color) so it's recognizable in under 1s. Avoid generic shots.
Label options with the place name only, 1-2 words, white bold sans with a black outline, in the exact same screen position (about 50% height, left of center) for every clip.
Alternate vibes (beach, city, culture, beach, festival, nature, history) so neighbouring options contrast and every viewer finds a pick.
Hold the final option about 2x longer (about 2s) to resolve the sequence, and keep total length under 12s to encourage loops.
Grade the intro cooler or duller than the destination clips so the first destination cut feels like a color 'arrival'.
Label it 'part N' to build a series and give viewers a reason to follow and search your profile.

study.format: Destination/cruise-ship montage that builds to an event payoff: a 'where I rang in the New Year' recap. Nine fast phone clips (about 1.9 s each) tour the ship's best features: sailaway, pool deck, splash zone, roller coaster, neon interior, ice-cream bar, ocean sunset and champagne. Then a long 7.8 s live clip of the on-deck New Year countdown acts as the climax. The only framing is one title card at the start; the countdown on the ship's giant screen finishes the story with no extra editing.
study.place: Carnival Celebration, Carnival's newest Excel-class ship (2022–23), sailing out of Miami on a New Year's Eve Caribbean cruise. The open shot shows the ship docked at a port with a chairlift over the water. What makes it special: a roller coaster at sea (BOLT), a WaterWorks splash park with a tipping bucket, a neon 'Chill & Tropical' interior, an ice-cream lounge styled as a vintage bus, champagne for everyone, and a huge LED screen on the main deck counting down to 2023 with thousands of glow sticks.
study.audience: Cruise fans, families with kids (splash park, ice cream), and anyone planning New Year's Eve travel. It makes them want to save it for next NYE, tag a partner or family ('we're doing this next year'), and look up the sailing. It reads as a real traveler or creator sharing their trip, not the cruise line. It's shaky handheld phone footage, with strangers and kids in frame and a security guard in shot.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0.0 s): the huge white-and-red Carnival Celebration fills the right half of the frame, seen from a moving chairlift over blue water, with empty chairs passing in front. Centered over the ship is a two-tier title: small white sans-serif 'Entering 2023 on' above a big pink neon-glow script/display 'Carnival Celebration'. A spoken audio clip starts on frame 0: 'Thank you for the help' (0.00–1.40 s). It stops the scroll because the title instantly sets up a promise ('how do you enter 2023 on a cruise ship?'). A giant ship seen from a moving chairlift is an unusual angle, and the movement of the lift (motion about 20–26) keeps the frame alive.

beats.what: Ship docked, filmed from a chairlift over the water; title 'Entering 2023 on Carnival Celebration' in pink neon; voice says 'Thank you for the help'.
Sailaway at sunset from the stern: wake, white railing, Miami skyline in orange-gold light, another ship docked as the camera pans.
Pool deck seen from an upper balcony past a security guard: blue pool, crowded loungers, the ship's red-and-white funnel; the camera pans right.
WaterWorks splash park: yellow-and-blue slides, kids waiting under the giant bucket.
The giant bucket tips and a wall of water crashes onto the kids (motion jumps from 9 to 45 between 6.5 and 8.0 s).
BOLT roller coaster on the top deck: guests film it with their phones as the car speeds along the track over the ocean; the camera tilts up to follow.
Quick 0.93 s look at the purple neon 'Chill & Tropical' sign with disco-ball ceiling decor.
Two girls pull soft-serve from a green military-bus-styled ice-cream machine in the Heroes Tribute Lounge; one walks off licking her cone.
Open-ocean sunset: golden horizon, dark rippling water, no railing in frame.
Trays of filled champagne flutes, staff popping and pouring bottles for midnight.
Main deck at night: giant LED screen shows '4' above a crowd waving glow sticks.
The screen reads 'Happy New Year 2023' and the crowd erupts.
The camera swings off the screen to packed upper decks, purple stage lights and people dancing on lit stairs; it ends mid-motion.

study.action_shots: 1) WaterWorks bucket dump, inside shot 5.23–8.0 s (2.77 s). Static-ish medium-wide filmed at kid height. The shot deliberately starts on the wait: motion drops to 9.0 at 6.5 s while the bucket fills. The tip at about 6.9 s and the splash at 7.0–8.0 s push motion to 32–46, and the cut lands at 8.0 just after the water hits, so the shot ends on the peak. Real speed. 2) BOLT roller coaster, 8.0–11.2 s (3.2 s). Handheld from the deck, tilting up to follow the car over the onlookers' heads and then under the track against blue sky. Motion is 40–58, the highest sustained section. Real speed. 3) Ice-cream pull, 12.13–14.4 s: small kid action, filmed handheld and walking. 4) Champagne pouring, 15.73–16.93 s. 5) Crowd waving glow sticks, 16.93–23 s. Locked on the screen (motion 4–8), so all the movement comes from arms and the numbers changing. 6) Final swing across the dancing decks, 23–24.7 s (motion up to 66.5). None of the cuts are synced to beats; the action is placed inside shots so each shot ends at its own peak.
study.views: Sailaway sunset over Miami at 1.87–3.7 s (1.83 s): a slow pan from the stern across the skyline in golden-hour orange, with the wake in the foreground. Pool deck seen from above at 3.7–5.23 s: a pan across bright blue water and the funnel. Roller coaster against deep blue sky with the ocean behind, 8.0–11.2 s. Open-ocean sunset at 14.4–15.73 s (1.33 s), a gentle handheld drift with no reveal move, used as the day-to-night bridge.
