The biggest 'view' is not scenery but the night deck with the giant LED countdown. It is held longest (7.79 s, 16.93–24.73) and placed last. The camera holds still on the screen for about 5 s and only pulls away after '2023' appears, which reveals the full multi-deck crowd.
study.how_place_is_shown: All handheld phone footage, mostly filmed from a guest's point of view (standing on deck, on the chairlift, at the railing), never staged. No creator on camera. The mix is mostly wides and medium-wides (ship, skyline, pool deck, splash park, coaster, crowd), with a few close-ish details (neon sign, ice-cream machine, champagne flutes). Strangers fill the frame: sunbathers, kids, coaster spectators, the security guard, staff pouring champagne. That makes the ship feel lively and real. The light follows a day-to-night arc: bright midday blues (port, pool, splash park, coaster) → golden-hour sunsets (Miami, open ocean) → warm indoor light (ice cream, champagne) → purple/pink night lights and glow sticks. The details are chosen as moments everyone recognizes from a cruise (free-flowing soft serve, champagne trays) and as signs of New Year's Eve (champagne, glow sticks).
study.info_and_value: Minimal. The title names the ship ('Carnival Celebration') and the occasion ('Entering 2023'). Everything else is shown, not told: features visible on screen include the BOLT coaster, the WaterWorks bucket, the Chill & Tropical sign, the Heroes Tribute Lounge sign and the free soft serve. No prices, dates or booking info. People save and share it because it signals 'this ship does NYE big' and shows its features.
study.pacing: Shots 1–9 run 1.87, 1.83, 1.53, 2.77, 3.2, 0.93, 2.27, 1.33, 1.2 s, about 1.9 s on average over the first 16.9 s (median 1.85 s overall). Then one 7.79 s held shot fills the last 31% of the video. Action shots get a bit more time (2.77 s for the bucket, 3.2 s for the coaster) so the payoff can land inside the shot. The 0.93 s neon sign is a pure accent. Cuts don't line up tightly with the audio hits (e.g. cut 3.7 vs hit 3.86; cut 8.0 vs hit 8.34). The rhythm comes from content rather than music. In the countdown shot the audio hits do follow the numbers (17.2, 18.87/19.11, 19.82, 20.54, 21.37, then a burst at 21.7–24.6). Overall it feels quick and breezy through the day, then slows into a real-time payoff.
study.speed: none. Everything plays at normal speed. Low motion around 6.5 s (9.0) is the real pause before the bucket tips, and 17–21.5 s (4–8) is a steadily held camera on the countdown screen, not slow motion.
study.on_screen_text: One title card, 0.0–1.87 s, gone at the first cut. Line 1 'Entering 2023 on' is a small white bold sans-serif in sentence case with a light shadow. Lines 2–3 'Carnival Celebration' are bigger, in a pink/magenta bubbly display font with a white inner stroke and pink neon glow. Text is centered horizontally, sitting just above the vertical middle over the ship's hull. 5 words in total, no emoji. The countdown numbers and 'Happy New Year 2023' are filmed on the ship's real LED screen, not overlaid.
study.audio: It opens with a spoken clip, 'Thank you for the help' (0.00–1.40 s), likely the intro of a trending sound or song. After that the track is music without transcribed words; only those 5 words are detected. Strong hits at 0.06–1.25 s mark the intro. Hits then fall roughly every 1–1.5 s through the montage (2.91, 3.86, 4.82, 5.77, 6.59, 8.34). There are few hits from 8.3 to 17 s, and then dense hits from 17.2 to 24.6 s, which match the countdown and the crowd roar/celebration. The final section's sound is either the live crowd or a drop timed to it. Either way the audio peaks with the '0 → 2023' moment.
study.transitions: hard cuts only. Every cut is a straight cut between unrelated locations (chairlift → stern sunset, pool → splash park, splash → coaster, coaster → neon interior, sign → sign at 12.13 (a jump cut within the same Chill & Tropical spot), ice cream → ocean, ocean → champagne, champagne → countdown).
study.effects: none added beyond the neon glow on the title text. No visible color grade: colors are stock phone (saturated blue sky and pool, warm sunsets, purple night lighting). No zooms, shakes, freeze frames or graphics added in the edit.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30 fps, 2.3 Mbps h264, so it's soft and compressed. All handheld phone footage with visible shake in the coaster and final crowd swing. The night shots are noisy and smeared. Skies and water are well exposed in daylight, and the golden-hour clips look good on their own. It looks like a real phone snapshot rather than a dream-trip production, and that is part of the appeal: authentic 'I was there' footage. The strong colors of the location (blue water, yellow slides, purple neon) carry it despite the low resolution.
study.ending: Ends on the climax itself: the countdown hits 0 at 21.4 s, 'Happy New Year 2023' appears at 22.6 s, and the camera swings to the cheering upper decks. It cuts abruptly at 24.73 s, about 2.1 s after the 2023 reveal, while the camera is still moving (motion 66.5). There's no CTA and no outro. The abrupt high-energy end invites a rewatch but isn't a seamless loop back to the daytime ship.
study.why_viral: 1) A clear promise paid off: 'Entering 2023 on…' sets up the countdown, and the video delivers it in real time on a giant screen with thousands of glow sticks. That is a shared, emotional moment everyone recognizes. 2) Fast tour of the wow amenities (roller coaster at sea, splash bucket, neon bars, free ice cream, champagne) at about 1.9 s each, which makes the ship look like a floating resort and theme park. 3) A day-to-sunset-to-night arc that feels like living the whole trip in 25 s. 4) Easy to tag a friend or partner ('NYE 2024 on a cruise?'), it's timely around New Year, and the brand name in the title makes it searchable.
lessons: Put the destination plus the occasion in a 2-tier title on the first frame ('Entering 2023 on' + ship name in a bold brand-colored glow font), centered over the hero subject, and remove it at the first cut (~1.9 s).
Open on the hero subject (the ship, resort or landmark) from an unusual moving angle (chairlift, boat, balcony walk) so the first 2 s have motion of ~20+ without needing effects.
Run the amenity montage at 1.2–2.0 s per shot, but give action shots 2.7–3.2 s and cut them right after the peak (splash lands, coaster passes). Never cut before the payoff inside a clip.
For action with a wait (a dumping bucket, a cliff jump), keep ~1 s of the calm wait before the release. The drop from still (motion ~9) to splash (~45) is what makes it hit.
Order clips as a light arc: bright midday blues → golden-hour sunset → warm indoor → night lights. Use a 1.3 s sunset shot as the bridge between day and night.

Save the single biggest moment for last and hold it 6–8 s, about 30% of the runtime. Let a countdown, fireworks or reveal play in real time with the camera steady, and only move the camera after the payoff.
Use 'universal' small details (free soft serve, champagne trays, a neon sign) as 0.9–2.3 s accents between the big shots. They add up to 'everything is included and fun'.
End within ~2 s of the climax while the energy is still rising. An abrupt cut on peak motion beats a fade-out and encourages rewatches.

study.format: Multiple choice / 'Choose Your Cruise Port' video. A title card over a docked cruise ship sets the question, then three ports play back to back. Each port is a mini montage of 4-5 phone clips under one persistent name + flag label. There are no numbers and no narration, and the viewer is implicitly asked to pick one in the comments.
study.place: Western Caribbean cruise ports seen from a Carnival cruise (Carnival Horizon's bow in the hook, Carnival ships docked in Cozumel). The three ports are Ocho Rios, Jamaica; Cozumel, Mexico; and the Cayman Islands. What makes it look special is the colour of the water in every option: a jungle waterfall over an emerald-green swimming hole in Ocho Rios, glass-clear pier water and snorkeling with fish in Cozumel, and turquoise sea plus a white-sand beach in Cayman. Cultural beats (Mayan-costumed dancers, carved masks, stone ruins, a distance signpost, black jagged limestone) make each port feel distinct.
study.audience: Cruisers and people planning a Western Caribbean itinerary, especially Carnival passengers. It is built to make them comment their pick, tag a cruise buddy ('which one are we doing?') and save it as a port preview. It reads as a cruise-loving creator or travel agent showing their own port-day footage, not the cruise line: it's handheld, with no logos or promo claims.
study.hook: Frame 1 is a low, upward angle on the huge blue hull of Carnival Horizon at the pier, with another Carnival ship behind and a big cloudy sky. Centred text reads 'Choose Your' (small, white, black stroke) over 'Cruise Port' (huge bold magenta with a thick white outline). A short vocal from the track starts at 0.22s; the transcription is garbled, so it is music, not narration. It stops the scroll because the instant 'choose your' question invites a decision before the viewer knows the options. The giant ship fills the frame, so cruisers self-identify in under a second, and the camera drifts along the hull so the frame is never static.

beats.what: Low angle on Carnival Horizon's bow at the dock with 'Choose Your Cruise Port' title; camera moves along the hull toward crew at the mooring line.
Option 1 label 'Ocho Rios, Jamaica' + Jamaican flag appears over the view from the ship's balcony of the green hills and port.
Continued balcony pan across the deep-blue harbour, the hillside town and the pier, with the ship's railing in the corner, into a sun-flared wide.
Waterfall and emerald pool seen through a red wooden railing.
From the top of the falls, the camera tilts down the rushing water and pans to reveal the glowing green swimming hole below; the cut lands on an audio hit (4.24).

POV over the edge of a stone platform toward the bright green water, then the camera goes down into the water until the frame is solid green (~7.6-8.0s). This works as a natural colour wipe out of Jamaica.
Option 2 label 'Cozumel, Mexico' + Mexican flag over clear shallow water with docked Carnival ships on the pier.
Underwater snorkel footage with hands reaching in and a swarm of striped sergeant-major fish.
Mayan-costumed dancers performing in a thatched-roof plaza.
Fast handheld sweep over a wall of colourful carved wooden masks in a shop (motion peaks at 100).
Stone Mayan ruins and steps under blue sky.
Option 3 label 'The Cayman Islands' + Cayman flag over turquoise water seen from a boat/pier, with sailboats and the shoreline.
Signpost with distances (London, Dallas 1,336, Toronto 1,683, 'Welcome To The Cayman Islands'), then a pan off the sign to the turquoise sea and rocky shore.
Field of black jagged limestone spires reflected in still water, under big clouds.
White-sand beach with swimmers in calm turquoise water; the camera sweeps left along the beach with loungers. The video ends here.

study.choice_format:
Question: 'Choose Your Cruise Port', shown only in the hook (~0-1.3s). There are 3 options, each labelled with the port name plus that country's flag emoji and no numbers or letters. The label is bold rounded sans in the upper third, coloured to match the flag:
- Ocho Rios: yellow fill with green outline.
- Cozumel: red fill with white outline.
- Cayman: blue fill with red outline.
The flag emoji sits centred just below the label. Time on screen per option:
- Ocho Rios: ~1.3-8.0s, ~6.7s, 4-5 shots.
- Cozumel: ~8.0-14.63s, ~6.6s, 5 shots.
- Cayman Islands: 14.63-23.67s, ~9.0s, 4 shots with longer holds.
Options are separated by a hard cut plus a label swap. Jamaica exits through an all-green underwater frame that acts as a colour wipe. The last option gets the most time and ends on the classic white-sand beach. Viewers are asked to answer only implicitly through the 'Choose Your' framing, with no on-screen 'comment 1, 2 or 3'. Comments would naturally name the port.
study.action_shots: POV toward and down into the Ocho Rios swimming hole from the stone platform, ~6.17-8.0s (~1.8s), at normal speed. It ends fully in the green water, and the transition to Cozumel rides on it. Snorkeling underwater, 9.2-11.13s (1.93s): close, chaotic handheld/POV with hands and fish crossing the lens, normal speed; motion 40-57. Mayan dancers, 11.13-12.27s (1.13s): static medium-wide watching the dancers spin, normal speed. Mask-shop whip, 12.27-13.4s: very fast handheld sweep, motion 100 at 12.5-13.0s, used as an energy spike rather than a real action. Beach walk/sweep, 21.07-23.67s: gentle pan with swimmers in frame. None is slowed, and cuts line up only loosely with the beat (4.23 lands on the hit at 4.24; 12.27 is close to 12.09; 16.87 is close to 17.06).
study.views: Ocho Rios harbour from the ship balcony, ~1.3-3.27s (~2s): slow pan across the hills and pier, ending in a sun-flared wide. Waterfall through the railing, 3.27-4.23s. Top-of-falls tilt/pan that reveals the emerald pool, 4.23-6.17s (1.93s). This is the most striking colour reveal, done by tilting from rushing water to the glowing pool. Cozumel pier with clear shallow water and Carnival ships, 8.0-9.2s (~1.2s): slight pan. Mayan ruins, 13.4-14.63s, with a small push. Cayman turquoise sea from the boat, 14.63-16.87s (2.23s): held, with a slow drift. Signpost-to-sea pan, 16.87-19.33s (2.47s): the reveal is the pan off the sign onto open sea and clouds, the longest-held shot. Black limestone field, 19.33-21.07s (1.73s): slow pan. White-sand beach, 21.07-23.67s (2.6s): the final and longest shot, a sweep along the beach. All views are handheld phone footage with no drone. The biggest blue-water moments are concentrated in the final Cayman option, so the video ends at peak paradise.
study.how_place_is_shown: Mostly wides and medium-wides, with a few details (the mask wall, the signpost). People appear only incidentally: crew at the mooring, snorkelers' hands and legs, dancers, beachgoers. The creator is never on camera and there are no couples posing, so it plays as the viewer's own POV. Everything is shot in bright midday sun: blue skies, puffy clouds and saturated turquoise/emerald water carry the entire video. Shots are handheld with phone stabilisation, and there is no drone or gimbal-grade movement. Details are chosen for 'what makes this port different': masks and dancers for culture, the distance signpost as a fun Instagram spot, ruins for history, fish for an excursion. There is no food, drinks or resort amenities.
study.info_and_value: Light. The only facts are the three port names with flags, plus what each port offers shown visually: waterfalls/swimming hole in Ocho Rios; snorkeling, Mayan culture, a market and ruins in Cozumel; clear water, a signpost, limestone formations and a beach in Cayman. The signpost incidentally shows distances (Dallas 1,336, Toronto 1,683). There are no prices, excursion names, tips or booking info. It gets saved and shared as a 'which port should we do' conversation starter and a quick visual preview of a Western Caribbean itinerary.
study.pacing: 14 detected shots in 23.67s (5.49 cuts per 10s); median shot 1.67s, shortest 0.97s (3.27-4.23 waterfall through the railing), longest 2.6s (final beach). The middle Cozumel section is fastest at 1.13-1.93s per shot, with motion peaking at 100 at 12.5-13.0s. The Cayman section slows to 2.23, 2.47, 1.73 and 2.6s, letting the final option breathe. Cuts mostly follow content rather than the beat, with a few landing near hits (4.23≈4.24, 12.27≈12.09, 16.87≈17.06). Overall the pace is brisk but not frantic, roughly 2 seconds per look.
study.speed: none — all clips appear to play at normal speed. The motion spike at 12.5-13.5s is a fast handheld pan in the mask shop, not a speed ramp.
study.on_screen_text:
Hook (~0-1.3s): 'Choose Your' in small bold white sans with a black stroke, above 'Cruise Port' on two lines in very large heavy magenta rounded sans with a thick white outline and a slight shadow, centred in the frame (~33-55% height). Port labels, which replace each other at each option change and stay on screen for the whole option, all in heavy rounded sans with a contrasting outline, placed upper third (~27% height) with the flag emoji centred below at ~33%:
- 'Ocho Rios, Jamaica': yellow with green stroke, Jamaican flag, ~1.3-8.0s.
- 'Cozumel, Mexico': red with white stroke, Mexican flag, ~8.0-14.63s.
- 'The Cayman Islands': blue with red stroke, Cayman flag, 14.63s-end.
Labels are 2-3 words each, colour-coded to the flag.
study.audio: A music track only, with no voiceover. A brief vocal at 0.22-0.92s is part of the song (the transcription is gibberish). Strong audio hits fall roughly every 0.4-1.6s (e.g. 2.16, 3.82, 4.24, 5.07, 7.13, 8.38, 9.63-10.86 in a dense run, 12.09, 13.75, 15.41, 17.06, 18.71, 19.97, 22.03-23.28). The dense run of hits at 9.6-10.9s coincides with the chaotic snorkel footage. Cut-to-beat sync is loose and only occasional. No natural sound (waves, falls) is audibly featured.
study.transitions: Hard cuts throughout. Exceptions: an undetected hard cut inside the first detected shot, from the ship hook to the Ocho Rios balcony view at ~1.2-1.5s; the Ocho Rios → Cozumel change uses the camera going into green water so the frame becomes a full green field (~7.6-8.0s) before cutting to Cozumel, which works as a natural colour wipe; and in-camera whip/pan energy in the mask shop at ~12.5-13.0s. There are no flashes, zooms or graphic transitions.
study.effects: Text-only graphics: outlined coloured titles and flag emojis. Colour appears to be the phone's natural vivid look, with possibly a mild saturation lift on the turquoise and emerald water. There are no zooms, glows, light leaks, freeze frames, maps or split screens.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, h264 ~3.3 Mbps. This is reduced resolution for a 9:16 upload, so fine detail (foliage, the mask wall) looks soft, and the fast mask pan smears. Stability is phone-handheld with OIS: acceptable on pans, shaky underwater. Exposure is midday: skies sometimes clip to white and there is sun flare at ~3.0s, but the water reads brilliantly blue and green, which is what sells it. It looks like a real traveler's phone camera roll rather than a commercial. The dream factor comes from the location colours, not the craft.
study.ending: Ends on the last option's biggest classic-paradise shot: a 2.6s sweep along a white-sand Cayman beach with swimmers in turquoise water under dramatic clouds. There is no answer, no ranking reveal, no explicit CTA and no outro card. It cuts mid-pan at 23.67s, which leaves the question open for comments and helps it loop back into the 'Choose Your Cruise Port' title.
study.why_viral: 1) 'Choose your…' format: the viewer has to form an opinion, which drives comments (port names), tagging cruise companions and rewatches to compare. 2) Every option is a strong water-colour payoff (emerald falls, glass-clear pier water, turquoise Cayman), so all three look like a dream and the choice feels genuinely hard. 3) There is a clear niche signal in frame 1 (a giant Carnival ship), so cruisers instantly self-select, and the ports are the most common Western Caribbean stops, making it relevant to people already booked. 4) It is short (23.7s) with ~2s shots and no talking, so it is easy to watch to the end and loop.
lessons: Open on the most recognisable symbol of the trip type (the ship's hull, the resort pool, the castle) with a 2-4 word 'Choose Your ___' title, and get the title on screen by frame 1, with the option label appearing by ~1.3s.

Label each option with name + flag/emoji in the upper third, keep it on screen for the whole option, and colour-code the text to the place (flag colours) so viewers can tell options apart without numbers.

Give each option ~6-7s and 4-5 shots, mixing one arrival/establishing wide, one 'signature' reveal (waterfall, fish, signpost), one people/culture moment and one detail; let the final option run longer (~9s) with 2.2-2.6s holds.
Put the most bankable view (white-sand beach, turquoise water) as the very last shot and end mid-motion with no CTA card, so the open question carries into comments and the loop.
Use an in-camera colour field as a transition: a camera going into water, a whip, or a pan into sky turning the frame one solid colour gives a clean seam between options without effects.
Reveal colour by tilting or panning: start on the waterfall, rocks or sign and move to the glowing water. A reveal of 1.9-2.5s beats a static wide of the same spot.
Keep shots around 1-2.5s (median ~1.7s), and use one very fast handheld sweep (~1s) mid-video to spike energy before slowing down for the finale.
Cut on a music hit when a shot change coincides with one (e.g. landing a reveal exactly on the beat, as at 4.23s); with no voiceover, music plus title text is enough for a choice video under 25s.

study.format: Narrated resort walkthrough / 'Let's stay at…' feature tour. It is built as a checklist of amenities, one sentence per amenity. Each sentence is spoken by a text-to-speech style voice (it mispronounces 'Cancun' as 'Cancane') and shown as a full-sentence text block. Each sentence gets 1–3 handheld phone clips. Order: pools → floating loungers → kids splash park → beach palapas → sunset → cabanas/hammocks → dining/bars → shops/kids club → ocean walkway → sign-off on the pool.
study.place: Azul Beach Resort Riviera Cancun, an all-inclusive family beach resort on Mexico's Riviera Maya. What makes it look special: winding turquoise pools under coconut palms with red umbrellas, in-pool loungers, a kids splash pad, thatched palapa beach beds on white sand, palm-silhouette sunsets over the Caribbean, white curtained daybeds, macramé hammocks, a swim-up/poolside bar under a thatched roof and an 'Azulitos' kids playhouse.
study.audience: Parents planning an all-inclusive family beach vacation. The pitch is 'pools without crowds', 'water park for the kiddos', shops next to the kids' play areas. It reads as a family traveler/creator sharing a stay, with a soft review tone. Its structure and positivity also suit a travel agent repost. It makes people save for later, send it to a partner ('let's do this'), and search the resort name. There is no explicit comment or booking ask.
study.hook: Frame 1 is a bright, saturated handheld shot of a turquoise pool lined with palms, red umbrellas and loungers under blue sky. Text sits mid-upper screen: a small white 'Let's stay at the' above a big red serif 'Azul Beach Resort Riviera Cancun' with white outline. The voice starts on word one at 0.00s: 'Let's stay at the Azul Beach Resort…'. The camera keeps moving (motion 40–50) across several pool angles inside 3.6s. It stops the scroll through instant blue-water payoff plus a named, searchable destination and an invitation framing ('let's stay'), so the viewer feels they're coming along.

beats.what: Moving pan across palm-lined turquoise pool, red/white title card 'Let's stay at the Azul Beach Resort Riviera Cancun', VO names resort
Girl in goggles at pool edge at dusk in front of a thatched-roof building jumps in; splash visible ~5.2s. Text: 'There were plenty of pool areas for the family without any large crowds'
Follow shot of the girl swimming across the near-empty pool at dusk, palms behind, proving 'no crowds'
Walking pan over in-pool loungers ('floating chairs') across a huge calm blue pool, 3.43s
Kids splash park: toddler with dad, bucket-dump sprayers, blue splash pad, older girl walking through. 'They even had a waterpark for the kiddos to play!'

study.how_place_is_shown: Mostly wides and medium-wides, with a few details: rolled towels on the daybed, stacked donut floats, bar bottles. People appear sparingly: the creator's kids (jumping, swimming, walking into the restaurant), a toddler and dad at the splash pad, the creator's shadow. Light mix: harsh midday blue sky for pools and the splash pad, dusk for the pool-jump clips, golden hour sunset, and one night restaurant scene with lens flare. study.info_and_value: Facts given: the resort's full name (spoken and shown at the start and in the sign-off), plenty of pool areas without large crowds, in-pool floating loungers, a kids water park, beach access, sunset views, private huts/cabanas and hammocks, multiple dining and drink options (the SIENA restaurant sign is visible), shops placed next to the children's play areas, and the Azulitos kids playhouse (sign visible). Save/share value comes from a family-focused amenity checklist plus a searchable name.
study.pacing: 17 shots in 45.7s, 3.5 cuts per 10s. Median shot 2.43s, shortest 1.03s (shop window, 33.87), longest 4.23s (final pool). Held shots are the hook pan 3.6s, beach walk 4.17s, ocean walkway 3.77s and closer 4.23s. Faster runs are 1.77s (sunset), 1.73s and 1.03s (shops). Cuts follow the voiceover sentence boundaries: 3.6 after the line ending at 3.24, 7.77 before 'Pools' at 7.84, 11.2 before 'They' at 11.04, 14.5 before 'Of course' at 14.26, 18.67 on 'The sunset' at 18.60, 22.87 on 'The resort' at 22.86, 32.13 on 'Don't' at 32.08, 41.43 near 'We can't' at 41.20. Each sentence runs ~3–5s and the camera is always moving (median motion 33), so it feels steady and calm rather than hype.

study.on_screen_text: Hook title (0–3.6s): 'Let's stay at the' in small white sans with shadow, then 'Azul Beach Resort / Riviera Cancun' in large red serif with thick white outline, centered in the upper-middle third. After that, one full-sentence block per beat in TikTok's native white sans with black stroke, centered at roughly 35–45% of frame height, 2–3 lines, 8–14 words at once. Each block appears on the cut that starts its sentence and stays until the next sentence. The blocks are: 'There were plenty of pool areas for the family without any large crowds', 'Pools also had floating chairs to relax in the water', 'They even had a waterpark for the kiddos to play!', 'Of course there was also access to the beautiful beaches as well!', 'The sunset views all around the resort were nothing short of GORGEOUS! 😍' (placed lower, ~60%, to clear the sun), 'The resort had even more areas to relax with private huts and hammocks', 'There were plenty of unique dining and drink experiences to choose from', 'Don't forget about the shops conveniently placed right next to the children's play areas! 👀', 'We couldn't get enough of the breathtaking views at every turn! 😍', 'We can't wait to visit the Azul Beach Resort again soon! 🤩'. Emphasis comes from all-caps 'GORGEOUS' and emoji on the emotional lines.
study.captions: No separate auto-captions. The overlay text is the script, and the TTS voice reads it nearly word-for-word, so the text works as captions. Each block is shown whole for the sentence's duration, with no word-by-word highlighting.
study.audio: TikTok-style text-to-speech voiceover from 0.00 to 44.72s, 127 words, almost no gaps. It reads the text (mispronounces 'Cancun' as 'Cancane'). A soft background music bed sits under it, with regular hits roughly every 1.6s (0.78, 2.68, 4.0, 5.6, 7.18…45.58), a steady mid-tempo pulse. Natural sound isn't prominent. Picture syncs to the voice: each new sentence brings a new location, and a few cuts coincide with music hits (5.67/5.6, 7.77/7.85, 32.13/32.21, 37.67/37.58). The splash at ~5.2s lands near the 5.6 hit.
study.transitions: hard cuts only. All 16 cuts are straight cuts between unrelated handheld clips, with no whips, zooms or wipes. Some are motion-to-motion (e.g. 5.67 continues the same pool and building from a similar angle, almost a match cut).
study.effects: none added beyond what the camera produced: no zooms, freeze frames, split screens or graphics. Colors look like a phone's punchy default/HDR, with saturated blue water and green palms. Natural lens flares appear in the hammock (25–27s) and night restaurant (28–29s) shots. The only design element is the styled red serif title card in the hook.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, h264, ~2.3 Mbps. Soft, compressed phone footage, handheld with walking bob and no gimbal. Daylight shots are bright, with blue skies mostly held and water rendered vivid turquoise, which carries the 'dream' feel. Weaker moments are the night restaurant shot (flare, noise, murky) and some dusk shots that are flat and grey-blue. Overall it reads as an authentic guest phone snapshot rather than a production, which adds credibility for a family-review audience.
study.ending: Ends on the final sentence 'We can't wait to visit the Azul Beach Resort again soon! 🤩' over a 4.23s pool pan (41.43–45.67). The voice ends at 44.72 and the video cuts ~0.95s later, on an audio hit at 45.58. Ending on the main pool echoes the opening pool shots, so it loops smoothly back to the hook. There is no explicit save/comment/book CTA; the resort name repeated at the end acts as the soft CTA.
study.why_viral: 1) Instant turquoise-pool-and-palms payoff plus a named, searchable resort in the first second, framed as 'Let's stay at…'. 2) A family-specific checklist (no crowds, kids water park, kids club, shops near the play areas) that parents save and send to a partner. 3) Constant movement and a new location every ~2.5s, with VO and text redundancy so it works muted or unmuted. 4) A sunset emotional peak mid-video and an authentic, real-guest feel with the creator's own kids.
lessons: Open with a moving shot of the most saturated water/palm view plus a big styled title naming the exact property, and start the voice at 0.0s.
Write one sentence per amenity, show it as a 2–3 line centered text block, and cut to new footage exactly where each sentence starts (within ~0.2s).
Give each amenity 1–3 clips totaling 3–5s; keep the median shot around 2.4s and never hold a non-view shot past ~4s.
Put a human action (jump, splash, swim) within the first 4–6s to prove the place is fun, and time the splash just before a music hit.
Place the golden-hour/sunset shot around 40% of the runtime as the emotional peak, hold it nearly still for ~2s, and move the text down so it doesn't cover the sun.
Order amenities from strongest visual (pools, beach) to practical (dining, shops, kids club), then end back on the hero pool so the video loops.
Tailor the copy to one audience. Here every line answers a parent's question (crowds, kids areas, convenience), which drives saves and partner shares.
Use emoji and one all-caps word only on emotional lines (GORGEOUS 😍, 🤩), not on factual ones.
Repeat the resort name in the final line so the last frame doubles as a search/booking prompt, and cut within ~1s of the last word.

study.format: POV comedy skit with a story arc (problem, gear-up, action, arrival), built as a mini 'how I got there' sequence. A spoken setup and a POV text card frame a real cruise-ship activity (the zip line) as a ridiculous shortcut to a cocktail party, then the cuts follow the journey in order: harness, helmet, launch, landing, gear off, fixing the dress, walking in, champagne in hand.
study.place: Royal Caribbean's Harmony of the Seas, a mega cruise ship, in bright midday sun with blue sky and open sea. What makes it special is the onboard zip line, which crosses high over the ship's open-air neighborhoods. The 'HARMONY' hull lettering, the stacked balconies and the netting show how huge the ship is. The trip ends at a glass-doored lounge where crew in light-blue polos hold trays of bright cocktails and champagne.
study.audience: Cruise fans, Royal Caribbean loyalists and people deciding which ship to book. It wants them to share it with a cruise buddy ('this is so us'), comment, and see the ship as a playground where you can zip line in a party dress. It reads as a real traveler or creator (a friend filming 'Carolyn'), not the cruise line, so it feels authentic and funny rather than like an ad.
study.hook: First frame (0.0s): Carolyn on a sunny pool deck in sunglasses and a loud multicolor geometric dress, a green umbrella and blue sky behind her. A three-line white caption sits mid-screen: 'POV: You're running late to a party on the other side of the Harmony of the Seas'. At 0.78s a friend's off-camera voice asks 'Carolyn, don't you have to be at a cocktail event in like two minutes?' The caption poses a relatable problem with a promised payoff (how will she get across a giant ship?). At 3.3–4.0s Carolyn's exaggerated open-mouth 'oh no' face sells the panic just before the cut.

Normal speed, motion 26–44. 2) Zip line launch, 8.33–10.73s (2.4s): a wide filmed from a distant deck. study.views: Views are background, not the star. 0–4s: blue sky, a green umbrella and the sea horizon behind her on the pool deck. 4–6s: the ship's glassy multi-level superstructure. 8.33–10.73s: the biggest and only true scenic beat, a far-side wide of the launch platform above the giant navy 'HARMONY' letters against a clear blue sky. At ~10.3–10.7s the camera pulls/pans wider to show stacked decks, balconies and the open sky for ~0.5s before the cut. 10.73–13.3s: the landing side shows rows of balconies and the netted sports deck. The biggest view lands at ~10.5s, almost exactly mid-video, right at the launch.
study.how_place_is_shown: All filmed by a companion on a handheld phone (no gimbal, no drone). The creator is in nearly every shot, and the bright dress is a visual through-line that makes her instantly trackable in wides. The mix is roughly: mediums (shots 1, 2, 6, 7), one close detail (helmet buckle), wides (launch, landing, lounge entrance). Crew members appear in several shots, which shows service and safety. The light is high midday sun: saturated blue sky, warm teak decks, then the cooler, even light of the indoor lounge at the end. The only food/drink details are the trays of colorful cocktails and the champagne flute, used as the reward at the finish line.
study.info_and_value: Very little explicit info. The ship name (Harmony of the Seas) is in the text card. The rest is shown, not told: Harmony has a zip line across the ship, staff harness and helmet you, and the 'Zip Line EXIT ONLY' sign is readable. There are no prices or booking details. The value is the 'I didn't know a cruise ship had this' discovery plus a funny, shareable scenario.
study.pacing: 8 shots in 22.33s, 3.13 cuts per 10s, median shot 2.37s. The setup shot is long (4.07s) so the dialogue and reaction can land. The middle six shots are a tight, even run of 1.93–2.6s that moves the story forward one step per shot. The final arrival shot is the longest (4.47s), giving the payoff room to breathe. Motion stays high (25–58) through the action middle, dips at the gear-off (13–19), spikes at 17.0s (70.9), then settles to 5–17 in the calm ending walk. Several cuts sit on or near audio hits: 8.33 (hit 8.46), 10.73 (hit 10.75), 15.67 (hit 15.5). Others are cut to the story rather than the beat. Speech ends at 3.06s, and the remaining ~19s is carried purely by visuals and music.
study.on_screen_text: One text card, 0–4.07s only: 'POV: You're running late to a party on the other side of the Harmony of the Seas'. It is 17 words in white sentence case, regular-weight TikTok-style font with a thin dark outline/shadow and no box, set across three lines centered just below mid-frame (~45–55% height) over her torso. It disappears at the first cut, and there is no other text after that. No emoji.
study.captions: none (the spoken line is not captioned; the POV card replaces it)
study.audio: Opens with natural sound and the friend's live off-camera voice, 0.78–3.06s ('Carolyn, don't you have to be at a cocktail event in like two minutes?'). Strong hits at 0.07, 1.26 and 2.74 sit under the dialogue. From ~7.2s a regular run of hits about 0.35–0.53s apart (7.23, 7.58, 8.46, 8.99, 9.34, 9.69, 10.22, 10.75, 11.38…) points to a rhythmic music track carrying the rest. The launch-to-landing cut at 10.73 hits 10.75 almost exactly. The final hits at 21.65/22.01 sit under the champagne walk-in. The track title cannot be identified from the data.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. Several work as story match cuts. At 4.07 she goes from the shocked face in the dress to the same dress with a harness on. At 15.67 she goes from walking off in gear to back in the dress on the sunny deck. At 17.87 she goes from walking down stairs to entering the lounge doors, which plays as continuous movement.
study.effects: No added effects, grade, zooms or graphics beyond the text card. The pull-wide around 10.3–10.7s is an in-camera zoom/pan, not a post effect. Color is the phone's natural punchy sunny look.
study.quality: 576x1024, 30fps, ~2 Mbps h264. That is modest: shots 5 and 8 look soft and compressed, as if re-encoded or zoomed from across the deck. Handheld throughout with small shakes. Exposure handles the bright sky and white ship well, with blue skies kept and no blown faces. It reads clearly as a phone snapshot, which suits the candid friend-filming-friend comedy. The authenticity sells the experience more than polish would.
study.ending: Ends on the payoff. She enters the cocktail event, takes champagne at ~19s, raises it at ~20.8s and walks toward the camera smiling. The video cuts mid-stride at 22.33s, about 1.3s after the glass-raise. There is no CTA. It loops reasonably well because the 'running late' opener follows the 'arrived in style' ending.
study.why_viral: 1) A relatable mini-problem ('late to a party') solved in an absurd, ship-specific way. The zip line becomes transport, which is funny and shows off a unique amenity. 2) A clear story arc in under 23s (setup, gear, launch, landing, champagne) with one step per ~2.3s shot keeps people watching for the arrival. 3) The party dress under a climbing harness is a visual gag and makes her easy to track in wide shots. 4) It shows the ship's scale and the 'cruise ships have zip lines?!' factor, which invites shares to cruise friends and comments.
lessons: Turn an amenity into a story: open with a tiny relatable problem in a POV text card (12–18 words, 3 lines, mid-screen) and let the activity be the solution.
Keep the setup shot long enough for the spoken line plus a reaction (about 3–4s), then drop the text at the first cut.
Cut the middle as one story step per shot at 2–2.6s each: prep, gear detail, launch, landing, aftermath.
Put the action's peak (launch, jump, drop) on a cut that lands within ±0.1s of a music hit, like the 10.73s cut on the 10.75s hit here.
Use a wide from a distance for the action so the setting's scale (hull lettering, decks, sky) shows. Let it widen for ~0.5s before cutting.
End on the reward (drink, view, arrival) and make it the longest shot, about 4–4.5s with the subject walking toward the camera. Cut ~1s after the triumphant gesture.
Use clothing or color continuity (here the loud dress) as match cuts across locations so jumps in time read as one continuous journey.
Candid handheld phone footage is fine for skit-style travel content. Keep exposure on bright skies and faces, and do not over-grade.

study.format: Fast cruise-ship tour / 'everything you need to see in 50 seconds' highlight reel. A title card over the exterior establishing shots promises a complete overview in a fixed time. It is followed by about 23 rapid shots that hop venue to venue across the ship. Many venues follow a 'sign shot → wide reveal' pair: the venue's own physical sign (Thrill Island, Music Hall, Overlook, AquaDome, Arcade, STAR OF THE SEAS) stands in for a text label, then the next shot shows the space. There is no voiceover and no list numbers; the music carries it.
study.place: Royal Caribbean's Star of the Seas, a new Icon-class mega cruise ship, docked at what looks like Perfect Day at CocoCay (pier with colorful shade sails, lighthouse, turquoise Bahamian water). It's a cruise trip that looks like a floating theme park and city. Highlights shown: the multi-level pool deck, Thrill Island water slides and tower, an infinity pool hanging over the ocean, the Music Hall, the glass-domed Overlook, the AquaDome/AquaTheater, Central Park, the Surfside family neighborhood (carousel, arcade, Splashaway kids' splash zone with the crown logo), and the Pearl atrium with its giant mirrored ship-name sign.
study.audience: Cruisers and families weighing whether to book the newest, biggest ship. It also serves people who just like 'look how huge this is' content. The goal is to make them save it as a ship preview, send it to a partner or family ('we need to do this'), and comment which area they'd hit first. It reads as a traveler/cruise creator: handheld 0.5x phone walk-throughs, no brand graphics, no price or booking push. It is not the cruise line's polished ad, which makes the hype feel authentic.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0–1.2s) is a calm wide from a sandy beach wall across turquoise water to two gigantic Icon-class ships side by side at the pier. Stacked white bold caps text sits in the upper third: 'EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO SEE ON / ROYAL CARIBBEAN'S / STAR OF THE SEAS / IN 50 SECONDS'. The ship name is the biggest, italic line. The audio opens immediately on a Spanish-language song lyric ('¿Qué te…' at 0.00s). At 1.2s it cuts to a dramatic low angle from the pier up the stern, showing the 'Star of the Seas' lettering. It stops the scroll for three reasons: the scale of the ships, a famous brand name, and a concrete promise with a time limit ('in 50 seconds') that tells viewers the payoff is short and complete.

study.action_shots: No sports or ride footage. The action is all camera movement through spaces. Walk-ins at 4.4s (Thrill Island arch), 19.67s (down the Overlook stairs), 27.37s (out to the atrium rail), 29.93s and 36.63s (through doors) and 32.77–36.6s (Central Park walk). Fast pans and orbits at 21.13s (dome), 38.93s (carousel) and 44.2–49.1s (Pearl and sign). All play at normal speed, handheld or gimbal with a wide lens. Motion peaks line up with these: 50–55 around 18.5–21.5s (Overlook dome), the video's maximum of 62.8 at about 33–34s (Central Park walk), and 49–57 at about 45.5–46s (the Pearl swing). The densest run of audio hits, 44.21–47.45s, falls on the final Pearl orbit, with the 44.2s cut landing on a hit at 44.21s. Slides are shown empty; nobody rides them.
study.views: Hero views: (1) 0–1.2s static beach wide of both ships, the scale shot. (2) 3.17s high pan over the pool deck. (3) 10.27–12.23s infinity pool with turquoise sea and island, held about 2s with a slow pan, the most 'dream vacation' frame. (4) 12.23–14.27s elevated pan across the deck out to the ocean. (5) ~13.8–14.5s near-aerial top-down onto the rainbow-sailed pier and turquoise water. (6) 19.67–23.33s glass-dome Overlook with ocean through the glass, about 3.7s across two shots, revealed by walking down the stairs then tilting up into the sun flare. (7) 25.47s AquaTheater blue dome, revealed after its sign. Interior reveals use doors: black frames parting at ~30s, Surfside frosted doors sliding open at 36.63s, and a walk-out from a covered deck to the rail at 27.37s. The biggest natural view (ocean infinity pool and pier) lands in the first third, 10–14.5s. The ending saves the most dramatic interior, the pink Pearl, for the last 4.9s.
study.how_place_is_shown: Mostly wides and mediums from a 0.5x ultra-wide phone lens, cut with medium sign close-ups that work as chapter headers: 6 signs out of about 25 shots. People appear only as background crowds (pool swimmers, a guest at the rail, performers, people on stairs). There's no creator on camera, no couple or family hero, and no face to camera. The shots are filmed walk-throughs at eye level, with low angles for scale (stern at 1.2s, slides at 7.73s). Light is midday bright sun and deep blue sky outside, then hard contrast moves inside to neon red (Music Hall), electric blue (AquaDome) and magenta (Pearl). That color variety keeps a sameness-prone walkthrough feeling fresh. There are no food, drink or cabin shots; it's all public venues and 'wow' architecture. Handheld with light stabilization; some shots wobble.
study.info_and_value: Light. The only text is the title naming the ship and line. Venue names come from the ship's own signage, so viewers learn the neighborhoods (Thrill Island, Music Hall, Overlook, AquaDome, Central Park, Surfside, Arcade, the Pearl) without overlays. No prices, sailing dates, ports, tips or booking info. The save value is the 'complete overview' promise: a reference viewers keep before booking or boarding.
study.pacing: 25 shots in 49.1s, about 4.9 cuts per 10s. Median shot 1.93s, range 1.07s (Arcade, 41.47s) to 2.83s (Central Park doors reveal, 29.93s). Very even rhythm: almost every shot is 1.4–2.6s, so it feels like a steady march rather than builds and drops. The first shot is the shortest opener (1.2s) and gets to motion quickly. Longer holds go to walk-through reveals (2.53s at 7.73s, 2.57s at 27.37s, 2.83s at 29.93s, 2.53s at 38.93s, 2.57s final). Some cuts sit close to audio hits (12.23 ≈ 12.1/12.34, 29.93 ≈ 29.77, 41.47 ≈ 41.72, 44.2 = 44.21), but many don't; cut rhythm matters more than strict beat sync. Motion stays in the 20–40 band almost throughout, with stillest moments at the AquaDome sign (~12 at 23.5–25s) and the opening (~10–12).
study.on_screen_text: One title block over the first two shots only (0–3.17s), centered in the upper third over the sky. Line 1, 'EVERYTHING YOU NEED TO SEE ON', is small white bold condensed caps. Lines 2–3, 'ROYAL CARIBBEAN'S / STAR OF THE SEAS', are large white heavy italic condensed caps. Line 4, 'IN 50 SECONDS', is medium white bold caps. Soft shadow, no box, 10 words, no emoji. It disappears at the 3.17s cut and no other text appears; physical venue signs do the labelling afterward.
study.audio: A music bed only, apparently a Spanish-language track; the transcript picks up its lyric '¿Qué te…' at 0.00–0.70s. No voiceover and no audible natural sound. Strong hits at 3.63/3.88, 12.1/12.34, 14.58–15.33, 24.05, 29.77–31.02, 37.24, 39.48, 41.72/42.47, and a dense cluster from 44.21 to 47.45 as the track builds. The Music Hall switch (~14.5s) arrives with the 14.58/15.08 hits, the doors-open reveal sits on the 29.77–31.02 hits, and the Pearl finale is cut exactly on 44.21 and rides the busiest stretch of the song.
study.transitions: Mostly hard cuts. The cut list shows no cut where the scene switches from the pier view (~14.5s) to the Music Hall sign, but the frames at 13.81 and 14.83s show a completely different scene. Most likely a quick cut timed near the 14.58s audio hit was missed by detection; the exact switch type can't be confirmed. In-camera wipes act as transitions: door frames parting at ~30s and frosted sliding doors at 36.63s. The 4.4s cut moves from a pan-right on the pool deck to a forward walk under the arch, which reads as continuous motion.
study.effects: No added graphics, zooms, freeze frames or overlays. Color looks punchy: saturated blue sky and turquoise water, vivid neon interiors. This is likely phone HDR or a light saturation boost, not a heavy grade. Natural lens flare from the sun through the dome at 21.13–23.33s.
study.quality: 720x1280 at 30fps, about 2.6 Mbps H.264. That's modest resolution and bitrate, but bright midday exteriors and strongly lit neon interiors hide it. The 0.5x ultra-wide lens exaggerates scale on the ship, slides and domes, which makes the place look enormous. Some shots are handheld-wobbly and slightly soft (the Music Hall interior, the carousel), so it reads as an honest phone walkthrough rather than a commercial. The dream-trip feel comes from the turquoise water, blue sky and architecture, not from cinematic camera work.
study.ending: The last shot (46.53–49.1s, 2.57s) orbits the iridescent 'STAR OF THE SEAS' letters in the pink Pearl atrium during the densest run of audio hits, then cuts out about 1.6s after the final hit (47.45s). The ship's name bookends the name on the hull in the first 3s, so it loops cleanly back to the title. There is no verbal or text CTA; the implied ask is to save, share or rewatch.
study.why_viral: 1) A concrete, time-boxed promise ('everything you need to see… in 50 seconds') on the newest, most-hyped cruise ship, which is instantly clear and feels complete. 2) Relentless variety at about a 1.9s median shot: water slides, an ocean infinity pool, a neon music venue, glass domes, a park, a carousel and a pink atrium. Color and indoor/outdoor switches mean nothing repeats long enough to bore. 3) Scale shots from an ultra-wide lens and low angles make the ship feel like a city, which is the selling point people share ('look at this thing'). 4) Real venue signs act as built-in chapter titles, so viewers learn the neighborhoods without reading overlays, and it loops back to the ship's name.
lessons: Open with the widest, biggest-scale shot (the whole ship, resort or skyline) for only about 1.2s under a title that names the place and promises a time-boxed overview ('…in 50 seconds'), and keep the title up for no more than about 3s across the first two shots.
Use the location's own signs as labels: cut a 1–2s sign close-up, then immediately a 1.9–2.5s wide of that space. This replaces on-screen text and makes it work as a guide.
Keep shots in a tight 1.4–2.6s band (median about 1.9s, roughly 5 cuts per 10s) and give the extra 0.3–0.6s only to walk-through reveals.
Move the camera in every shot (walk in, pan, orbit, tilt up) so motion stays around 30–40 and nothing sits still. Save the biggest orbit or pan for the final shot.
Alternate light and color moods every 2–4 shots: bright blue exteriors, then neon interiors, then glass and sun, then pink. This keeps a long walkthrough from feeling repetitive.
Use doors, door frames and walking out to a rail as free reveal transitions. Start a shot on the closed or covered frame and let the space open up within the first second.
Shoot the scale subjects (hulls, slides, domes, towers) from a 0.5x ultra-wide at a low angle; it makes the place feel huge, which is the share trigger.

Put your best natural view (ocean or pool) in the first third (around 10–14s) to hold viewers, and land the most dramatic interior plus the place's name on the densest part of the music for the last 4–5s, ending within about 1.5s of the final hit so it loops.

study.format: Text-list 'listicle' over a single piece of B-roll. It is a 'where NOT to travel' warning list: one airplane-window clip carries a headline plus a bulleted list of 9 destinations that build in line by line. The second segment swaps the overlay for a brand logo and a CTA card. The content is in the text, not the footage.
study.place: No single destination. The footage is a generic airplane-window shot: a white wing over a sunlit bay or lake with a city coastline below, in daytime blue-sky light. The 'places' are named only in text: Kerala, Tokyo, Kyoto, Mt. Everest, Scotland NC500, NYC, Venice, Barcelona and Phi Phi Islands. These are famous bucket-list and overtourism hotspots, and that is what makes the list provocative.
study.audience: Made for general travelers planning 2025 trips. It reads as a brand, a travel podcast, shown by the purple microphone-in-passport logo. It wants viewers to comment (to defend a place on the list, or answer 'Where are you traveling in 2025?'), to save the list, to share or tag someone going to one of these places, and to follow or seek out the podcast for the 'full list… and WHY'.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0-0.3s) shows the plane wing out the window with the headline 'Where NOT to Travel in 2025' at the top. It is in bold white letters on a red outlined box, and 'NOT' is capitalized. A music beat starts right away, with the first strong hit at 0.62s, and there is no voice. The negative 'NOT' flips the usual 'where to go' post into a warning. Viewers immediately ask 'is my trip on it?' Then the first two destinations pop in before 1s, so there is an instant payoff to keep reading.

beats.what: Airplane-window wing shot with headline 'Where NOT to Travel in 2025' (white text, red box) at the top.
'Kerala, India' and 'Tokyo, Japan' pop in with red map-pin icons, by about 0.9s.
'Kyoto, Japan' added.
'Mt. Everest, Nepal/China' and 'Scotland NC500, Scotland' added, both visible by about 2.2s.
'NYC, United States' added, visible by about 2.8s.
'Venice, Italy' and 'Barcelona, Spain' added, visible by about 3.4s.
'Phi Phi Islands, Thailand' added. The full 9-item list is complete by about 4.0s.
The full list is held for about 5s over the slowly drifting wing-and-water view, giving time to read or screenshot.
Hard cut to the same window view with a purple podcast logo and the text 'Get our full list of destinations to avoid in 2025, and WHY! Where are you traveling in 2025?', held to the end at 13.0s.

study.choice_format: Not a choice video. It is a cumulative unranked list. There are 9 items, each labelled with a red map-pin emoji and written as 'City, Country'. The text is white with a dark outline, left-aligned and stacked under the headline in the upper half. Items appear roughly one per music beat (about 0.5s apart, sometimes two at once), and all 9 are on screen within about 4s. Nothing separates the items except their pop-in appearance; there are no cuts. The list is not ordered best-last. The viewer's answer is requested at the end: 'Where are you traveling in 2025?'
study.action_shots: None. The only movement is the plane's gentle drift and bank seen through the window. Motion stays between 5 and 12 for the whole video, with no people, rides or sports.
study.views: One continuous aerial-from-the-plane view: the wing in the upper right, a city coastline at the top, and a large sunlit expanse of water filling the bottom half. Sun glints on the water around 5-8s. It is held for the full 13s with no reveal technique. The camera just drifts handheld as the plane moves, and the coastline slides up and down in frame. There is no 'biggest view' moment; the view is a backdrop for the text.
study.how_place_is_shown: A single wide POV out the window, handheld from a seat, in bright midday light with blue sky and silver-blue water. No people, food or details. The wing gives an instant 'I'm traveling' cue, and the empty water gives clean negative space for a long text list.
study.info_and_value: Gives 9 named destinations to 'avoid' in 2025 as text only. No reasons are given. The 'WHY' is deliberately withheld and pushed to the podcast ('Get our full list… and WHY!'). This curiosity gap, plus a list that names beloved places like Kyoto, Venice and Barcelona, drives screenshots and saves, arguing comments, and profile clicks.
study.pacing: 2 shots, of 9.0s and 4.0s, with 0.77 cuts per 10s, so the pace is very slow. The energy comes from text pop-ins in the first 4s, about 0.5s apart on the beat. The list then sits still for about 5s of reading time before the CTA card holds for 4s. The cut at 9.0s lands right next to an audio hit at 9.05s.
study.on_screen_text: Headline: 'Where NOT to Travel in 2025', in a bold rounded sans-serif. It is white with a red background box or stroke, centered at the top on two lines, from 0s to 9s. List: 9 lines with a red 📍 pin plus 'Place, Country', in a white bold sans with a dark shadow. It is left-aligned below the headline and builds from 0.6s to 4.0s, holds to 9s, and has up to 9 lines (about 30 words) on screen. The CTA from 9-13s has a purple circular podcast logo (a microphone in a book) at the top center. Below it is 'Get our full list of destinations to avoid in 2025, and WHY!', then a blank line, then 'Where are you traveling in 2025?', in lavender or white text with a purple outline, centered mid-screen.
study.audio: A music track only, with no voiceover and no natural sound. Strong hits come about every 0.53s (around 113-114 BPM) from 0.62s to 12.99s. List items pop in roughly on these hits, and the cut to the CTA at 9.0s sits on the 9.05s hit.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. There is one cut at 9.0s, and it is essentially an overlay swap on matching airplane-window footage, so the background barely changes.
study.effects: Text pop-ins for the list items, and a logo graphic on the end card. Color is natural or slightly bright, with no visible grade, zooms or other effects.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, about 2.3 Mbps h264. It is soft, phone-shot window footage with a slightly hazy, bright sky and window glare. It is stable enough, but it reads as a phone snapshot rather than a cinematic dream trip. That is acceptable here because the text carries the video.
study.ending: Ends on the 4s CTA card (logo plus 'full list… and WHY' plus a comment question) and cuts at 13.0s on the last beat. The background is the same wing-and-water view as the opening, so it loops almost seamlessly into the hook, which encourages rewatching and rereading.
study.why_viral: 1) The contrarian 'Where NOT to travel' headline, with the capitalized NOT, flips the usual inspo format and triggers 'is my trip on it?' 2) It names beloved hotspots (Kyoto, Venice, Barcelona, NYC), which provokes debate and defensive comments. 3) A dense list that builds fast and then holds invites screenshots, saves and rewatches, and the loop helps. 4) Withholding the 'WHY' plus a direct question pushes comments and podcast visits.
lessons: Lead with a contrarian or negative headline ('Where NOT to…', 'Skip these…') in bold, high-contrast boxed text in the top third from frame 1.
Build list items in one per music beat (about 0.5s apart) so the full list is on screen within about 4s.
After the list completes, hold it still for 4-5s so viewers can read or screenshot it before any CTA.
Use one calm, low-motion travel clip (plane window, horizon, water) as a backdrop when text carries the content, and keep about half the frame as empty negative space for text.
Prefix each list item with a 📍 pin and a 'City, Country' format for instant scannability; aim for 8-10 items.
Withhold the reasons and point to the full version ('…and WHY!') to create a curiosity gap that drives follows and clicks.
End with a 3-4s CTA card that asks a direct comment question ('Where are you traveling in 2025?'), and put the cut on a beat hit.
Keep the end-card background the same as the opening shot so the video loops seamlessly into the hook.

study.format: Educational tips explainer in a numbered series ('Tips for First Time Cruisers Part 2'). It is built as voiceover plus B-roll: one calm narrated sentence per shot, with each sentence repeated as a centered text card, laid over 6 handheld phone clips of cruise ships. It is a single-topic 'what to expect' explainer (the muster drill), not a list or a tour.
study.place: Cruise ships in general rather than one ship. The footage mixes lines: a Disney ship seen from a car in a palm-lined Florida port parking lot, a packed Carnival lido deck with its red/blue waterslide, a Royal Caribbean Oasis-class hull with yellow lifeboats seen through a terminal window, open ocean with sun glare, a '...of the Seas / Nassau' life ring on a teak deck, and a Disney top deck (enclosed tube waterslide, Mickey-red funnel, big poolside screen showing Finding Nemo, pool). What makes it look special is the sheer scale of the ships, the blue water and the bright sun.
study.audience: First-time or nervous cruisers, often families, planning a first sailing. It wants them to save the tip for embark day, follow for the rest of the series (Part 2 implies Parts 1, 3...) and send it to a travel companion. Because footage from several cruise lines is mixed, it reads as a cruise tips creator or travel agent account, not a cruise line.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0.0s) is a moving shot from a car window: a giant cruise ship towers over a palm-lined port parking lot under a blue sky. A dark blur from the window edge or a finger sits at the top of the frame. Two lines of text are already on screen. A small white outlined line reads 'Tips for First Time Cruisers Part 2:' and below it is a large white 'Muster Station Drill' with a strong cyan glow. The voiceover starts on the very first frame: 'Tips for First-Time Cruisers Part 2, Muster Station Drill' (0.00–3.88s). It stops the scroll because the 'arriving at the port' POV plus the words 'First Time Cruisers' instantly flag the target viewer, and 'Muster Station Drill' names a mandatory thing they are unsure about.

beats.what: Drive-by POV of the Disney ship at port, with the glowing title card 'Tips for First Time Cruisers Part 2: Muster Station Drill' and the VO reading the title.

High wide of a packed Carnival lido deck: hundreds of passengers gathered, decks of railings full of people, waterslide and blue sky behind. VO: 'Before the fun begins, every passenger must report for their Muster Station Drill.'
Walking past terminal window mullions toward a Royal Caribbean hull with yellow lifeboats hanging at its side. VO: 'This is where you'll assemble in case of an emergency.'

Ocean from the ship's rail. The shot opens into sun glare and silver water, then pans down and left until it settles on deep blue sea and a clean horizon. VO gives the key tip: muster location is on your room keycard or in the cruise line app.

Fast handheld walk along an upper deck rail, past a standing passenger, ending on a close detail of an orange life ring ('...of the Seas, Nassau'). VO: 'A crew member will be there to give you instructions.'

Sweeping pan across the Disney top deck: the tube waterslide over the ocean, the big screen showing Finding Nemo, the pool, then the red funnel. VO: 'it only takes a few minutes before you can go and enjoy the ship.'
Ends mid-pan on the funnel about 0.8s after the last word ('ship' @25.26). There is no spoken or written CTA.

study.action_shots: There are few true action shots. (1) 0–4.2s: a lateral car-window tracking move past the ship, at real speed. The motion graph sits steady at about 16–24, reading as a smooth drive-by. (2) 9.4–12.67s: a walking POV past window mullions. The bars sweep across the frame, which gives a parallax 'wipe' feel. (3) 18.57–21.57s: a brisk handheld walk-through along the deck rail. This is the motion peak of the video at 61.9–69.3 around 18.5–19.5s, settling to about 48 at 20s and 19 at 20.5s, then nearly still at about 11 on the life ring at 21s. (4) 21.57–26.07s: a sweeping deck pan with motion around 35–47, ending up at 45–54 at 25–26s. Everything plays at normal speed. There is no beat drop. Cuts follow the voiceover sentences, not the music.
study.views: The ocean shot at 12.67–18.57s is the biggest and longest view (5.9s, the longest shot). It opens backlit into the sun, with silver glittering water and a lens flare. A slow handheld pan then moves away from the sun, down and left, until the frame clears to saturated blue sea and a crisp horizon around 17.3–18.5s, a gentle 'glare-to-blue' reveal. The lido crowd wide at 4.2–9.4s is held for 5.2s with only a slight drift. The final Disney deck pan at 21.57–26.07s (4.5s) sweeps across slide tubes, the ocean, the pool and the funnel against a deep blue sky, using a pan as its reveal. The opening ship-from-the-car shot (4.2s) is an establishing scale shot. There is no drone and no aerial.
study.how_place_is_shown: Mostly wides (port, crowd deck, ocean, top deck), one medium (lifeboats through glass) and one detail (the life ring, chosen because it literally reads 'safety'). People appear only as a crowd or as anonymous passersby. There is no creator on camera and no couple or family shots. It is all filmed POV-style on a phone, handheld, with no gimbal-smooth or drone footage. The light is midday sun with blue skies and white clouds, plus one backlit late-day ocean shot with glare. Footage from different ships and lines is mixed freely to illustrate a generic process, and ship features (slides, pool, big screen) are used to visually promise 'the fun after the drill'.
study.info_and_value: The facts given are: every passenger must attend the muster drill before the fun begins. It's where you assemble in an emergency. Your muster station location is printed on your room keycard or shown in the cruise line app. A crew member gives instructions. It only takes a few minutes. All of it is delivered twice, by voiceover and as matching text cards. The keycard/app tip is the saveable insider nugget. 'Part 2' of a numbered first-timer series pushes follow and save behavior, and the reassuring tone ('only a few minutes') makes it shareable with anxious first-timers in a travel group.
study.pacing: There are 6 shots in 26.07s, about 1.9 cuts per 10s, which is slow for travel content. Shot lengths are 4.2, 5.2, 3.27, 5.9, 3.0 and 4.5s (median 4.35s). Cuts are placed by narration: each cut lands 0.3–0.6s after a sentence ends (3.88→4.2, 9.06→9.4, 12.08→12.67, 18.16→18.57). The exception is the last cut at 21.57, which falls mid-sentence after 'And it only'. The VO runs almost continuously from 0.00s to 25.56s with tiny gaps of 0.1–0.4s, so there's no dead air. Calm static wides (crowd, ocean) are held longest, and the motion-heavy walk shot is the shortest. Background-music hits fall every 0.5s (about 120 BPM pulse), but the cuts only loosely coincide with them (e.g. 9.52, 12.52, 18.52), more by chance than by design.
study.on_screen_text: Title card (0–4.2s), centered in the upper third. Line 1 is small white bold condensed sentence-case text with a black outline, 'Tips for First Time Cruisers Part 2:'. Line 2 is large white bold 'Muster Station Drill' with a strong cyan/blue outer glow. After that, each narrated sentence appears as a full sentence card: white regular-weight sans-serif with a soft dark shadow, centered at about 30–35% from the top, 2–3 lines and 9–23 words at once. The cards are 'Before the fun begins, every passenger must report for their Muster Station Drill' (4.2–9.4), 'This is where you'll assemble in case of an emergency' (9.4–12.67), 'You can find your Muster Station location on your room keycard or in your cruise line app' (12.67–18.57) and 'A crew member will be there to give you instructions, and it only takes a few minutes before you can go and enjoy the ship!' (18.57–end, covering two VO sentences). Each card changes exactly on the cut. No emoji.
study.captions: There are no separate word-by-word captions. The sentence-level text cards serve as captions, matching the VO nearly verbatim, one card per shot. The last card shows two spoken sentences at once from 18.57s.
study.audio: Calm, even narrator voiceover (75 words, starting at 0.00s) that sounds polished and possibly text-to-speech. It carries the whole video under a soft background music bed with a steady pulse; audio hits fall every 0.5–1s from 2.02 to 23.52s. No natural sound or sound effects stand out. Sound and picture line up by sentence (one sentence per shot), not by beat drops.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. They come at 4.2 (car POV → crowd deck), 9.4 (crowd → lifeboats through glass), 12.67 (lifeboats → ocean glare), 18.57 (blue ocean → deck walk) and 21.57 (life ring → Disney slide tube/ocean). The text card swaps on the same frame as each cut. The window mullions sweeping across shot 3 act as an in-camera wipe but are not a transition.
study.effects: The cyan outer glow on the 'Muster Station Drill' title is the only stylized graphic. A drop shadow sits on the sentence text. The color is bright with slightly boosted saturation: punchy blue skies and blue water, and the red Disney funnel and orange life ring pop. There is a natural lens flare and sun glare in the ocean shot. No zooms, shakes, freeze frames, maps or split screens.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, h264 at about 3 Mbps, so it is moderately soft and compressed. All footage is handheld phone video. Shot 1 is shot through a car window with a dark blur intruding at the top. Shot 3 has glass reflections and mullions. Skies stay exposed and blue except for the intentional backlit ocean shot. It reads as an authentic 'real cruiser's phone' snapshot rather than a cinematic dream trip. That suits a practical tips video, where credibility matters more than polish, and the strong blue sky and water carry the visual appeal.
study.ending: The VO's final words 'go and enjoy the ship' (25.26s) play over the Disney top-deck pan of the slide, pool and funnel, so the payoff line lands on the most fun-looking footage. The video cuts about 0.8s after the last word, mid-pan on the red funnel. There is no spoken or written CTA; the 'Part 2' label implies the series continues. Ending mid-motion with no outro makes it loop easily back to the arrival shot.
study.why_viral: 1) It names a specific audience and a specific worry in the first second ('First Time Cruisers' + 'Muster Station Drill'), and first-timers search for and save exactly this. 2) There is one genuinely useful, quick-to-act tip: the station is on your keycard or in the app. 3) The reassuring arc goes from 'mandatory' and 'emergency' to 'only takes a few minutes, go enjoy the ship', ending on slides, pool and ocean, so the anxiety turns into excitement to book. 4) The numbered 'Part 2' series format drives follows and binge-viewing of other parts.
lessons: Put the series label and topic on frame 1 as a two-tier title: a small 'Tips for First Time [Travelers] Part N:' line plus a large glowing topic line. Start the voiceover at 0.0s reading it.
Give each narrated sentence its own shot. Cut 0.3–0.6s after the sentence ends and swap the on-screen sentence card on the same frame.
Hold calm wides (crowd scenes, ocean) for 5–6s under longer sentences. Keep handheld walk-throughs to about 3s.
Match B-roll literally to the words: crowds for 'every passenger', lifeboats for 'emergency', a life ring for 'crew instructions'. Literal visuals make dry info watchable.
Place the most practical, saveable tip (where to find the info: keycard/app) over the most beautiful shot (the ocean), so the longest-held view coincides with the key fact.

End on the payoff and the fun visuals (pool, slides, ocean, iconic funnel). Have the final line resolve the worry ('only takes a few minutes... enjoy the ship'), then cut within about 1s of the last word, mid-pan, so it loops.
Keep text cards at 30–35% from the top in white with a shadow, max 3 lines. Use the colored glow only on the title so the topic stands out from the body text.

Footage from different trips or ships can be mixed for a generic how-to explainer, as long as every shot has a blue sky or water and a clear subject. Cut away dark window-edge or finger intrusions where possible.

study.format: Single 'cruise tip you never knew' insider-tip video. A 2.5s hook title card is stacked over a scenic establishing shot. It is followed by three short night-time B-roll shots of the pool deck, while the tip text builds up line by line, ending on a held atmospheric wide. There is no voiceover; the text carries the whole message.
study.place: An ocean cruise ship, likely a large Royal Caribbean-style ship, judging by the pool deck, the funnels with steam and the stacked decks. It opens on a balcony view at sea at sunset, with the wake churning beside the white hull. It then moves to the top-deck hot tub under a blue-lit canopy, the main pool glowing turquoise at night (depth marker '1.45M/4ft 9in') and rows of red-lit loungers. What makes it special is the empty, glowing, almost private pool deck at night, which is the 'secret' being sold.
study.audience: First-time and repeat cruisers planning a sailing, especially adults and couples who want to dodge crowds and kids. It is built to be saved for the trip and sent to a cruise partner ('we're doing this'). It reads as a cruise-fan creator or traveler account sharing hacks, not the cruise line.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0-0.24s) is a sunset-at-sea view from a balcony: an orange horizon, dark blue water, white wake foaming along the curved hull on the right. At 0.24s, white bold monospace-style text with a black outline appears mid-frame: 'Cruise Tip That You'. By 0.72s a red serif line, 'Never Knew', pops in under it, and by 1.68s a blue line, 'You Needed:', completes it. It stops the scroll because of the curiosity-gap phrasing plus a dreamy, instantly recognizable cruise-balcony sunset, and because the sentence builds word by word so you wait for it to finish.

beats.what: Balcony sunset view over the wake and ship hull; title line 1 'Cruise Tip That You' appears at 0.24s
Red serif 'Never Knew' added
Blue 'You Needed:' added; the colon promises the payoff
Quick dissolve to a night hot tub under a blue-lit canopy; handheld orbit. The tip appears: 'Hit the pools/hot tubs during popular dining hours for less crowds and kids.'
Cut to the wide main pool at night, glowing turquoise with the lit superstructure behind; second line 'They're open late and beautiful at night.'
Jump cut within the pool footage (depth marker, a lone person in red), quickly moving to red-lit loungers
Row of empty red-lit loungers, the pool and the funnels venting steam; third line 'It's the perfect opportunity to relax peacefully!'
Near-still hold on the empty lounger wide until the end at 7.67s (motion drops to 2.0)

study.action_shots: No real action. The only movement is the camera's: the churning wake in shot 1 (0-2.5s, motion 8-16), a handheld orbit/pan around the hot tub (2.5-3.93s, motion ~14-16), and a slow handheld drift across the pool (3.93-5.33s). A person standing at the pool edge in red is incidental. The final shot settles almost still.
study.views: Shot 1 (0-2.5s) is the scenic money shot: a sunset horizon and wake from the balcony, static handheld, held 2.5s under the title. It is used as the hook rather than saved for the end. The night pool wide at 3.93s is revealed by a hard cut and drifted over for 1.4s. The final empty-lounger-and-pool wide (5.33-7.67s, ~2.3s, the longest-feeling hold) has a slow drift settling into stillness. It is the emotional payoff view that shows the 'peaceful, no crowds' promise.
study.how_place_is_shown: All handheld phone footage, filmed POV-style without the creator on camera. There is one golden-hour exterior, then everything is night: saturated blue LED canopy, turquoise underwater pool lights, red lounger lights and warm deck lamps. The shots are mostly wides and mediums of the amenity. Details like the mosaic tile, the depth marker and the empty chairs show emptiness. People are almost absent (one figure by the pool), which is the point: proof of no crowds and no kids.
study.info_and_value: One actionable tip, given entirely as on-screen text in three lines: go to the pools/hot tubs during popular dining hours for fewer crowds and kids; they're open late and beautiful at night; it's the perfect chance to relax peacefully. It is simple, free and immediately usable on any cruise, which makes it a classic save-and-share-with-your-cruise-buddy hack. There are no prices, ship names or booking info.
study.pacing: 4 shots in 7.67s (3.9 cuts per 10s, median shot 1.88s). The hook shot is longest at 2.5s, long enough to read the 3-line title. The B-roll shots are 1.43s and 1.4s, then the final shot holds about 2.33s for reading. Cuts land near music hits: 2.5 (hits at 2.42/2.59) and 5.33 (hit 5.42). The 3.93 cut sits between hits. Overall it is quick but reading-paced: text lines arrive about every 1.4-1.8s.
study.on_screen_text: Hook title, centered at upper-middle: line 1 'Cruise Tip That You' in white bold monospace with a black outline (0.24s); line 2 'Never Knew' in red serif with a white outline (0.72s); line 3 'You Needed:' in blue bold monospace with a white outline (1.68s). It is 3-4 words per line in mixed fonts and colors, and it fades out through the 2.5s dissolve. The tip text uses TikTok's classic white sans with a soft shadow, left-aligned, placed upper-middle, and stacks cumulatively. 'Hit the pools/hot tubs during popular dining hours for less crowds and kids.' appears at 2.5s (13 words). 'They're open late and beautiful at night.' is added at 3.93s, indented. 'It's the perfect opportunity to relax peacefully!' is added at about 5.4s. All stay to the end. There are no emoji.
study.audio: No speech. It is a music track, likely a trending lo-fi or upbeat sound, with dense hits about every 0.17-0.33s from 2.08s to the end (2.08, 2.42, 2.59... 7.59). The first hit at 2.08s comes just before the hook-to-tip transition, so the beat kicks in as the payoff starts. There is no audible natural sound design.
study.transitions: 2.5s: a short cross-dissolve; the before frame shows the title text ghosted over the hot tub shot. 3.93s: hard cut from the hot tub to the pool wide. 5.33s: jump cut within the pool footage that quickly moves into the lounger wide.
study.effects: No added effects beyond the text. The color appears straight from the phone: saturated blue and red LED tones at night and a soft orange sunset. There is no grade, zoom, freeze or graphics.
study.quality: 576x1024, 50.5 fps, about 1.6 Mbps h264: low-res and compressed. The night shots show noise and slight motion blur, and the sunset is a bit washed out. It looks like a phone snapshot, which here reads as authentic traveler footage. The vivid LED colors carry the 'dreamy' feel despite the low sharpness.
study.ending: It ends on the near-still wide of empty red-lit loungers and the glowing pool, with all three tip lines on screen, about 2.3s after the last cut. There is no spoken or written CTA. The quiet, empty frame acts as the payoff and lets viewers finish reading. It is short enough (7.7s) to loop naturally back to the sunset hook.
study.why_viral: The 'tip you never knew you needed' curiosity hook is built line by line over an iconic sunset-at-sea balcony shot, so viewers stay to read it. The payoff is a free, instantly usable insider hack that cruisers save and send to their travel partners. The empty, neon-lit night pool footage proves the claim visually and sells a calm, private-feeling luxury. At under 8 seconds with stacked text, people rewatch to finish reading, which boosts completion and loops.
lessons: Open on your single prettiest establishing shot (sunset, ocean, balcony) and hold it about 2.5s under the title. Don't make viewers wait for the scenic shot.
Build the hook title in 3 staggered lines about 0.5-1s apart (0.24s, 0.72s, 1.68s here), with the key words ('Never Knew') in a contrasting color and font.
End the hook text with a colon or open phrase so the cut to the payoff feels like the answer, and time that cut to the first strong music hit (here about 2.4-2.6s).
Deliver the tip as stacked, cumulative text lines, adding one line per shot about every 1.4s, so each new clip reveals a new piece of information.
Match each B-roll shot to the claim. 'Less crowds' needs empty pools and empty loungers; avoid footage with crowds that contradicts the text.
Keep B-roll shots at 1.4-1.5s and give the final shot about 2.3s with almost no camera motion, so viewers can finish reading before the loop.
Use naturally saturated night lighting (LEDs, underwater pool lights) as the visual hook for night-amenity tips; it hides low resolution and feels exclusive.
Keep single-tip videos under 8s so the stacked text forces rewatches and saves; one concrete, free, actionable tip beats a vague list.

study.format: Educational tip in a numbered series: 'Tips for First-Time Cruisers Part 3: Cruise Line Apps'. It is a short how-to built from voiceover over B-roll. The structure runs: title card over a hero shot of the ship (0-4s), then the claim over a scenic balcony shot (4-7.8s), then the how-to as a phone screen recording of the App Store (7.8-12.5s), then the payoff as a fast montage of what the app unlocks (show, deck party, fireworks, food, pool deck; 12.5-19.9s), and finally a one-line CTA over a water-coaster action shot (19.9-22.5s). There are 4 voiceover sentences plus the title, and each one gets its own text block and its own visual section.
