study.action_shots: These are mostly walking and lifestyle movement, not adrenaline. Shot by shot: 4.93-~6.5s walk-away follow up the Kyoto street (about 1.5s, normal speed). ~6.5-8.27s turning walk among the Barcelona columns. 8.27-~9.3s follow from behind toward Ross Castle. ~9.3-10.67s walk into the mossy forest (motion jumps to 23-35 around 7-8s as these walks cut). ~29.7s wave in the business-class seat. 32.73-~34.5s standing still in Shibuya crossing while the crowd moves; this is the motion peak of the video (47.2 at ~32.5-33s), with the creator as the still centre. 44.53-~46.5s handheld selfie walk in Akihabara (motion ~27-29). ~53-54.8s POV rolling the carry-on through the terminal. 57.0-~58.3s gimbal-style follow across the checkerboard terrace. ~58.3-59.4s side wide in the cactus garden. All play at normal speed. Cuts follow the voiceover phrases rather than music drops.
study.views: Big Ben and Parliament at golden hour (2.87s, ~1.3s, static). Soumaya facade from a low angle (~4.2s). Kyoto pagoda at dusk (4.93s, walk-in reveal). Plane-wing view over mountains and a sea of clouds (27.8-29.73s, almost static, motion ~1). Sunset over the airport apron (~31s). Cliffs of Moher in blue water and sky (~35s). Eiffel Tower framed by POV legs (36.27-38.27s, slight handheld drift). Kylemore Abbey (38.27s). Benbulben over the lough (40.53-42.53s), the longest-held static landscape: motion 1.7-2.2 for about 2s, a calm breather. Lantern-lit Tokyo alley at blue hour (42.53s). Chapultepec terrace with the city skyline (57.0s). There are no drone shots; reveals are walk-ins, POV framing or simple holds. No single 'biggest view' climax: the strongest landmark shots are front-loaded in the first 10s to sell credibility.
study.how_place_is_shown: Mostly medium-wide shots with the creator in frame, either from behind walking toward the landmark or facing camera smiling in front of it. That is the classic 'girl in front of landmark' travel-creator look. She is alone in almost every shot; friends appear once in the café mirror. Mixed with POV (lying in Paris, rolling luggage, phone in hand) and pure screen recordings for the Google Maps demo, roughly 10-27.8s. The light varies: golden hour in London, dusk in Kyoto and Tokyo, overcast Ireland, bright Mexico City. Shot handheld or on a phone gimbal, phone-native. Details are chosen to serve each rule: phone screen and list counts for planning, the coffee shop dog and bookstore for the 'local' rule, suitcase brands for packing. The apartment scenes with the suitcase frame the whole video as trip prep.
study.info_and_value:
Five concrete rules, each delivered twice: once by voiceover and once as a short persistent text card at the top.
1. Save places in a Google Maps saved list before the trip, then look at what's nearby on the ground. Proven with real lists and place counts (211, 95, 75).
2. Hours of travel = minimum days at the destination. A memorable formula.
3. Avoid popular destinations May–September, naming Paris, Rome and Amsterdam, and visit nearby small cities instead.
4. Check that accommodation is near a local coffee shop, not chains.
5. Carry-on only, packing neutrals to mix and match. Brands listed: Monos Travel, Nomad Land, Away, Calpak.
The calls to action are 'Let me know if you want any of the maps' (a comment bait and lead magnet) and 'stay tuned for more' (follow). It works as a save-for-later checklist.
study.pacing: 25 detected cuts over 61.9s (3.88 per 10s). Median shot 2.4s, range 1.6-3.53s, but the frames show extra undetected changes inside several shots (2.87-4.93, 4.93-8.27, 8.27-10.67, 29.73-32.73, 32.73-36.27, 44.53-47.93, 51.33-54.8, 57.0-59.4). Real B-roll pace is therefore roughly one new location every ~1.3s in the intro montage. It slows to 2-3s shots in the Google Maps demo, then goes back to ~2s location shots. Cuts land on voiceover phrase boundaries ('Rule number two' at 27.56 vs cut at 27.8; 'Rule four' at 44.54 vs cut at 44.53; 'And rule number five' at 51.32 vs cut at 51.33) rather than musical beats. The voiceover is dense: 285 words in 62s, about 4.6 words per second, with no pauses. That density drives the speed more than the cutting does.
study.speed: none visible. Everything appears to play at normal speed, and the still-looking shots (plane wing ~27-28.5s, Benbulben ~40-42s, ending ~59.5-61s) are simply static framings, not freezes.
study.on_screen_text:
Persistent header cards in white, thin-to-regular TikTok-style sans with a dark shadow and no box. They are centred in the upper third, 2-3 lines and 6-12 words each, and stay up for the whole section until the next rule:
- 0-~10.6s: 'travel rules I live by' (larger, bold), plus '(that will help you plan better trips)' and 🗺️📍✈️🌎. Absent on the 8.27-10.67s Ireland shots.
- 10.67-18.47s: 'Rule #1) save places to visit on Google Maps list BEFORE you get there' (it drops off during the full-screen recordings).
- 27.8-~35s: 'Rule #2) amount of hours flying = amount of days to spend in destination'.
- ~35-44.5s: 'Rule #3) I never travel to popular destinations May-September'.
- 44.53-51.3s: 'Rule #4) Book accommodation near a local coffee shop'.
- 51.33-~54.8s: 'Rule #5) Pack carry-on only!'.
- 54.8-57.0s: 'Favorite brands:' with 'Monos Travel / Nomad Land / Away / Calpak' as a vertical list.
The cards summarize the rule more bluntly than the voiceover does ('I never travel' vs the spoken 'I personally avoid').
study.captions: Present for the entire voiceover. Small white sans with a black shadow, centred in the lower-middle (~65-70% height), in 1-2 line phrase chunks of 3-8 words that change with each phrase. Some contain light rewording or punctuation ('rule #5) … you knew this was coming!').
study.audio: A continuous first-person voiceover from 0.00s to 61.78s, upbeat and conversational, carrying all the information. Any background music sits low under the voice; the strongest audio hits (e.g. 0.46, 3.32, 8.03, 10.22, 13.82, 28.17, 45.64, 57.06) mostly line up with stressed words and rule announcements rather than visual drops. There is no prominent natural sound or sound effects. Rule transitions are marked verbally ('Rule number one/two/three…'), and the picture cuts within about 0.25s of those words.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. Between locations they are straight cuts; across the Google Maps screen recordings, the zoom-ins from the Japan overview to Tokyo pins (20.27-25.07s) are in-app zooms joined by hard cuts. There are no whips, flashes or match cuts. The only clever join is structural: the outro cuts back to the same apartment setup as the opening.
study.effects: No added graphics beyond text. The map zooms are native screen-recording movement, not editor push-ins. The colour is a natural phone look with mildly bright, clean saturation; no heavy grade, light leaks, freeze frames or split screens.
study.quality: Delivered at 576x1024, 29.18 fps, ~1.7 Mbps H.264, so it is compressed and slightly soft. The source footage is clearly modern-phone quality: well exposed skies at Big Ben and the Cliffs of Moher, stable gimbal-like walks, and flattering golden-hour and blue-hour light in London, Kyoto and Tokyo. It looks like a polished creator archive rather than cinematic drone work; the aspiration comes from locations and light, not resolution.
study.ending: The VO ends 'I have so many more specific travel rules, so stay tuned for more' (59.40-61.62s) over the opening apartment shot, with a thumbs-up and her grabbing the suitcase handle. The video cuts at 61.93s, only ~0.3s after the last word. Because the final frame matches the first frame's set, it loops seamlessly into the hook. The ask is to follow, plus the earlier comment ask about the maps.
study.why_viral: 1) An authority-plus-promise hook ('40 countries', 'I promise your next trip will be better') proven within 3s by a landmark montage. 2) Practical, saveable rules, including a quotable formula (hours flying = days) and a contrarian take (skip Paris/Rome/Amsterdam in summer) that sparks debate in comments. 3) A real proof demo (her own Google Maps lists with 211 saved places) plus a 'want my maps?' comment bait that boosts engagement. 4) Constant visual reward: a new iconic location roughly every 1.3-2.5s, so even people skimming the advice get the travel fantasy.
lessons: Start the voiceover at 0.0s with a credential number plus a promise ('after X countries… your next trip will be better') and back it up with your 3-4 most iconic landmark shots inside the first 10s.
For a numbered-tips video, put a persistent 2-3 line header card ('Rule #N) …') in the upper third for the whole section, and cut to the next section within ±0.25s of the spoken 'Rule number N'.
During montage or intro stretches, change location every ~1.2-1.5s; during an explanation or demo, let shots run 2-3s so the viewer can read.
Prove at least one tip with a screen recording or a real artefact (lists, counts, bookings). Specific numbers like '211 places' make the advice feel real and saveable.
Match B-roll loosely but literally to keywords: flight rule → wing/cabin/airport, 'local coffee shop' → café and bookstore, 'carry-on' → rolling-suitcase POV and a brand list.
Add one comment-bait offer mid-video ('let me know if you want my maps') around the 40% mark, and end with a follow ask ('stay tuned for more').
Bookend the video: open and close on the same setup (e.g. packing in the apartment) and cut within ~0.3s of the last word so it loops back into the hook.
Insert one near-static wide landscape held ~2s mid-video as a breather between busy crowd and walking shots.
Run speech captions in 3-8 word chunks in the lower-middle, separate from the topic card up top, so the screen carries both the headline and the line-by-line voiceover.

study.format: Ranked countdown list ('5 best places in Arizona') narrated by a travel creator. It opens with an 8.1s intro montage of the best clips from every location under a contrarian claim ('most underrated state'). It then counts down #5 to #1, with each item opened by the spoken and captioned label 'Number X is [name]', followed by 1–2 sentences of opinion or tip over 2–6 clips. One item (Lake Powell kayak to Antelope Canyon, the implied #2) is never numbered and is delivered as an insider hack instead. The video ends on #1's best reveal shot.
study.place: Arizona and its border red-rock country, as a road-trip and hiking destination. Locations: The Wave / Coyote Buttes (swirled striped sandstone), Lake Powell (cliff jumping, kayaking between white-and-red canyon walls), an Antelope-style slot canyon, Sedona's Subway Cave and Birthing Cave, and Horseshoe Bend at sunset. It looks special because the landscapes look unreal: candy-striped rock, glowing orange slot walls, turquoise water under a hard blue sky, a sunset river bend, and a keyhole cave window framing green valley and red buttes. That backs up the 'another planet' / 'won't believe you're in the U.S.' line.
study.audience: Made by a travel creator (@findingfiona) for young US travelers, hikers and couples planning a Southwest trip. It is built to be saved as a ready-made bucket list, shared or tagged with a travel partner ('we're doing this'), and commented on (people defending their own favorite Arizona spot or asking about the lottery and kayak logistics). It reads as an authentic traveler and creator, not a tourism board: selfie clips, a boyfriend/partner in frame, and personal 'I think you should go' framing.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0–~1s) is a wide of The Wave, a woman in black walking along a sweeping candy-striped sandstone ridge under clouds. A selfie of the creator lounging on red rock follows before the first detected cut at 2.0s. Voiceover starts on the very first frame: 'Arizona is by far the most underrated…'. The caption 'Arizona is by far the MOST underrated state but...' sits in the upper third, with 'MOST' in caps. It stops the scroll on two fronts: the image looks like another planet, and the claim is a debatable opinion that invites agreement or argument. An audio hit at 1.85/2.02s lands on the cut to the Lake Powell cliff-jump clip.

Front POV over the creator's legs on the kayak gliding between cliffs.

Pan inside Birthing Cave from rough red wall to the keyhole-shaped opening framing green valley and red buttes. Held to the end: 'of the most epic views, you won't even believe you're in the US'.

study.choice_format: Ranked countdown, 5 items, counted down from #5 to #1 with the best last. Labels are spoken ('Number five is…') and shown as captions with a hashtag-number style ('#5 is The Wave', '#4 is Subway Cave', '#3 is Horseshoe Bend', '#1 is Birthing Cave'). They use the same white caption font as the rest of the subtitles, upper-center, with no separate title card. The #2 slot is never labelled: Lake Powell/Antelope Canyon by kayak is slipped in as an 'instead of a guide' hack. Each new item cuts within about 0.1–0.3s of the word 'Number' (5: VO 7.84 / cut 8.13; 4: VO 16.22 / cut 16.2; 3: VO 22.06 / cut 22.07; 1: VO 36.32 / cut 36.2). Time per item: #5 8.07s over 6 shots; #4 5.87s over 4 shots; #3 5.93s over 3 shots; implied #2 8.2s over 6 shots; #1 5.7s over 2 shots. The intro runs 8.13s. Items are separated only by hard cuts and the spoken number, with no sound effect. There is no explicit ask to comment or vote; the debatable 'most underrated' and 'best' rankings do that job implicitly.
study.action_shots: 2.0–3.67s (1.67s): cliff jump at Lake Powell, wide from the water, normal speed. The jumper is mid-air around 3.0s, and the shot follows an audio hit at 2.02s. 3.67–~4.3s: walk-away follow through The Wave corridor, handheld or gimbal, normal speed. 7.07–8.13s (1.07s): kayak paddling POV from behind, normal speed. 10.87–12.73s (1.87s): POV of feet stepping across striped rock, looking down. ~13.9–14.8s: woman hiking away across rippled rock, follow from behind. 17.27–19.0s (1.73s): follow shot of the partner on the Sedona trail. This is the highest-motion moment in the video (46.5 at 17.5s), as the camera walks and tilts up to the butte. 28.0–34.47s: a 6.47s run of kayak POVs (behind the paddler, front over the legs, water-level glide past walls, pointing finger, beach landing), with motion 15–25 throughout. 34.47–36.2s: partner walking into the slot canyon. 36.2–38.83s: walking selfie on the trail. All play at normal speed. Cuts in the kayak run land on audio hits (28.12, 29.54, 32.08, 34.23).
study.views: The Wave wide at 0s (about 1s, the opener). Sedona butte wide/aerial ~4.3–6.0s, slow drift. Slot-canyon glow 6.0–7.07s, almost static. Wave amphitheater with a tiny person for scale at 12.73s (~1.2s). Coyote Buttes beehives under storm clouds 14.8–16.2s (1.4s, gentle push or drift). Subway Cave framed by dark rock 16.2–17.27s, near-static at motion 1.4: a silhouette 'window' reveal. Seated cave silhouette 19.0–22.07s, a tripod-still 3s (motion 1.5–5.4), the calmest stretch. Horseshoe Bend 22.07–28.0s at sunset: first with the creator on the rim, then a clean static wide 23.8–25.6s (motion about 3), then a slow pan along the rim 25.6–28.0s (2.4s). Canyon walls from the water 28–34s. The biggest view is saved for the last 3.07s (38.83–41.9), the longest shot in the video: a handheld pan inside Birthing Cave sweeps from the red wall into the keyhole/heart-shaped opening, revealing green valley and distant red buttes. Motion falls to 4.5 at 41.0s as it settles on the framed view under the line 'you won't even believe you're in the US'.
study.how_place_is_shown: About 60% wides or landscapes, 30% medium people shots, and about 10% details (feet on striped rock, a pointing finger, a kayak nose). People are in almost every location: the creator (posing, silhouetted, selfie), her partner walking ahead (a couple's-trip read), and tiny figures for scale in the big wides. The mix of POV (kayak, feet, selfie, finger point) and filmed-by-partner shots makes it feel like 'you could do this'. Light varies by location: harsh midday blue sky and turquoise water at Lake Powell, soft overcast and storm clouds at The Wave, blue-hour silhouettes at Subway Cave, golden sunset at Horseshoe Bend, and an even overcast glow at Birthing Cave. Most clips are handheld phone or gimbal; the silhouettes and the Horseshoe wide are tripod-still, and the Sedona butte looks like drone footage. There are no amenity or food details; the 'details' are rock textures, which prove the colors are real.
study.info_and_value: Delivered entirely by voiceover, mirrored in captions. Place names: The Wave, Subway Cave, Horseshoe Bend, Lake Powell, Antelope Canyon, Birthing Cave. Insider facts: The Wave requires winning a permit lottery ('you do need to win the lottery to hike this'). Subway Cave involves real hiking. Horseshoe Bend is 'the easiest hike you'll do in Arizona'. The money-saving hack is to skip the Antelope Canyon guide and rent a kayak at Lake Powell to paddle there yourself. These are save-worthy logistics (permit, difficulty level, DIY alternative to a paid tour) packed into 42s, plus a numbered itinerary people screenshot for trip planning. No prices or booking links are given.
study.pacing: 25 detected shots in 41.9s, 5.73 cuts per 10s. Median shot 1.53s, range 1.0–3.07s, and at least two extra visual changes (~1s and ~4.3s) that the detector missed in the intro, so the opening montage runs at roughly 1s per clip. Voiceover is fast and constant: 156 words, about 3.7 words/s, starting at 0.00s with almost no gaps. Fast shots (1.0–1.4s) carry action and transit (kayak, trail). Longer holds go to the payoff views: the Horseshoe rim pan at 2.4s, the #1 selfie at 2.63s, and the Birthing Cave reveal at 3.07s. The video gets slower and calmer at the end, with the final two shots the longest. Cuts are driven by speech, falling on 'Number X' and on phrase ends. Many also coincide with audio hits: 2.0/2.02, 25.6/25.58, 28.0/28.12, 29.47/29.54, 36.2/36.28, 38.83/38.85.
study.speed: none (no visible slow motion, ramps or timelapses; all clips appear to play at real speed).
study.on_screen_text: No separate graphic titles. The only overlay is the subtitle line, which doubles as the list labels ('#5 is The Wave', etc.) and carries emphasis words in all caps ('MOST', 'SO', 'EVEN MORE', 'EASIEST'). See captions.
study.captions: Present for the entire video. TikTok-classic sans in white, sentence case with selective ALL-CAPS emphasis words, and a thin dark outline/shadow with no box. Centered in the upper third (about 25–28% from the top), where it stays out of the subject and the sky reveals. Shown in phrase chunks of 3–9 words, one or two lines, each changing about every 1–2s in sync with the VO and often carrying across cuts. Numbers are written as '#5', '#4', '#3', '#1'. The captions correct the mis-heard names ('The Wave', 'Birthing Cave') and slightly paraphrase the speech ('it truly feels that you are').
study.audio: Dominated by the creator's fast, upbeat voiceover from 0.00s to 41.78s, opinionated and conversational. There appears to be a low background music bed (regular audio hits through the video), mixed well under the voice, with no clear beat-drop moments. No sound effects. Little natural sound beyond the selfie and talking clip at 36.2s, where the speech appears to be live to camera rather than VO. Sync is tied to the voice: each 'Number X' lands on or within about 0.3s of a cut, and the final line 'you won't even believe you're in the U.S.' lands exactly on the settled #1 view.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. There are likely two fast hard cuts inside the detected first and third shots: Wave wide to selfie around 1s, and Wave corridor to Sedona butte around 4.3s, which the cut list doesn't register. No whips, zooms or flashes.
study.effects: No zooms, shakes, freeze frames or graphics. The color grade is warm and saturated, pushing the red and orange sandstone, with strong blue skies and turquoise water at Lake Powell, plus a pastel sunset gradient at Horseshoe Bend. Phone HDR keeps the skies from blowing out. The look is consistent across locations so the montage reads as one trip.
study.quality: 576x1022 at 30fps, about 1.6 Mbps H.264: a recompressed, modest-resolution file with some softness and banding in the skies. The source footage is clean modern phone or gimbal capture: steady holds on the views, well-exposed skies with HDR, and rich color. Several shots are deliberately composed (silhouettes in cave openings, tiny figure for scale, rim sunset with the subject). Those compositions make it feel like a dream trip despite the low bitrate; the selfie and walking clips keep it relatable, like a phone snapshot.
study.ending: Ends on the #1 payoff, the Birthing Cave keyhole view: the longest shot at 3.07s, revealed by a pan and settling still at the end. The last word, 'U.S.', ends at 41.56s and the video cuts at 41.9s, only about 0.3s later, with no CTA, outro or text card. The red-rock-to-red-rock bookend (Wave opener, cave closer) and the abrupt end encourage a seamless loop or rewatch.
study.why_viral: 1) The debatable claim on frame one ('Arizona is the MOST underrated state') plus an unreal-looking Wave visual both stops the scroll and invites comments. 2) A numbered countdown with the best saved for last keeps people watching to #1, and #1 is the biggest framed reveal held longest. 3) It is packed with save-worthy insider info (the Wave permit lottery, the easiest hike, kayaking to Antelope Canyon instead of paying for a guide), which turns it into a trip-planning bookmark. 4) A couple or creator in nearly every location shows real people doing it (cliff jumps, kayaking, cave silhouettes), making viewers want to tag a partner and go.
lessons: Start the voiceover at 0.0s with an opinionated claim about the place ('most underrated', 'nobody talks about') and put it as a caption in the upper third over the single most unreal-looking clip.
Open a list video with a 6–8s teaser montage of 1–1.7s clips pulled from every item, including at least one action clip (jump, splash, paddle), before announcing 'here are the X best…'.
Cut to each new list item on the word 'Number' (within 0.1–0.3s) and show the label as '#X is [Name]' in the caption, so the structure is readable with sound off.
Give each item about 6–8s and 2–6 clips: a wide establishing view, a person-in-frame shot for scale, then a POV or detail. Hold the calm view shots 2–3s and keep transit or action clips at 1–1.5s.

Save the best place for #1 and its best shot for last: make it the longest shot (3s or more), revealed by a pan or walk into a framing element (cave mouth, doorway, arch), and end within 0.5s of the final word.
Attach one concrete insider fact to each item (permit or lottery, difficulty, a cheaper DIY alternative to a paid tour). Facts like these make viewers save the video rather than just watch it.
Frame people as silhouettes inside dark openings or as tiny figures in huge landscapes. Shoot these on a tripod or held still (motion near 0) to give the eye a rest between handheld action clips.
Keep one consistent warm and saturated grade across locations shot at different times of day so a multi-stop trip reads as one cohesive dream trip.
Place captions in the upper third with white text and a thin shadow, ALL-CAPS only on 1–2 emphasis words per line, changing every 1–2s with the VO.

study.format: Travel hack 'I tested it' POV vlog / proof video. A creator tells a little-known airline policy (Delta's 20-minute bag guarantee) and documents testing it in order: setting the timer on landing, the flashback to the gate-check, deplaning, the timer hitting 0:00, bags arriving late, the claim form, the 'Thank You' confirmation, and a happy wrap-up selfie. It is built as a problem → rule → test → result → payoff story, with continuous voiceover over handheld phone clips and inserted phone screen recordings.
study.place: A Delta domestic flight and a bright, modern US airport: the plane cabin, the gate's carry-on size check, the jet bridge, a long glossy concourse, and the Bag Claim 6 carousel under a big Delta screen. It ends in a car on a sunny day with desert hills outside. This is not a scenic destination. What makes it special is the insider money-saving angle, not the views.
study.audience: Frequent and casual US flyers, especially Delta/SkyMiles members and people who get forced to gate-check carry-ons. It makes them save it for their next flight, tag or send it to a travel partner ('do this next time'), and comment their own experience. It reads as a relatable traveler/mom creator sharing a hack, not as a brand or agent.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0.0s): a phone held up in front of a Delta seatback screen with the Timers app open, and white overlay text 'Setting a 20 min timer when the plane lands ⏰'. The voiceover starts on frame 0: 'As soon as the boarding door is open, I hit my 20-minute timer.' (0.00–2.54s). It stops the scroll because it is an odd, specific action with no explanation. Viewers wait to learn why. The '20 min' plus the alarm-clock emoji promise a clever trick.

beats.what: Phone in front of the seatback screen; finger sets a timer (19:59 visible at ~1.5s); text 'Setting a 20 min timer when the plane lands ⏰'; VO starts on the first word.
Cabin aisle shot of passengers standing up to deplane: the 'boarding door is open' moment.

Flashback to the gate: an agent tags a red carry-on at the 'CARRY-ON SIZE CHECK' sizer. Three quick shots (cuts 2.93, 3.6) while VO says 'we did end up having to check our carry-ons on our recent Delta flight.'
Jet bridge: red, pink and purple suitcases being left at the plane door next to a Delta bin.
VO lays out the rule: 'if bags don't arrive within 20 minutes, you're entitled to 2,500 points' (6.20–11.50), over the deplaning clips.
POV feet walking out of the aircraft door onto the jet bridge.
Low-angle selfie walking through the terminal with a smiling companion, ending in an in-camera whip pan (~10.0s) to a wide of the glossy concourse.
Screen recording of the lock-screen timer counting 0:02 → 0:01 → 0:00 while VO says 'And today I wanted to test that.' The screen darkens as the cut arrives at 12.9.
Tilt-up to the 'BAG CLAIM 6' board beside a big DELTA logo. VO: 'The timer actually did go off and the bags still weren't there.'
Longest shot (6.37s): companion pulls suitcases off the carousel, then the creator kneels over a navy bag holding the tag. VO: 'They did show up a few minutes later. So on our drive home…'
Screen recording of the delta.com claim form (name, SkyMiles #, departure date 01/28/2025, terms mentioning 2,500 bonus miles). VO: 'easily submitted this form within 2 minutes.'
Quick 0.67s shot of the red SUBMIT button.
Delta 'THANK YOU' page: 'your submitted claim was successful and miles have been posted'. VO: 'and was immediately awarded 2,500 points.'
Car selfie, grinning with her chin on her hand, sunny desert hills outside. VO: 'That is definitely the easiest points that I've scored.'

study.action_shots: 1) 1.77–~2.4s: cabin aisle of people standing up, handheld medium-wide, normal speed. 2) ~2.5–4.6s: the gate agent pulling a tag strip and wrapping the red bag. Three handheld close shots (0.4–1.0s each), normal speed, motion 17–25. 3) 6.53–8.0s: POV walk out the aircraft door, camera pointed at her feet, normal speed (motion ~22–37). 4) 8.0–~10.0s: walking selfie with the friend, low angle, then a fast whip pan at ~9.5–10.0s (the motion peak of the video, 48.3/41.7) that lands on the concourse wide by 10.7s. 5) 13.9–20.27s: carousel bag-grabbing, handheld wide-medium follow, normal speed, motion 9–21. None of these are cut to a beat drop. They are cut to the voiceover sentences: the gate shots sit under 'check our carry-ons', and the deplaning walk sits under the policy line.
study.views: No beauty views in the usual sense. The 'reveal' moments are functional. There is a concourse wide at ~10.2–11.0s, revealed by the whip pan off the selfie and held about 0.8s. There is a tilt-up reveal of the BAG CLAIM 6 board and DELTA screen at 12.9–13.9s, held 1.0s. The only scenic touch is the sunny window with desert hills behind her in the final car selfie, 24.27–25.7s (1.43s). The biggest 'view' is really the proof shot, the Delta THANK YOU confirmation at 22.87–24.27s.
study.how_place_is_shown: Everything is handheld iPhone. There is no gimbal and no drone. The mix: POV and close details for the gate tag, timer and feet; mediums for the carousel; one wide of the concourse; and two front-camera selfies (terminal and car) that put the creator's face in. People are in almost every shot (gate agent, travel companion, creator), which keeps it human and relatable. The light is even, bright, cool airport fluorescent and daylight, with warm sun in the car at the end. Details are chosen as evidence, not decoration: the timer app, the luggage tag, the 'CARRY-ON SIZE CHECK' sign, the Delta bin, the bag claim board, the countdown hitting 0:00, the form, the SUBMIT button and the confirmation page. They prove each step of the claim.
study.info_and_value: All of it is delivered by voiceover, backed by screen recordings. The facts: Delta has a policy that if checked bags don't reach the carousel within 20 minutes, you're entitled to 2,500 points. The tip is to start a 20-minute timer when the boarding door opens. Gate-checked carry-ons qualify in her case. You submit a form on delta.com, which she says took 2 minutes from the car. Points were 'immediately awarded'. The on-screen form terms add that you must be a SkyMiles member and file within three days of the flight, but these are readable only by pausing. The value is concrete (a number of points), easy to repeat, and proven with receipts. That drives saves ('do this next flight') and shares to travel partners.
study.pacing: 14 shots in 25.7s, 5.06 cuts per 10s, median shot 1.45s, shortest 0.67s, longest 6.37s. The first 8s are fast: 6 cuts plus one undetected cut around 2.5s. Shots run 0.67–1.93s while the setup and flashback are explained. Mid-video it slows: the 3.0s walk and selfie, the 1.9s timer countdown with motion near 0 at 11.5–12.0s (a deliberate still hold so the 0:00 lands), then the 6.37s carousel hold while the VO tells the outcome. The proof section speeds back up: 1.93s form, 0.67s SUBMIT, 1.4s THANK YOU, then a 1.43s end selfie. Cuts follow the VO sentence breaks, not the music. For example, the cut at 11.0 lands just before 'And today' (11.66), the cut at 12.9 lands right on 'The timer' (12.94), and the cut at 20.27 comes just before 'this form'.
study.on_screen_text: One overlay only: 'Setting a 20 min timer when the plane lands ⏰'. It is white sans-serif in regular weight and sentence case, with a soft drop shadow and no box, set as two centered lines in the upper-middle of the frame (about 18–21% down). It shows 0.0s to ~6.5s (gone at the cut to the jet-bridge walk), 9 words plus the alarm-clock emoji. After that there is no text. The screen recordings (timer 0:00, form, THANK YOU) do the job of text.
study.audio: A continuous first-person voiceover from 0.00 to 25.32s, 114 words, starting on the very first frame with no music intro. It is calm and conversational. Under it, the audio hits recur roughly every 0.6s from ~12.4–16.1s (12.43, 13.06, 13.69, 14.36, 14.97, 15.43, 16.1), which suggests a quiet rhythmic music bed. It sits well under the voice, and picture cuts aren't synced to it. There are no obvious sound effects. The countdown screen recording plays silently under 'And today I wanted to test that', so the 0:00 lands on the VO's 'The timer actually did go off'.
study.transitions: Mostly hard cuts: 1.77 seat→aisle, ~2.5 aisle→gate, 2.93 and 3.6 gate jump cuts, 4.6 gate→jet bridge, 6.53 jet bridge→door POV (near match cut, as both frames show the same door threshold and feet), 8.0 jet bridge→terminal selfie, 11.0 concourse→lock-screen recording, 13.9 board→carousel, 20.27 carousel→form recording, 22.2 and 22.87 jump cuts within the screen recordings, and 24.27 THANK YOU→car selfie. There is one in-camera whip pan at ~9.5–10.0s from the selfie to the concourse. At 12.9 the lock screen visibly darkens/dims just before cutting to the bag claim board, which reads as a quick fade or dip out of the timer.
study.effects: The screen recordings (lock-screen timer, delta.com form, THANK YOU page) are scaled down slightly and placed over a blurred, stretched copy of themselves, so blurred edges fill the 9:16 frame. The THANK YOU page slides sideways between 22.95 and 24.17s, which looks like her horizontal scroll or a slow pan rather than an added zoom. There is a dim/darken on the timer screen right before 12.9. No color grade, light leaks, freeze frames, maps or graphics; it is natural phone color.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, h264, ~1.1 Mbps. That is low resolution and bitrate, so the footage is a little soft, with some blown highlights on the windows and ceiling lights. It is all handheld and shaky in the walking shots. It looks like a phone snapshot on purpose, and that authenticity is the point: it reads as a real traveler's receipts, not an ad. The crisp screen recordings in the second half add credibility where it matters.
study.ending: The proof beat (THANK YOU page, 22.87–24.27s) is followed by a 1.43s car selfie where she grins with her chin on her hand, and the VO closer 'That is definitely the easiest points that I've scored'. The last word lands at 25.02s and the video cuts about 0.7s later at 25.7s. There is no spoken or written CTA to save or comment. The satisfied face is the CTA. It loosely loops: the end (driving home, done) leads back into the start (setting the timer on the plane).
study.why_viral: 1) A specific, money-like reward anyone can claim (2,500 Delta points for a 20-minute bag delay) that most travelers don't know about, so people save it and send it to whoever they fly with. 2) A self-contained test story with a ticking clock: the timer hitting 0:00 while the bags still aren't there is a mini twist. 3) Receipts at every step (timer, tag, carousel, form, confirmation page) make it believable and easy to copy. 4) A curiosity hook in the first second: an odd action stated as fact before it's explained.
lessons: Start the voiceover on frame 0 with the strange action, not the explanation ('I hit my 20-minute timer'), and back it with a one-line text overlay of the same action for sound-off viewers; keep that overlay up through the first ~6s.
Structure hack videos as setup → rule → test → result → proof; put the rule with its exact number (2,500 points, 20 minutes) before 12s so people know what they're watching for.
Cut on voiceover sentence breaks: 0.6–2s shots during the setup, then hold a 5–6s shot under the result while the story resolves.
Insert screen recordings as proof (countdown hitting 0:00, the claim form, the confirmation page) and scale them over a blurred copy of themselves to fill the 9:16 frame.
Hold a near-still 1.5–2s shot on the key number moment (timer 0:02 → 0:00) so the twist lands before cutting on the next line.
Use an in-camera whip pan or POV walk to move between locations (plane → terminal) instead of adding edit transitions; it keeps raw phone footage feeling continuous.
End within about 1s of the last word, on a satisfied face, with no dead air.
Show only details that prove the claim (tag, sign, carousel board, submit button); every cutaway should make the tip more believable and repeatable.

study.format: Creator resort-recommendation montage built on a 'deal hook + it's not X, not Y… it's Z' twist. A scripted voiceover (94 words in 23.3s, about 4 words/s, starting at 0.00s) carries everything. A price question hook (0–3.1s) leads into the name and location (3.2–4.9s), then the price ($200/night, 5.0–7.8s). A 'what makes it incredible is NOT…' rundown follows, where each feature (rooms, dining, tubing, shows, beach, price) gets roughly one sentence fragment and one to two clips (7.9–16.6s). The emotional twist, 'it's the people who work here' (16.7–20.0s), plays over a run of waving and smiling staff. It closes on a 'save this video' CTA over a sunset (20.0–23.3s). Every voiceover phrase is matched to B-roll that literally illustrates it.
study.place: SeaGarden Beach Resort, Montego Bay, Jamaica. It is an all-inclusive Caribbean beach resort sold as 'affordable luxury'. What makes it look special: an iconic thatched-roof gazebo with red curtains standing on a rock in shallow turquoise water, a private terrace with loungers over the sea, castle-crenellated walls, tropical gardens with a fountain, and white colonial-style buildings with palms. Activities shown include snorkeling, tubing, catamaran cruising and cultural dance shows at night. A plane landing over the turquoise sea signals 'just a flight away'.
study.audience: Budget-conscious couples, friend groups and families who want a Caribbean all-inclusive but assume it costs too much. It reads as an authentic traveler/creator (two girlfriends filming selfies, reacting, sipping a coconut), not the resort itself, which makes the price claim and the 'hospitable staff' claim more believable. The main intent is to save for later (explicit 'SAVE' CTA). Secondary intents are to tag a travel partner and to look up the resort by name.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0.0s) is a postcard wide: a palm frond framing the left edge, a thatched gazebo on a rock in clear turquoise shallows, pale sand and a deep blue sky. Voiceover starts on the very first frame with 'Want a luxury, all-inclusive…', and a centered white text line reads 'Want a luxury all inclusive'. Within about 1.9s it flashes through two more postcard clips: a woman in a white crochet dress with a straw bag walking along a dock above bright aqua water (~0.9s), then a jet coming in low over turquoise sea (~1.5s) under the text 'Caribbean vacation that won't break the bank???'. It stops the scroll because it is a direct yes/no question that names a desire (luxury) and an objection (price) at once, over three of the most saturated turquoise images in the video, with no silent lead-in.

study.views: 1) 0.0s: opening gazebo postcard wide, about 0.6s, near-static, with a palm frond as a foreground frame. 2) 1.5s: plane-over-turquoise wide. 3) 2.73–3.43s: the strongest reveal. A door swings open from inside, showing a sliver of turquoise, then the camera steps out to a full terrace with loungers and an unbroken sea horizon (a door plus walk-out reveal in 0.7s). 4) 4.13–4.83s: high wide over the castle walls, gazebo and bay, 0.7s, slight drift. 5) 9.0–9.67s: curtains flung open to bright light (an interior reveal). 6) 14.47–15.2s: the gazebo postcard returns, 0.73s, static, with a bird crossing. 7) 18.33s: sunset sky with pink clouds behind the crew. 8) 22.03–23.27s: the biggest and longest-held view, an orange sun disc through palm silhouettes over the sea, held 1.24s near-static (motion drops to 14.1 and then 11.0). It is the only warm-orange frame in the video and lands on the final words 'luxury vacation'. No drone footage is evident; the high wides look like they were shot from a building.
study.how_place_is_shown: About 40% wides/establishing shots, 45% people mediums (selfies, staff, guests), and 15% details (the sign, fruit tray, soup, coconut). People are in frame in most shots: the two girlfriend creators (selfie POV, filmed walks, a reaction), then staff and other guests (couples, a young pair of guys), which proves the 'people' payoff. The first half is mostly bright daytime with saturated blue sky and turquoise water. The night dance show and the dinner/soup shots add variety. The ending shifts to golden/orange sunset. Footage is a handheld/gimbal phone mix plus an underwater action cam. Details are chosen to prove claims: the sign proves the name, the 'ASSORTED FRUITS' tray and the 'enjoy' soup prove unlimited dining, and the coconut and catamaran drink sell the lifestyle.
study.info_and_value: Facts are given by voiceover and mirrored in on-screen text. Resort name: SeaGarden (Beach) Resort, also shown on the gazebo sign at 3.43s. Location: Montego Bay. Type: luxury all-inclusive. Price: rooms for two under $200 a night. Included and nearby: unlimited dining options, tubing, cultural shows, beach, and catamaran/boat outings. Selling point: very hospitable staff. Booking details and dates are not given. The concrete, searchable name plus a price anchor under $200 for an all-inclusive makes it worth saving as a reference. The explicit 'you need to SAVE this video' plus the 'affordable luxury' framing turns it into a bookmark.
study.pacing: 25 detected shots in 23.3s (10.3 cuts per 10s, median 0.73s, shortest 0.67s, longest 1.9s). Several detected shots actually contain two to three clips (0–1.9s holds three postcards; 6.93–8.3s, 15.87–17.3s, 17.3–18.33s and 20.37–22.03s each change scene inside). The real clip rate is therefore roughly one every 0.6–0.7s. The rhythm is a near-metronomic 0.7s grid from 2.73 to 6.93s and again 8.3–12.63s. The only holds are the final sunset (1.24s) and the dance show (1.1s). Cuts follow the voiceover phrase changes more than the music. Some land on audio hits (1.9≈2.0, 5.53≈5.56, 6.93≈6.83, 8.3≈8.46, 18.33≈18.26, 20.37≈20.47). Median motion is 18.9 and fairly constant; the only dip is at the end.
study.speed: none clearly visible; all clips appear to play at normal speed. The sunset ending is a near-static hold, not slow motion.
study.on_screen_text: The voiceover script is broken into phrase-sized text overlays. They use a thin regular white sans (TikTok default style), mostly lowercase sentence case, with no box and only a faint shadow. The text is centered horizontally at about mid-frame (y≈50%) and wraps to 1–2 lines of 2–6 words. Sequence: 'Want a luxury all inclusive' (0–~1.4s); 'Caribbean vacation that won't break the bank???' (~1.4–3.4s); 'this is SeaGarden Resort in Montego Bay' (3.4–5.2s); 'you can find rooms here for two people' (~5.2–6.2s); 'for less than $200 a night' (6.2–8.0s); 'what makes this place incredible'; 'is not the luxury rooms'; 'for the unlimited dining options'; 'or tubing'; 'or the cultural shows'; 'it's not even the breathtaking beach'; 'or insane price tag'; 'it's the people who work here'; 'this is one of the most hospitable places'; 'I've ever stayed and'; 'you need to SAVE this video'; 'for your next affordable'; 'luxury vacation' (22.0–23.3s). Emphasis comes only from the triple '???' and the capitalized 'SAVE'. There are no emoji.
study.captions: The overlay text above effectively serves as the speech captions. It is a manually placed, phrase-by-phrase transcription of the voiceover in the same white thin sans at mid-frame, switching on each phrase boundary (about every 1–2.5s). It is not word-by-word highlighted.
study.audio: A continuous voiceover from 0.00s to 22.98s with almost no pauses (gaps under 0.15s) drives the edit. It is fast, conversational and confident, with deliberate rhythmic list cadence ('or… or… or…') and a pause-free pivot into 'It's the people who work here' at 16.68s. A music bed under it produces regular hits (0.52, 2.0, 4.03, 4.51, 5.56, 5.92, 6.6, 6.83, 8.16, 8.46, 11.53, 12.16, 13.16, 14.02, 15.02, 15.69, 16.08, 16.24, 18.26, 18.44, 19.01, 19.53, 19.76, 20.47, 21.69). Several cuts sit within 0.1s of a hit (1.9, 5.53, 6.93, 18.33, 20.37), and the tubing and catamaran motion peaks line up with the 12.16 and 14.02 hits. No natural sound or SFX is clearly featured; the VO dominates.
study.transitions: Hard cuts throughout. The door-open at 2.73s works as an in-camera reveal (the door acts as a wipe into the terrace view) but is still joined by a hard cut. The curtain throw at 9.0s is an in-shot reveal. The jump from the buffet guests to the sunset at 22.03s is a hard cut with the biggest frame change (motion 45.3 at 22.0s). No whips, zooms or flashes are visible.
study.effects: Strong saturation and blue/turquoise boost on daytime clips, with skies near pure cyan-blue and water glowing aqua (especially 0.0–4.8s and 13.7–15.2s). The sunset is pushed deep orange with crushed black silhouettes. There are no zooms, shakes, freeze frames, split screens or graphics.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, h264 at about 1.8 Mbps, so modest resolution and visible compression in the dark night and sunset shots. Daytime footage still reads as dreamy because of bright exposure, stabilized phone/gimbal movement, clean horizons and the heavy turquoise grade. Selfie clips are intentionally phone-snapshot (fisheye arm-length, wobble) and add authenticity rather than polish. The mix says 'real guest' while the postcard wides say 'dream trip'.
study.ending: The last spoken line 'save this video for your next affordable luxury vacation' runs 20.02–22.98s. The final clip (22.03s) is a sunset through palms carrying the text 'luxury vacation', held 1.24s, and the video cuts about 0.3s after the last word. The open-sun-over-the-sea frame visually rhymes with the opening beach postcard, so it loops smoothly back to the turquoise gazebo and the question 'Want a luxury all-inclusive…'.
study.why_viral: 1) The hook names a universal desire and the main objection in one question ('luxury all-inclusive… won't break the bank???'), then answers it with a hard, searchable fact (SeaGarden, Montego Bay, under $200/night) within 7.8 seconds. 2) The 'it's not X, not Y, not even Z… it's the people' list builds suspense over 9 seconds and lands on an emotional, unexpected payoff. Real staff dancing, waving and grinning make it warm and shareable, and it differentiates the resort from every other turquoise-water video. 3) Relentless 0.6–0.7s clips that literally illustrate each spoken word (tubing → tubing clip, soup → soup) pack about 30 scenes into 23s, so viewers rewatch and feel they have toured the whole resort. 4) The explicit 'SAVE this video' CTA, tied to 'affordable luxury', converts a pleasant watch into a bookmark.
lessons: Open with a yes/no question that pairs a desire with an objection (e.g. 'luxury… that won't break the bank???') over your single most saturated postcard shot, with voice and text starting at 0.0s.
Say the place name and a concrete price within the first 8s (here name at 3.2s, '$200 a night' at 6.8s), and cut to the property's sign on screen when the name is spoken.
Match B-roll literally to each spoken noun: when the VO says 'tubing', show tubing; 'dining', show a labelled buffet tray. Give each item 0.7s and one to two clips.
Use a 'not X, not Y, not even Z… it's ___' list to build anticipation for 8–10s, then reveal an emotional differentiator (people, service, a story) and back it with 4–6 quick clips of real faces.
Cut on a steady 0.65–0.75s grid for list sections, and reserve the only long holds (1.1–1.3s) for the final hero view.
Put in-camera reveals (a door swinging open onto the sea, curtains thrown open) in the first 10s. They act as transitions and deliver a view payoff in under 0.7s.
Mix about 60% filmed or selfie shots of people with about 40% empty postcard wides, so the video feels like an authentic guest experience but still sells the dream.
End on the warmest, most different-looking frame (sunset) with the last CTA words on screen, cutting about 0.3s after the final word so it loops back to the opening view.
Keep text overlays at 2–6 words, centered mid-frame, switching on each VO phrase, and capitalize only the action word ('SAVE').

study.format: Travel hack / quick tutorial. It is built as a scenic 'proof I'm traveling' selfie hook (3.73s), then a 10.7s iPhone screen recording. The recording shows the hack step by step: open Calculator, long-press to the Convert toggle, pick currency, search 'Mex' for Mexican Peso, type a local price and see the USD equivalent. It is a one-tip 'things you didn't know' format with no voiceover. The screen itself does the explaining.
study.place: A jungle swimming hole or cenote-style lagoon with vivid turquoise-green water, vine-covered rock walls, a limestone ledge and bright midday sun. The later switch to MXN (Mexican Peso) implies Mexico, likely a cenote/river trip. The place itself isn't named. The scenery is only a backdrop to prove the creator is abroad and to make the hack feel needed.
study.audience: Travelers heading abroad, especially Americans going to Mexico or Europe, who struggle with mental currency math. It's made to be saved ('travel hack I'll never forget again'), sent to a travel buddy, and commented on ('I didn't know this!'). It reads as a traveler/creator sharing a personal discovery, not a brand or agent.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0.0s): the creator's selfie in a neon-yellow life vest, filling the lower half, with glowing turquoise lagoon water and a vine-draped cliff behind. A white two-line caption reads 'The ONE travel hack I'll never forget again!!'. The first sound is the lyric 'Somebody's watching' (0.00–1.18s). It stops the scroll three ways: the saturated turquoise water reads as instant vacation envy, 'ONE travel hack' promises a fast and useful payoff, and the lyric adds playful intrigue. Within the first 1.5s the camera already swings off her face toward the water, so the frame is moving and not a static talking head.

beats.what: Selfie at turquoise jungle lagoon with headline text 'The ONE travel hack I'll never forget again!!'; lyric 'Somebody's watching'.
Camera pans off the creator onto the open lagoon: limestone ledge, green water, vines, swimmers far right by 3.3s.
Hard cut (on audio hit at 3.72) to iPhone screen recording: Calculator opens from black.
Calculator shows a trip-budget sum 4,320.48−873.43 = 3,447.05.
Long-press on calculator icon reveals menu: Basic / Scientific / Math Notes / Convert toggle (lands on audio hits 5.31–5.77).
Convert on: 3,447.05 USD = 3,185.76 EUR appears instantly.
Value cleared to 0 USD / 0.00 EUR, ready to change currency.
Cut to currency list (Currency tab, Euro checked, Yahoo Finance rates).
Search field typed 'M'… 'Mex' → Mexican Peso MXN.
Cut to converter now USD ⇄ MXN at 0; swap so MXN is the input (~12.3s).
Types 800 MXN → 39.49 USD shown; held to the end.

study.action_shots: Only one physical-motion shot: 0–3.73s, handheld selfie/POV. It starts on the creator's face and swings right/down across the lagoon (motion 34–45 the whole shot), at normal speed. It ends on a cut at 3.73 that lines up with the audio hit at 3.72. Everything else is screen-recording 'action': taps, a long-press menu at ~5.1–5.7 synced to hits at 5.31/5.58/5.77, list scroll at ~8.5 (motion 12.0), search typing ~9.5–10.5 (motion 7.8–10.3), and the number entry at ~13.5.
study.views: One view only: the turquoise lagoon, 0–3.73s (3.73s total). It is revealed by a handheld pan away from the selfie. By ~2.1s the creator has left frame, and the lagoon fills the screen with the vine wall top and limestone ledge bottom. Swimmers appear in the distance at ~3.3s. There is no drone, sunset or room view. The biggest (and only) view lands in the first 4 seconds as the hook, not as a payoff.
study.how_place_is_shown: Filmed by the creator handheld on a phone at bright midday. The water is a strong blue-green, with sunlit leaves and harsh light on the rock ledge. The creator is in frame for ~1.5s (face, braids, yellow life vest that signals an excursion). The rest is a wide of the water. No food, drinks or amenity details. After 3.73s the 'place' is entirely the iPhone UI: a dark-mode calculator with orange buttons and a visible touch-indicator dot so viewers can follow each tap.
study.info_and_value: The hack: the iPhone Calculator has a built-in currency converter. Long-press the calculator icon (bottom-left) → toggle Convert → tap the currency label → Currency tab → search (e.g., 'Mex') → Mexican Peso, then type a local price. Concrete example numbers: 3,447.05 USD = 3,185.76 EUR; 800 MXN = 39.49 USD. Rates are shown as Yahoo Finance–sourced. Everything is taught visually with no text or voiceover, so viewers save it to replay the steps later and share it with travel companions.
study.pacing: 4 shots in 14.4s (2.08 cuts per 10s; shots 3.73 / 4.87 / 2.13 / 3.7s; median 3.71s). The opening 3.73s is high-motion (34–45). After the first cut, motion drops to near zero (median 0.9) with small spikes only at taps and scrolls (12.0 at ~8.5s, 7.8 at ~9.5s, 10.3 at ~10.5s). The dead time in the screen recording was trimmed into three jumps: after the clear at 8.6, after 'Mex' at 10.73, and a held final result. The first cut sits on an audio hit (3.72). The later cuts (8.6, 10.73) fall near hits at 8.83 and 11.16 but not exactly on them.
study.on_screen_text: One overlay: 'The ONE travel hack I'll never forget again!!' (9 words). It is white sentence case with 'ONE' capitalized for emphasis, a medium-bold TikTok classic font, a soft dark shadow and no box. It sits center-upper, over the vine wall, on two lines. It is on screen from 0.0s until the cut at 3.73s and is gone for the screen recording. No emoji.
study.audio: A trending song clip whose first audible lyric is 'Somebody's watching' (0.00–1.18). There is no voiceover and no natural lagoon sound. Strongest hits are at 2.79, 3.72, 5.31, 5.58, 5.77, 6.97, 7.9, 8.83, 9.04, 9.3, 11.16 and 11.84. The cut from scenery to the calculator lands on the 3.72 hit. The cluster at 5.31–5.77 roughly coincides with the hidden Convert menu popping open, the 'secret' moment.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. At 3.73 the selfie clip ends on a brief iPhone home-screen frame, then cuts to the Calculator launching from black. At 8.6 it goes from the cleared converter to the currency list (jump cut within the screen recording), and at 10.73 from the search result 'Mexican Peso' to the converter set to MXN (jump cut).
study.effects: none: no zooms, grade or graphics added. The iOS screen-record touch indicator (grey dot) serves as a natural pointer.
study.quality: 576x1024, 30fps, h264 at ~949 kbps: a modest, compressed phone upload. The lagoon footage is bright and saturated thanks to midday sun on turquoise water, but it is shaky, handheld and partly blocked by the creator's face. The screen recording is crisp and readable with large numerals. The video looks like an authentic phone snapshot, not a dream-trip production, and that fits a 'real traveler tip' credibility.
study.ending: Ends on the payoff: 800 MXN = 39.49 USD, typed at ~13.5s and held still ~0.9s until 14.43. There is no CTA, text or voiceover. The abrupt end loops straight back to the turquoise lagoon and headline, which encourages a rewatch to catch the long-press step.
study.why_viral: 1) A universally useful, low-effort hidden feature that most iPhone travelers don't know. It is highly saveable and shareable to travel partners. 2) The hook pairs vacation-envy turquoise water with a clear value promise ('The ONE travel hack'), so you get both escapism and utility in 3.7s. 3) Silent screen-recording steps with real numbers (800 MXN → $39.49) are easy to follow and prompt rewatches and saves. 4) The short 14s runtime with an abrupt end on the answer drives loops.
lessons: For tip/hack videos, open with the most beautiful 3–4s clip from the trip (water, view) plus a value headline; cut to the tutorial on a music hit (here 3.72s).
Keep the headline to about 9 words, white with a shadow in the upper third, and capitalize one key word ('ONE') for emphasis. Remove it once the demo starts.
Screen recordings: show taps with the touch indicator and trim dead time into 2–5s jump cuts (here 4.87s, 2.13s, 3.7s) so the steps never stall.
Use concrete, locally relevant numbers in the demo (a real local price like 800 MXN → $39.49), not abstract examples. Real prices drive saves.
Line up the 'secret reveal' moment (hidden menu, toggle) with a cluster of audio hits so the payoff feels punchy.
End on the result held about 1s, with no outro, so the video loops back to the scenic hook and gets rewatched.
Keep a utility video under 15s; one tip, one example, then done.
Let the creator appear for only ~1.5s, then pan to the view. A face adds trust, and the scenery adds desire.

study.format: Cruise ship tour in the '[ship] in 60 seconds' format. It is a fast neighborhood-by-neighborhood walk-through with continuous voiceover. Each named area (Pearl, Royal Promenade, AquaDome, Thrill Island, Central Park, Surfside, pools, Royal Theater, Absolute Zero) gets 1–3 shots and one superlative or fact. It ends with a question and a follow CTA. It works like a list, but there are no on-screen numbers. Structure comes from spoken signposts: 'As soon as you board', 'Up front', 'Now we're at', 'Next up', 'Families, this one's for you', 'Finish your day'.
study.place: Royal Caribbean's Icon of the Seas, billed as the biggest cruise ship in the world. The stern reads NASSAU, and it is shown docked with the Miami skyline and Biscayne Bay visible. It's a mega-ship cruise vacation. It looks special because the ship plays like a floating theme park/city. The visuals stack up: neon-pink and purple interiors (the Pearl sculpture, the Royal Promenade); a giant glass AquaDome with ocean views; candy-colored water slides on Thrill Island; a real tree-lined Central Park open to the sky; a pastel Surfside family zone with a carousel; a suspended infinity pool; and an ice arena with a rainbow-lit rink.
study.audience: Made for cruise-curious travelers, Royal Caribbean fans and families weighing the ship. It reads as a cruise creator (thecruisevibe_ style first-person 'come with me', 'that had such good food'), not the cruise line, even though the opening drone shot looks polished/official. It makes people save it as a ship overview, tag a partner or family ('families, this one's for you'), comment whether they've sailed ('Have you cruised on board the Icon of the Seas?'), and follow for the series.
study.hook: Frame 1 is a bright, high-angle drone shot of the ship's stern: water slides, the pool deck, the arch and the 'Icon of the Seas / Nassau' lettering, with blue sky and blue water. A two-line white all-caps title 'ICON OF THE SEAS IN 60 SECONDS' sits mid-frame. The voiceover starts at 0.00s: 'Come with me on a one-minute tour of the biggest cruise ship in the world.' It stops the scroll for three reasons. The giant colorful ship is an instant 'wow' wide. The time promise (60 seconds) makes it feel low-commitment. And the superlative 'biggest cruise ship in the world' lands by 3.0s.

beats.what: Drone aerial of the stern and top decks with the title 'ICON OF THE SEAS IN 60 SECONDS'; VO: 'one-minute tour of the biggest cruise ship in the world'.
