study.choice_format: not a choice video. The only question is the yes/no hook ('did this luxury cruise line change your mind?') and the closing comment prompt ('would you give this kind of cruise a try?').
study.action_shots: There is very little real action. It is a lifestyle and amenity reel. Motion moments: 4.8-7.07s, a cheese-pull reaction, filmed medium and static, with low motion (3-5) so the face reads. 17.6-18.47s, a 0.87s walk along the jogging track filmed from behind/above, with the couple's shadows as the subject. 23.13-23.93s, a dancers' stage show, 0.8s wide from the audience. 23.93-24.87s, a smoke cloche reveal, close and 0.93s, with smoke as the 'action'. 31.13-35.07s, a handheld walk around the pool deck. 35.07-39.53s, a POV walk with feet in frame on the curving track that tilts up to the wake; motion climbs from about 27 to a peak of 47 around 37.5-38.5s, the most kinetic moment of the video. All of it plays at normal speed. Nothing is cut to a beat drop, because the edit follows the voiceover phrasing.
study.views: 0-2.73s: the opening sunrise from the balcony, a slow push-in toward the sun (motion 12-16), held the full 2.73s. It is the hook view. 2.73s: island and turquoise water off the balcony rail (0.87s). 15.07-16.73s: the gym facing deep-blue sea. 18.47s: the night pool lit electric blue with the cinema screen (0.87s). 21.0s: binoculars over open sea with the wake visible below (0.87s). 21.87s: mountains through the balcony door behind breakfast. 28.67-31.13s: the sunset terrace with the sun on the horizon and a reflection path on the water, a slow push-in held 2.47s, revealed by a straight cut. 31.13-35.07s: a pool-deck walk-around, 3.93s, revealed by handheld pan. 35.07-39.53s: the biggest view lands here, near the end. It is a walk-out along the track, then a tilt-up revealing the open Mediterranean and white wake stretching to the horizon, held 4.47s, the longest shot in the video. 39.53-41.43s: a doorway-framed reveal of the balcony and sea, with a dark door frame and curtain as a frame within the frame, nearly static (motion about 1). So the bookends are the two calmest balcony-over-sea shots, and the longest, widest shots are saved for the last 12 seconds.
study.how_place_is_shown: Roughly 40% details (whisky cart, cocktails, logo, pastries, Dyson, binoculars, cloche, towel swans), 40% mediums (tables, rooms, people), and 20% wides (lobby bar, night pool, sunset, pool deck, stern). People are in about 7 shots: the creator (soup reaction, cocktail, reading on the balcony), the husband (balcony daybed), the couple in robes, the couple's shadows on the track, and the show audience. This keeps it human and couple-oriented. Most of it is filmed by them; there is a POV feel in the walks (feet and shadows in frame). The light mix moves from sunrise gold at the open, to midday hard blue sky and deep-blue water, to warm tungsten interiors at night, to an electric-blue pool at night, to sunset gold, and back to soft daylight blue. Most shots are handheld phone, some gimbal-smooth, with no drone; the ship's own height stands in for aerials at the stern. The details are chosen as luxury signals people recognize instantly: the Dyson, champagne bucket, Japanese whisky, art, towel swans and the smoke cloche read as 'boutique hotel', not 'cruise buffet'. That directly supports the non-cruiser pitch.
study.info_and_value: All of it is delivered by voiceover, mirrored in word captions; there are no info graphics. Facts: the brand name 'Explora Journeys', said 3 times at 3.18s, 11.84-15.48s and 22.78s, plus the 'EXPLORA II' logo shot at 13.93s; positioning as a 'luxury hotel at sea'; the cruise benefit 'see the world and only have to unpack once'; the route 'started in Athens and ended in Venice'; 'three different countries'; a standout perk, '24-hour in-suite dining'; 'our very own private terrace'; and 'best ways to view the sunset and sunrise'. There are no prices, inclusions list, or booking info. The save/share value is mostly the brand name plus a dream picture to send a partner, and the qualifier 'if you're someone who loves boutique luxury hotels, exceptional food, and exploring new destinations' lets viewers self-identify and tag someone.
study.pacing: 41.4s total, 25 shots, 5.79 cuts per 10s, median shot 1.27s, shortest 0.8s, longest 4.47s. It has three tempos. Hook and early tour (0-11.27s): shots of 2.73, 0.87, 1.2, 2.27, 1.67, 1.67, 0.87s, with longer holds on the hook and the soup reaction. Rapid-fire middle (15.07-25s): eight shots at 0.8-1.27s while the voiceover lists the route and countries, the fastest section, with a cut almost every phrase. Slowdown finale (27.4-41.4s): 1.27, 2.47, 3.93, 4.47, 1.9s, opening up for the sunset, pool and wake. Cuts follow voiceover phrases more than music: 4.8 lands on 'hotel', 18.47 on 'Venice', 25.28 on 'dining', and the cut at 27.4 falls just before 'private terrace'. Several cuts sit near audio hits (15.07 vs 15.14, 35.07 vs 35.0, 8.73 between 8.44 and 8.99). Overall it moves fast but calms down at the end, so the payoff views can breathe.
study.speed: No visible slow motion, speed ramps or timelapses. Everything appears to play at normal speed. The motion rise in the final walk (about 27-47 between 35-39.5s) comes from the handheld walk and camera tilt, not a ramp. The near-zero motion at 40-41.4s (1.5, 1.3, 0.9) is a static locked-off hold.
study.on_screen_text: One overlay only: 'POV: you're not a cruiser but did this luxury cruise line change your mind?' It is black sentence-case sans-serif on white rounded rectangle boxes, one per line, in TikTok native text style, over 3 lines of about 4-5 words each (14 words total), centered horizontally in the upper-middle of the frame. It sits from 0s through the second shot (visible at 3.02s) and is gone by the cut at 3.6s, so about 3.6s on screen. No emoji.
study.captions: Present throughout, from 0.46s to the end. Bold all-caps white sans-serif with a thin dark shadow; the currently spoken word is highlighted yellow (karaoke style). 2-3 words at a time, small, centered at about 72-75% of frame height (lower third), updating in sync with each word. Minor inconsistencies: British spelling 'FAVOURITE', and at about 40.1s the caption reads 'YOU GET THIS' while the voiceover says 'you give this'.
study.audio: A continuous first-person voiceover (135 words, starting at 0.46s and running to 41.14s with almost no gaps) is the main audio. The tone is warm, slightly conversational and confessional ('I finally understand what cruisers mean…', 'Oh, and on our very own private terrace'). There is likely a soft background music bed underneath; audio hits at 0.8, 3.29, 5.09, 15.14, 27.73, 35.0 and later sit close to cuts or word stresses, but no beat drop drives the picture. No natural sound or effects stand out. Picture is matched to words rather than beats: 'luxury hotel' gets the champagne suite, 'at sea' the restaurant, 'Explora Journeys' the logo wall, 'Venice' the night pool, 'in-suite dining' the cloche and breakfast, 'private terrace' the couple in the suite, 'sunset and sunrise' the sunset shot, and 'would you give this…a try?' the balcony reader.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only at all 24 listed cuts (2.73, 3.6, 4.8, 7.07, 8.73, 10.4, 11.27, 13.93, 15.07, 16.73, 17.6, 18.47, 19.33, 20.13, 21.0, 21.87, 23.13, 23.93, 24.87, 27.4, 28.67, 31.13, 35.07, 39.53). Two shot segments contain an undetected internal change: the lobby bar to Malt Whisky cart (7.07-8.73) and spin bikes to rowers (15.07-16.73), likely quick cuts or fast blends the detector merged. No whips, zooms or flashes.
study.effects: A warm, punchy grade: boosted saturation and contrast, with sunrise and sunset pushed to deep orange with bloom around the sun. Mediterranean water and sky are pushed to deep cobalt, and the night pool to electric blue. Interiors are warm amber. Slow digital push-ins on static shots: the hook sunrise (0-2.73), suite table, breakfast (21.87-23.13), towel swans (24.87-27.4) and sunset (28.67-31.13), which add life to still frames. Glow and starburst on the bedside lamp and LED candles. No freeze frames, split screens, maps or graphics.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 29.93fps, h264 at 1469 kbps, so it is low resolution and compressed, and fine detail softens on patterned floors and art. Still, the hero shots (sunrise, sunset, stern wake, pool) look like a dream trip because of strong color, clean horizons, exposure set for the sky so the sun doesn't clip badly, and smooth movement. Some inserts look like phone snapshots (Dyson in a drawer, workout mat, wobbly gallery walk at 11.27-13.93). That mix makes it feel authentic and 'real guest' rather than a brand ad. Exposure on interiors is warm and slightly dim but readable.
study.ending: It ends on the calmest frame: a doorway-framed static shot of the creator reading on the balcony facing open sea (39.53-41.43), while the voiceover asks 'I'm curious, would you give this kind of cruise a try?' The final word 'try' lands at 41.0s, and the video cuts about 0.4s later. The CTA is the comment question. The blue, calm image echoes the opening balcony sunrise, so it loops softly back to the balcony hook.
study.why_viral: 1) An identity callout plus an open question in the first frame ('POV: you're not a cruiser but…did this change your mind?') pulls in the large anti-cruise audience and invites debate in the comments. 2) A rapid stack of recognizable luxury signals (champagne, Dyson, whisky bar, art gallery, smoke cloche, towel swans, private terrace) reframes a cruise as a boutique hotel in under 30s. 3) A human couple and reactions (cheese-pull face, robes dinner, reading on the balcony) make it aspirational and easy to tag a partner. 4) The longest, biggest views (sunset 2.47s, pool deck 3.93s, stern wake 4.47s) are saved for the final third, so the payoff arrives right before a simple yes/no comment ask.
lessons: Open on your single best view (sunset or sunrise from a balcony) with a slow push-in for 2.5-3s, and lay an identity-callout question over it ('POV: you're not a ___ but…'). Keep the box text to about 14 words and remove it by about 3.5s.
Cut B-roll to the voiceover phrase, not the music. Swap the shot on the key noun ('luxury hotel', 'Venice', 'in-suite dining') so each image literally illustrates the word being spoken.
Use three tempos: about 2-2.7s holds for the hook and one reaction shot, a 0.8-1.3s rapid-fire middle for amenity lists, then 2.5-4.5s holds for the final 2-3 big views.
Put the longest and widest shot (a walk-out reveal ending on open ocean or a wake) in the last 10s, not the first. Let the camera tilt up from feet or deck to the horizon for the reveal.

Mix about 40% details that read as status signals (branded tech, champagne, smoke cloche, towel art) with people shots. Include at least one genuine reaction (cheese pull, first bite) held about 2s at low motion so the face reads.
Add slow digital push-ins (about 5-10% over the shot) to every static room, food or view shot so stills don't feel dead under fast cuts.
Say the brand or place name at least 3 times and show its logo once as a 1s insert, so viewers can find it later.
Grade for the dream: warm golds on sunsets and interiors, saturated cobalt on water. Expose for the sky on horizon shots.
End on a calm, near-static frame (motion near 0) that mirrors the opening location, with a spoken yes/no question timed to finish 0.3-0.5s before the cut so the video loops cleanly.
Use word-by-word captions in bold caps with yellow highlight on the active word, 2-3 words at a time in the lower third, and proofread them against the audio.

study.format: Narrated hotel showcase / 'where to stay' recommendation. A single voiceover script runs over a fast montage of about 22 short clips. The order is: city skyline hook, then the hotel's rooftop pool and tower, then the nearby attractions (stadium, concert, Arizona Center, farmers market), then the hotel's public spaces (restaurant, lobby, front desk), then the gym, and finally the guest room and bathroom. It is built as 'neighborhood reasons first, hotel second'. The location-tag CTA lands mid-tour and a follow CTA closes it. The cut detector only logged 3 hard cuts (2.13, 5.17, 7.7) because most scene changes are short crossfades. The frames show a new scene roughly every 0.6–1.3s.
study.place: Sheraton Phoenix Downtown, a city hotel in downtown Phoenix, Arizona, pitched as an event and convention base. What looks special: a blue-hour skyline with orange horizon and mountains, framed by tree branches. A rooftop pool lit by color-cycling LEDs (blue, then purple, then red) against lit office towers. A big-name neighbor in Chase Field (Diamondbacks game inside). The neon Arizona Center sign, a night farmers market and a giant Day-of-the-Dead Catrina figure. A warm, plant-filled restaurant with a fire pit. A dramatic atrium with a suspended wave sculpture. A Sheraton Fitness gym and a clean modern room with a backlit vanity mirror.
study.audience: People with a Phoenix trip already planned, especially for a game, concert or convention, who need somewhere to sleep downtown. It reads as an affiliate travel creator (@thecruisingblonde) rather than the hotel itself: first-person 'Follow me for amazing places to stay', polished but personal footage, and a monetized 'tap the location tag to check rates' booking push. Desired actions: tap the location tag and book, save for an upcoming trip, follow.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0–2.13s) is a blue-hour Phoenix skyline. City lights glitter under an orange horizon band and silhouetted mountains, framed by dark tree branches top and right. Serif text fades in at the top: 'Heading to Phoenix soon?' in cream, then 'Here's where to stay downtown.' in white by ~0.9–1.5s. The voiceover starts at 0.00s with no lead-in: 'If you're planning a trip to downtown Phoenix…'. It stops the scroll because the direct second-person question self-selects anyone going to Phoenix, the text promises a useful answer, and the sunset city is a beautiful first frame.

study.action_shots: Few true action shots; motion comes from camera glides and the montage rate. 6.0–7.2s: wide static-ish view of a live baseball game with players on the field (~1.2s, normal speed). 7.2–8.2s: dancers spinning on stage in an over-the-shoulder audience angle (~1s, normal speed). The 7.7 hard cut lands exactly on an audio hit at 7.71, mid-dance. 2.13–3.6s: pool LED color changes act as 'motion' in a static frame. 19.1–20.3s: slow upward glide/tilt in the atrium (motion spike 33.6/30.0 at 19.0–19.5s is the scene change). Lobby and gym shots are slow handheld/gimbal walk-pans.
study.views: Biggest view lands first: 0–2.13s blue-hour skyline with orange horizon, held 2.13s, near-static with slight drift, framed by foreground branches. Second view: 3.6–5.1s, the Sheraton tower lit at dusk from a hilltop, also branch-framed, held ~1.5s. That ties the hotel back to the opening vantage point. The rooftop pool (2.13–3.6s) works as a night view with towers reflected in the water, revealed by a hard cut. Chase Field exterior (5.2–6.0s) gives a bright blue-sky contrast. Interior 'view' is the atrium sculpture tilt at ~19.1s. There are no drone shots and no room-window reveal.
study.how_place_is_shown: Mostly wides and mediums of spaces, with a few details (necklaces, Catrina, bike sign, fire pit, door lettering). People appear only incidentally: crowds at the game, the concert audience, bar patrons. The creator is never on camera and only shows up in the voiceover. All filmed, not POV, apart from the over-the-shoulder concert shot. The light runs night to day to night and back: dusk and night for skyline, pool, Arizona Center, market and restaurant (warm amber, neon, LED). Bright daylight for Chase Field and the jewelry table. Evening warm lobby light, then flat fluorescent gym, then soft room light. Shot handheld/gimbal on a phone. The details are chosen as proof of claims: the stadium sign proves 'sporting event', 'Let's CRUISE' bikes and the 'Sheraton Fitness' lettering prove amenities, and the fire pit and lanterns sell the atmosphere.
study.info_and_value: Given by voiceover and mirrored in captions. Names: Sheraton Phoenix Downtown. Implicit neighbors shown by signage: Chase Field, Arizona Center, Downtown Farmers Market. Use cases: sporting events, concerts, conventions, exploring downtown. Positioning: 'right in the middle of everything', 'perfect home base'. Booking path: 'Tap the location tag to check rates for your dates and see current promotions'. No prices, no inclusions, no specific tips. The value is the location argument plus a one-tap booking route, which suits event-goers who save it for later.
study.pacing: Only 4 hard-cut 'shots' were detected (2.13, 3.03, 2.53, 19.63s), but the 19.63s 'shot' is really ~16 clips joined by crossfades. Real scene length is about 0.6–1.5s, averaging ~1.2s across ~22 scenes. The hook holds longest (2.13s); the pool runs ~1.5s; most later clips run 1.0–1.3s. Median motion is 13.3 with no long still holds; the low point of 2.0 at 18.0s is the static elevator hall. Scene changes follow the voiceover clauses rather than the music: Chase Field on 'Whether you're in town', the game on 'sporting event', the concert on 'a concert', Arizona Center on 'convention', the market on 'explore downtown', the front desk on 'Tap the location tag', the bed on 'destinations'. The 7.7 cut coincides with an audio hit at 7.71. Overall the feel is brisk but smooth, with ~3.9 spoken words/s.
study.on_screen_text: Hook title only, in an elegant serif (Cormorant/Garamond-like), regular weight, mixed case, top-center, with a soft shadow and no box. Line 1, 'Heading to Phoenix soon?', is cream/pale gold, partly visible at 0.3s and fully legible by 0.9s. Lines 2–3, 'Here's where to stay downtown.', are white and fade in from ~0.9s to 1.5s. It stays over the pool shot and is gone by 3.34s (~3.3s total, 8 words). No emoji. 'Sheraton Fitness' at 21.5s is real door lettering, not an overlay.
study.captions: Present throughout. Same white serif family, sentence case, small size, bottom-center in the lower ~15% of frame. They reveal word by word with a soft fade/typewriter effect synced to the VO. Lines build up to 3 lines (e.g. 'the Sheraton Phoenix / Downtown puts you right in / the middle of everything.'), then clear and restart at the next sentence (~4.3s, 8.2s, 12.9s, 16.5s, 19.3s, 22.6s). The final caption block finishes 'trip for.' at ~26.9s.
study.audio: Voiceover carries the video: calm, polished narration starting at 0.00s and ending at 26.90s, 105 words with almost no gaps, possibly AI or studio-read. Strong audio hits at 0.84, 1.22, 1.44, 2.0, 2.5 and every 0.5–1s after suggest a soft music bed under the voice, but no song is identifiable. Natural sound is not prominent. Sound-to-picture sync is mostly VO-to-scene (each noun gets its clip); the clearest beat alignment is the 7.7 hard cut on the 7.71 hit.
study.transitions: Hard cuts at 2.13s (skyline to pool), 5.17s (into Chase Field; the frame at 5.16 shows a Chase Field/Sheraton blend, so effectively a fast dissolve) and 7.7s (jump within the concert). The rest are short cross-dissolves, visible as double exposures in the frames at 5.16 (stadium over Sheraton tower), 8.20 (Arizona Center over concert), 23.39 (equipment rack over gym) and 25.21 (bed over gym). Each lasts roughly 0.2–0.4s. There are no whips, zooms or flashes.
study.effects: Warm, slightly lifted grade with gentle contrast, giving a soft 'luxury' feel. Night scenes keep saturated LED/neon (pool blue/purple/red, Arizona Center pink/gold). Foreground tree branches give natural vignette framing in the two dusk views. Cross-dissolves create brief double exposures. There are no graphics, maps, freeze frames or split screens.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, ~2 Mbps h264, which is modest for a delivery file. Night shots show some noise and softness, but the footage is stable (gimbal/steady handheld) and well exposed, with no blown skies in the daylight stadium shot. The warm grade, elegant serif type and smooth dissolves make it feel like a boutique hotel ad rather than a phone snapshot, even though it is phone footage.
study.ending: Ends on the bathroom vanity with its backlit mirror. The follow CTA ('Follow me for amazing places to stay, destinations to explore, and experiences worth taking a trip for') runs over the gym, bed and bathroom from 22.56s to 26.90s. The video cuts at 27.33s, ~0.4s after the last word. The booking CTA came earlier (19.3–21.9s). No designed loop, though the short tail lets it roll back into the skyline hook.
study.why_viral: 1) The hook targets a high-intent audience: anyone with Phoenix plans hears 'If you're planning a trip to downtown Phoenix' over a gorgeous blue-hour skyline and a 'here's where to stay' promise. 2) It sells location before the room by putting recognizable landmarks (Chase Field, Arizona Center, live concert, farmers market) on screen in 1-second proof clips matched to each spoken use case, which makes it relevant to event travelers. 3) There is a new visual every ~1.2s with soft dissolves and a striking color-changing pool early, so it never stalls. 4) A one-tap booking CTA ('check rates… see current promotions') turns interest into a save or booking.
lessons: Open on your single most beautiful wide (dusk/blue-hour skyline) for ~2s with a direct question overlay like 'Heading to [city] soon?' and start the voiceover at 0.0s.
Put a visually changing amenity (color-cycling pool, fire pit, neon) in the first 3s right after the hook to name the hotel. It earns retention before any room shots.
Match every noun in the voiceover to its own 0.8–1.3s proof clip, ideally showing the actual sign or landmark name (stadium, convention center, market) so the viewer can verify it.
Sequence it as neighborhood, then public spaces, then amenities, then room. For city hotels, location is the reason to book and the room is the closing reward.
Use 0.2–0.4s cross-dissolves between same-mood clips for a premium feel, and save hard cuts for strong audio hits (here 7.7s on a hit at 7.71s).
Keep the hook text to under ~10 words in one elegant serif family, fade it in over ~1s, and remove it by ~3.3s. Captions sit bottom-center in the same font, revealed word by word, max 3 lines.
Place the booking CTA ('tap the location tag to check rates and promotions') at ~70% of runtime over the lobby/front desk, then use the final 4–5s for a follow CTA over the room and bathroom.
Frame dusk views with foreground branches or railings for depth, and reuse the same vantage point to show the hotel tower so the viewer links it to the opening view.

study.format: Travel-agent room tour told as one continuous walk-through. It is a handheld phone tour of a single room in 5 long shots. A talking-head-free voiceover lists the amenities, then pivots at 39s to 'a little secret': agent-only VIP perks. It ends on a comment-to-get-a-quote CTA. It is built like an ad script: name and room type, luxury features, who it's for, exclusive perk, CTA.
study.place: Le Blanc Spa Resort Los Cabos, Mexico: an adults-only, all-inclusive luxury beach resort. The room is the Royal Deluxe Partial Ocean View Room. It looks special because of the marble floors and counters, a freestanding soaking tub, a stocked minibar with Lavazza pods and snacks, wall-mounted top-shelf liquor dispensers (vodka, whiskey, Black Label), Bvlgari toiletries, monogrammed robes, and a rose-petal heart on the bed with anniversary balloons. It finishes on a balcony overlooking white resort buildings, palms and a saturated blue Sea of Cortez.
study.audience: Couples planning honeymoons and anniversaries, girls' trips and destination-wedding groups who want an upscale adults-only all-inclusive. It clearly reads as a travel agent (vibrantsuntravels): 'plan your stay with me', 'I'll send you a free quote with our most current promotion'. The desired actions are to comment 'LeBlanc' (a lead-gen keyword), share with travel buddies, and save for trip planning. The perk list gives a reason to book through her instead of direct.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0-0.9s) is a wide handheld view down a glossy marble entry hallway. A bathroom with a wood-grain stone wall sits on the left, and the far end opens to a bright window and colorful balloons. Centered at mid-frame is a white-box title, 'Le Blanc Los Cabos Full Room Tour 😍'. The voice starts at 0.98s: 'Let's do a quick room tour at LeBlanc Los Cabos.' It stops the scroll because the long marble corridor pulling toward a sunlit window promises a reveal. The title names a famous luxury brand, and 'quick room tour' sets a low time cost. The camera swings into the bathroom with its freestanding tub by 1.9s.

study.views: Views are rationed and back-loaded. 0-1.5s: a bright window at the end of the hallway, teased but not revealed. 45.5s: the hard cut from a dark closet door into the sunlit bedroom wide, the first big bright shot, held ~1s before panning to the bed. 50-50.5s: a sliver of ocean through the balcony door behind the desk. study.how_place_is_shown: About 70% details and mediums (drawers, bottles, toiletries, robes, minibar contents). Wides are only the opening hallway, the bathroom, the bedroom from 45.5s and the balcony ending. No people on camera, except the creator caught in mirrors holding her phone (6.8s, 10.6s, 31.8s), which adds authenticity. It is all POV with her hand entering frame to open doors and drawers. The first 45s is warm tungsten interior light, a bit dim and orange. The last 15s switches to bright daylight with white walls and blue sky, so the room 'opens up' visually as the pitch peaks. Handheld phone, lightly stabilized, no gimbal or drone. Brand-name details (Lavazza, Don Ramón tequila, Bvlgari, Black Label, Nespresso) are chosen to prove 'top-shelf' and 'ultra-luxe' without saying a price. The rose-petal heart and anniversary balloons sell the couples/celebration audience.
study.info_and_value: All given by voiceover, with key nouns repeated in on-screen text. Resort name: Le Blanc Los Cabos, adults-only, all-inclusive. Room category: Royal Deluxe Partial Ocean View Room. Inclusions: personal butler (unpacks, draws baths), unlimited in-room minibar with premium drinks, top-shelf liquor, wine, espresso machine. Use cases: quick getaway, honeymoon, anniversary, girls' trip, destination wedding. The insider 'secret': booking through her adds VIP perks (free room upgrades, early check-in, late check-out, resort credit, airport transfers on 4+ night stays). CTA: comment 'LeBlanc' and share with travel buddies to get a free quote with the current promotion. No prices are given. The value is the exclusive-perk list, which gives a concrete reason to comment and book via the agent, plus 'share with your travel buddies' to drive group tags.
study.pacing: Very long takes: 5 shots in 59.8s (0.67 cuts per 10s). Shot lengths are 21.07, 9.9, 14.53, 9.6 and 4.7s (median 9.9s). Pace comes from the voiceover (180 words, ~3 words/s, starting at 0.98s) and constant handheld movement (median motion 21.9), not from editing. Each amenity gets ~1.5-3s of screen as the camera moves on when the VO names the next thing. The quietest stretch is 32-35s (motion dips to 6.4 on the shower). The busiest is 20-25s (whips around the minibar). Cuts land on sentence or section changes, not beats. 30.97 comes just after 'espresso machine' at the start of 'So whether you're...'. 45.5 lands as 'free room upgrades' begins. 55.1 falls mid-CTA. The final shot is the shortest (4.7s) and carries the payoff view.
study.on_screen_text: Sparse label cards: black regular-weight sans-serif sentence case in a white rounded box, centered at roughly 45-55% screen height. (1) 'Le Blanc Los Cabos Full Room Tour 😍', 2 lines, ~0-5s. (2) 'Royal Deluxe Partial Ocean View Room', 2 lines, ~8-13.5s, appearing as the VO says the room name. (3) A stacked 4-line list 'Honeymoon / Anniversary / Girls getaway / Destination Wedding' placed higher (~15% from top), ~34-38.5s. (4) 'A little secret 🤫', ~40-43.5s. (5) 'Comment Le Blanc', ~52.5-57s. Each card holds 3.5-5s and appears only at a section change, so it works as a chapter marker that echoes the VO.
study.captions: Yes, for the whole voiceover. Bold all-caps sans-serif in white with a dark outline/shadow. One keyword per chunk is highlighted yellow (e.g., 'QUICK room tour', 'LUXURY vibe', 'UNLIMITED premium drinks', 'ROOM upgrades', 'COMMENT le BLANC'). Chunks are 2-3 words, positioned in the lower third (~73% down), and switch word-synced with the speech.
study.audio: Voiceover-led, a friendly, upbeat agent pitch in first person, starting at 0.98s and running almost wall to wall until 57.9s, then 'Thank you' at 59.6s. The audio hits mostly track speech stresses (e.g., 14.24 'amenities', 26.88 'top-shelf', 46.19-48.01 the perk list, 57.1 'promotion') rather than a music drop; any background bed is low and not cut to. No sound effects. Picture follows words: the room name card appears on 'Royal Deluxe', the liquor dispensers on 'top-shelf liquor', the balloons and rose petals during the celebration and perk lines, the 'Comment Le Blanc' card on 'comment LeBlanc'. One mismatch: 'butler... draw you a bath' plays over the minibar.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only, but two are disguised. 21.07 is a jump cut on the same minibar from the door-opening to the straight-on open fridge. 30.97 goes from an upper cabinet/mirror to the bathroom doorway, a cut on a panning camera that reads as continuous movement. 45.5 is a near object wipe: the frame is filled by a dark wood closet door, then a hard cut to the bright bedroom wide, used as a dark-to-light reveal. 55.1 is a straight cut from the desk wide to a table-top detail. No whips are added in editing; the in-camera whip pans at 22-25s do the energy work.
study.effects: none beyond a likely light brightness/saturation lift. The balcony sky and sea are a strong saturated blue, and interiors are warm. No zooms, graphics, maps or freeze frames.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, h264 ~1.2 Mbps: soft, phone-snapshot resolution with visible compression. Handheld with some stabilization; clear motion blur and smear during the 22-25s minibar whips. Interior exposure is warm and slightly dim through the first 45s, then the bedroom and balcony are bright and clean with a deep blue sky that isn't blown out. It reads as real and trustworthy (an agent who was actually there) rather than cinematic. The dream-trip feeling is carried by the marble, brands and the final ocean view, not by production polish.
study.ending: The CTA ('comment LeBlanc... free quote with our most current promotion') ends at 57.9s. Simultaneously the camera walks out onto the balcony for the biggest view of the video: ocean, blue sky, resort below. It is held ~2s more with a quick 'Thank you' at 59.6s and cuts at 59.8s. It doesn't loop to the start, but ending on the ocean view leaves the strongest want-to-go image right as the viewer decides whether to comment.
study.why_viral: A recognizable luxury brand plus 'adults-only all-inclusive' instantly targets honeymoon and anniversary couples. Concrete, brand-name proof (unlimited top-shelf liquor dispensers, Bvlgari, snack drawers, butler) makes 'all-inclusive' tangible and save-worthy. The 'little secret' turn at 39s gives exclusive value (upgrades, credit, transfers for 4+ nights) that rewards finishing and makes commenting the keyword feel worth it. Holding back the bright bedroom and ocean balcony until 45-60s pays off the hallway window teased in frame one and keeps people watching.
lessons: Open on the longest leading line you have (a hallway toward a bright window) with a 3-5 word title card naming the place plus 'Full Room Tour', and start talking within 1s.
Say the exact room category name and put it on screen as a card for 4-5s; viewers save tours to look up that specific room.
Shoot amenities as hand-opened reveals (drawers, cabinets, fridge) and give each 1.5-3s timed to when the voiceover names it; reaching in to open things feels like being there.
Save the brightest wide and the ocean or balcony view for the last 10-15%: cut from a dark door or closet into the bright room, then walk out the door onto the balcony for a final 2-3s hold.
Insert a 'here's a little secret' turn at roughly 65% of runtime with its own text card (🤫) to re-hook viewers before the pitch.
For agent or lead-gen content, end with a single keyword comment CTA ('Comment Le Blanc') shown as text for ~4s plus 'share with your travel buddies', and let the best view play under it.

Caption every word in 2-3 word bold uppercase chunks in the lower third with one yellow keyword per chunk; keep separate label cards in white boxes mid-frame and only at section changes (about every 10-15s).
Show who it's for with a stacked text list (honeymoon / anniversary / girls' trip / wedding) held ~4s so viewers self-identify and tag someone.

If footage is long continuous handheld takes, you can keep cuts to 4-6 per minute as long as the voiceover runs at ~3 words/s and the camera never stops moving; trim stretches where motion drops to near zero for more than 2s.

study.format: 'Things you didn't know' / travel-hack tutorial with 2 numbered tips. The creator talks to her front camera, and each tip is shown as a screen recording of her iPhone floating over the talking-head shot (green-screen style). The structure is: promise hook, then Tip 1 said, demonstrated and recommended, then Tip 2 said and demonstrated, then a 'part two?' CTA.
study.place: No destination is shown. It is filmed in a plain, bright bedroom or home office with a window onto trees and a ceiling fan. The lock screen reads Sydney and the carrier is Telstra, so the creator is Australian. The 'trip' is generic international travel, and the value is pure utility: world clocks on the lock screen, and the offline currency converter built into the iPhone calculator.
study.audience: iPhone-owning travelers and people with family abroad. It is made to be saved for the next trip, shared with a travel buddy or a parent with relatives overseas, and commented on ('part two please'). It reads as an individual creator or traveler giving friendly insider tips, not a brand or agent.
study.hook: Frame 1 is a medium close-up selfie of the creator mid-gesture, already talking at 0.00s ('Okay, here are some things that I use my iPhone for when I'm traveling that you probably didn't even know already exist on your phone'). Small lowercase text sits top-center: 'my favourite iphone hacks when i travel <3'. It stops the scroll through a curiosity gap ('you probably didn't even know') combined with a universal object (your own phone). There is zero dead air: the first word lands on frame 1.

beats.what: Talking head plus title text 'my favourite iphone hacks when i travel <3'. She promises hidden features already on your phone.
Jump cut. 'One, and probably my favorite thing…' The title text clears around 7s.

Screen recording overlay of the lock screen showing Vancouver -17hrs 10:56 pm and Sydney 3:56 pm. At about 8.5s an orange hand-drawn circle highlights the two clocks while she says 'time zones on my lock screen'.
Walkthrough: long-press the lock screen, tap Customise, and enter widget edit mode while she explains why it helps (friends or family abroad, best times to call).
City Digital clock widget city list scrolling (A cities).
She adds widgets on screen: Detroit -14hrs, then picks Kathmandu from the list. VO: 'put your next location in to help your body adjust'.
Widgets set to Detroit and Kathmandu. Edit screen shows 'Saving…'.
0.93s trimmed flash of the wallpaper gallery, skipping the wait.
Finished lock screen held 3.33s, showing Detroit 1:56 am and Kathmandu 11:41 am under the clock.
Back to talking head with two quick jump cuts (0.63s, 1.3s): 'So highly recommend.'
Peace-sign gesture: 'Second thing is if you jump into your calculator top right…'
Calculator screen recording. She taps the top-right icon, a menu opens (Basic/Scientific/Maths Notes/Convert), she picks Convert, and the USD/AUD converter appears. The currency list scrolls.
She switches currency to Euro while the VO says other apps need internet and are 'a nightmare'.
She types 5 USD and it shows 4.36 EUR, proof it works. VO: 'you do not need internet'.
Smiling talking head: 'Let me know if you want a part two', with a peace sign at 'two things I cannot live without when I'm traveling'.

study.action_shots: No physical travel action. The 'action' is on-screen phone interaction: lock-screen taps and widget additions (15.3–21s, motion spikes 17.6 at 9s, 26.2 at 15s, 20.1 at 20.5s from screen transitions), list scrolling (12.87–15.3s and 39–46s), and typing 5 USD → 4.36 EUR (~48s). All of it is shown full-speed in the floating screen-recording window. Her hand gestures (counting 'one', the peace sign for 'second' and 'two things') act as visual beat markers. There is no music to sync to.
study.views: none. The only scenery is trees through the bedroom window behind her. The 'reveal' moments are the finished lock screen with the two world clocks (25.0–28.33s, held 3.33s) and the converted result 5 USD = 4.36 EUR (~48–49.5s).
study.how_place_is_shown: Front-camera handheld selfie at chest-up framing in soft, even daylight from a side window: neutral, bright, airy room. The creator is in frame the whole time, in the background of the overlays and filling the frame in the talking segments. The screen recordings are real POV of her own phone, including a cute dog wallpaper that adds warmth and personality. The details used are the clock widgets and calculator UI, because the 'place' here is the phone.
study.info_and_value: All delivered by voiceover with on-screen demonstration. Tip 1: add the Clock 'City Digital' widget to the lock screen to show other time zones (examples Vancouver -17hrs, Detroit -14hrs, Kathmandu -4:15hrs). Use it to know when family abroad is sleeping, find the best times to call, and pre-set your next destination to help your body adjust. Tip 2: in the Calculator app, tap the top-right calculator icon, then Convert, to get a built-in currency converter (rates shown from yahoo finance) that works without internet, unlike downloaded apps. Proof: 5 USD = 4.36 EUR. This is very saveable, because the steps are exact enough to follow later. It is shareable to anyone traveling, and the 'part two?' CTA drives comments.
study.pacing: 14 shots in 54.8s, 2.37 cuts per 10s, median shot 3.17s. The talking-head bits are tight jump cuts (5.9, 1.57, 0.63, 1.3, 1.77, 4.43s) with breaths and pauses removed. The demos are held long (5.4, 5.77, 9.1, 9.27s) so viewers can follow taps. Dead UI waits are trimmed out (0.93s gallery flash at 24.07, cut at 12.87 into the loading list). Cuts follow speech phrases (e.g. 30.27 right on 'Second', 50.4 right before 'Let me know'), not music. Speech is near-continuous at ~4 words/s (218 words).
study.speed: none. Everything plays at normal speed. Time is compressed by trimming UI waits and pauses rather than speed-ups.
study.on_screen_text: One title: 'my favourite iphone hacks when i travel <3', all lowercase, thin pale-yellow/cream sans-serif with no box or stroke, 2 lines (~7 words), top-center above her head. On from 0s to about 7s, then gone. Plus one orange hand-drawn circle annotation around the lock-screen clocks at about 8.5s. No other text and no emoji beyond '<3'.
study.audio: Voiceover only (direct-to-camera speech recorded with the video, continuing over the screen recordings). No music or sound effects are evident. The strongest audio hits are speech stresses, e.g. 5.71 'One', 30.12 near 'Second', 50.74 'Let me know'. The tone is casual and enthusiastic ('so handy', 'it's a nightmare', 'literally inbuilt').
study.transitions: Hard cuts only. Jump cuts within the talking head (5.9, 28.33, 28.97, 30.27, 50.4). A hard cut into the overlay at 7.47 and 32.03 (the screen recording appears instantly over her). Hard cuts inside the screen recording to skip loading (12.87, 15.3, 21.07, 24.07, 25.0, 41.13).
study.effects: Picture-in-picture or green-screen composite: the phone screen recording sits centered at about 75% of frame width over the live talking-head shot, so her hair and hand stay visible at the edges and she keeps 'presenting' it. An orange hand-drawn circle highlights the time-zone widgets at about 8.5s. There is no color grade beyond natural phone processing, and no zooms or graphics.
study.quality: 576x1024, 30fps, h264 at just 680 kbps, so it is soft and compressed. The front-camera footage is clean thanks to bright, even window light, and the screen recordings stay crisp because UI is high-contrast. It looks like an authentic phone selfie, which fits a utility hack video: trust and relatability matter more than cinematic polish.
study.ending: Ends on the talking head with the CTA 'Let me know if you want a part two' (50.76s) and a recap, 'two things that I cannot live without when I'm traveling'. It cuts about 0.4s after the last word (54.42 → 54.8). Ending mid-energy in the same framing as the opening lets it loop smoothly back into 'Okay, here are…'.
study.why_viral: 1) A curiosity hook about something everyone already owns ('you probably didn't even know already exist on your phone'), so the payoff feels free and instantly usable. 2) Proof on screen: real screen recordings with exact taps and a visible result (5 USD → 4.36 EUR, Detroit/Kathmandu clocks), which makes it highly saveable and shareable. 3) A genuine pain point solved, with the offline currency conversion framed against 'downloading a whole other app… a nightmare'. 4) A comment-baiting 'part two?' CTA plus a short, numbered 2-tip structure that people watch to the end.
lessons: Start talking on frame 1 (first word at 0.00s) with a curiosity line that promises a hidden benefit the viewer already has access to.
Put a short lowercase title (≤8 words) top-center for the first ~6-7s, then remove it so it doesn't compete with the demo.
Number tips out loud and with a hand gesture ('one', a peace sign for 'second'), and cut so each number lands at the start of a shot (e.g. the cut at 30.27s on 'Second').
Show, don't tell: overlay a screen recording or B-roll at about 75% width over the talking head within ~1.5s of naming the tip, and keep the speaker visible behind it.
Add one highlight annotation (a colored circle or arrow) within 1s of the demo appearing to point at the exact feature.
Hold demo shots long (5-9s) so steps can be followed, but trim every loading screen or wait with hard cuts (sub-1s bridges like the 0.93s gallery flash).
Always end each tip on the finished result held 2-3s (the completed lock screen, '5 USD = 4.36 EUR') so viewers screenshot or save it.
Jump-cut the talking head to remove pauses (0.6-1.8s shots), keeping overall pacing around 2-3 cuts per 10s for a ~55s tip video.
Close with a 'want a part two?' comment CTA in the last 4-5s and cut within 0.5s of the last word so it loops.

study.format: Destination/resort montage built on a 'This is not Bali… This is… Phuket' misdirect-and-reveal. It is a fast slideshow of about 15–17 clips of one jungle hillside resort, run under a three-step text sequence. There is no voiceover; the only words are a song lyric.
study.place: A luxury hillside jungle resort in Phuket, Thailand (the resort is not named). It has thatched wooden villas stacked up a forested slope, each with a private plunge pool and walls covered in vines, plus a hillside funicular, a stone waterfall staircase, and green-wall buildings with warm evening lights. Interiors include a lantern-lit open-air restaurant, a stone bathroom with a rose-petal tub, and a timber lobby lounge. What makes it look special: it reads as 'Bali-style' treehouse luxury, which is exactly what the text plays on.
study.audience: Couples and honeymooners, plus Southeast Asia travelers who assume this look means Bali. It makes them want to save it and tag a partner ('we need to go'). It also starts comment debates ('Is this Bali?', 'Name of the hotel?'). It reads as an aggregator or inspiration creator reposting resort and drone footage, not as the resort itself and not as a first-person traveler.
study.hook: Frame 0: a lush drone wide of villas stepping up a misty jungle hillside, with turquoise pools in the foreground. Small white centered text reads 'This is not Bali'. A sung lyric starts at 0.18s ('For you…'). It stops the scroll because the image screams Bali while the text contradicts it, creating an instant 'then where?' question that only a later reveal can answer.

beats.what: Drone wide of the hillside villa complex; text 'This is not Bali'.
High-angle drone looking down the symmetrical villas, waterfall channel and terraced pools.
Two torch fire performers flanking a pool at dusk.
Text changes to 'This is...' on an audio hit. Drone shows a villa with a man in the plunge pool holding a floating breakfast tray.
Top-down shot of a person swimming the length of a private plunge pool.
Stone waterfall staircase between wooden cabins, lit from below.
POV down the steep funicular rail through a steel frame toward green-wall buildings and a city skyline.
Text resolves to 'Phuket' and stays to the end.
Drone of the funicular tracks beside a stacked villa with a pool and a swimmer.
Moving drone over a villa, its pool, the lounger deck and lagoon-style terraced pools.
Wide of the whole hillside of villas with drifting mist and smoke.
Evening shot of a vine-covered building with warm window lights, with a waterfall in the foreground.
Wide of the villas climbing the slope, with misty mountains behind.
Repeat of the floating-breakfast plunge-pool villa drone shot.
Top-down aerial over a grid of pool villas and the main pool.
Open-air restaurant with a lantern cluster chandelier and a set table.
Stone bathroom with a rose-petal-filled freestanding tub and a carved stone sink.
Warm, dim timber lobby lounge with tall windows onto ferns; the video ends on this.

study.action_shots: Very few, and all subtle. A man floats in the plunge pool with a breakfast tray at about 2.1s and again at 8.6–9.4s, filmed from a wide drone angle at normal speed. A top-down swimmer glides the length of the pool at about 2.7s for about 0.3s at normal speed. Fire-torch performers stand at the pool at 1.67s for about 0.4s. A POV ride down the funicular rail runs 3.33–4.4 (1.07s), forward-moving and front-facing. The drone shot at 5.27–6.07 carries the video's peak motion (35.3 at 5.5s). The action is atmosphere rather than thrills; the cut to the swimmer and waterfall lands near the 2.91s audio hit.
study.views: Views are the whole video. Drone wides of the hillside appear at 0, 4.4, 6.07 and 7.8s. Top-down aerials appear at 0.93 (high angle), about 2.7 and 9.4s. The POV funicular reveal at 3.33s is framed by steel beams, a 'window' that opens onto the city skyline. Each view is held only 0.8–1.07s, with slow drone drift or push-in rather than big moves. The biggest scale view is the misty full-hillside wide at 6.07s, and again at 7.8s with clouded mountains. There is no door or curtain reveal; reveals come from the text change, not the camera.
study.how_place_is_shown: About 70% wides and aerials, with medium interiors in the last third (restaurant, bath, lobby) and few true close-ups. People are tiny or absent: one man in a pool, one swimmer, two fire performers, and no creator on camera. Everything is filmed or drone footage, except the single funicular POV. The light is overcast daytime with soft diffuse greens and teal pools, then blue-hour and night shots with warm tungsten lamps (6.87s, 10.27s on). The look moves from lush day to cozy night. The details used — the floating breakfast, the rose-petal tub, the lantern chandelier — are classic luxury-honeymoon signifiers. Camera work is drone plus smooth gimbal.
study.info_and_value: Minimal. The only fact is the location, 'Phuket', delivered as on-screen text after the 'not Bali' tease. The resort name, prices and booking details are not given. That absence drives 'what's the name?' comments, while the 'hidden alternative to Bali' angle drives saves.
study.pacing: 15 detected shots in 12.73s, about 11 cuts per 10s. Median shot is 0.8s, longest 1.2s (which likely hides 2 extra fast cuts at about 2.1 and 2.7s), shortest 0.47s at 2.87–3.33. From 4.4s on, the rhythm is almost metronomic at 0.8–0.93s per shot, matching the song's beat. Motion falls from the mid-20s/30s early to single digits at the end (4.1, 2.6), so the edit calms down as it moves into still interiors.
study.speed: none — all clips appear to play at normal speed. The drone moves are slow by nature; there are no ramps or timelapses.
study.on_screen_text: Three states, one at a time, in white sans-serif (medium/bold, sentence case) with a light drop shadow. The text is small, centered horizontally and sits just above the vertical middle. 'This is not Bali' runs 0–about 2.1s (4 words). 'This is...' runs about 2.1–3.7s (2 words plus an ellipsis, appearing on an audio hit). 'Phuket' runs about 3.7s to the end (1 word). No emoji, no box.
study.audio: A trending emotional song. The only recognized words are the lyric 'For you I bring myself' at 0.18–2.44s; there is no voiceover and no natural sound is audible from the data. Audio hits at 2.1s line up with the text switch to 'This is...', and hits at 2.91 and 3.21 line up with the cut to the waterfall at 2.87 and the funicular at 3.33. The final hit at 12.71s is at the very end of the clip.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only, cut on the beat. There are likely 2 undetected hard cuts inside 1.67–2.87s (fire dancers → floating-breakfast villa → top-down swimmer). No whips, zooms or wipes.
study.effects: A strong color grade: boosted greens and teal pool water, slightly lifted contrast, and warm amber on the night and interior shots. Some clips look heavily sharpened or enhanced. No zoom effects, freeze frames, maps or split screens.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, 2546 kbps h264, so it is low resolution and a recompressed repost. Still, the source footage is professional: stable drone and gimbal work, clean exposure even under overcast skies, and rich saturated color. Composition and grade carry the 'dream trip' feel despite the soft resolution and compression.
study.ending: Ends on the warm lobby lounge (11.87–12.73s, 0.87s), with the 'Phuket' text still on screen. There is no CTA. The last audio hit falls at 12.71s, right at the cut-off. The short length and the open, ambient final shot let it loop back easily to the 'This is not Bali' opener.
study.why_viral: 1) The 'This is not Bali' contradiction over an image that looks exactly like Bali creates an instant curiosity gap, paid off in under 4s. 2) Every shot is a luxury fantasy signifier (private plunge pools, floating breakfast, rose-petal bath, jungle funicular), shown at 0.8s each, so viewers rewatch to take it in. 3) Leaving out the resort name and price provokes comments and saves ('name?!', 'tagging you'). 4) Hard cuts locked to an emotional trending song give it a polished, dreamy rhythm.
lessons: Open with your most 'iconic-looking' wide, held 0.9–1.0s, and overlay a contrarian line like 'This is not [famous place]'.
Run the reveal as a 3-step text sequence (claim → 'This is...' → answer), with each text change on an audio hit and the answer landing by about 4s.
Keep a single centered text line in small white sans-serif with a shadow, placed just above mid-frame so it never covers the subject, and leave it up for the rest of the video.
Once the reveal is done, cut on the beat at a steady 0.8–0.9s per shot; use a 0.4–0.5s quick cut around the first musical accent for energy.

Order the footage from aerial scale (drone wides and top-downs) to signature experiences (pool, floating breakfast, ride or POV) to cozy night interiors (dining, bath, lobby), so it closes calm and warm.
Include 1–2 tiny-scale human moments, like a swimmer or someone in the pool, inside wides so the luxury feels inhabitable without showing faces.
Grade greens and pool water up for saturation and push night shots warm and amber, so day and night footage reads as one dreamy palette.
Leave out the hotel name if you want comments, or put it in the caption; either way, end on a low-motion shot that loops cleanly into the hook.

study.format: Single-hotel 'save this for your trip' montage: a 13s beat-synced slideshow of 13 shots of one property, with one save-bait hook line followed by a persistent name and location title card. There is no voiceover, no prices and no list structure. The edit is built purely on dreamy views of the villas plus a trending song.
study.place: La Lanna, a boutique jungle villa hotel in Chiang Mai, Thailand. Its special features: private kidney-shaped and round jacuzzis on decks among tall jungle trees, and villas raised on stilts. It also has sculpted stone-look exterior walls, round rattan daybeds and beds, and porthole windows. Floor-to-ceiling sliding walls open the bedrooms to the deck. Shallow turquoise private pools have glass 'water wall' cascades, and a corridor with a curved walkway over glowing green water ends at a waterfall window. It reads as a hidden, design-led, Instagram-bait jungle retreat rather than a beach resort.
study.audience: Made by a travel creator (kelseyinlondon) for young women and couples dreaming of or planning a Thailand trip. The explicit goal is the save ('Save this hotel for your trip to Thailand...'), with secondary goals of tagging a partner or friend ('we need to go here') and searching the hotel name. It reads as an aspirational creator or influencer post, not a hotel ad: the creator is posed in most shots and nothing is sold.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0.0s): a woman in a white bikini sits on the edge of a bubbling, glowing turquoise kidney-shaped jacuzzi on a white deck. Tall jungle tree trunks and a round daybed sit behind her in bright sun. White serif text centered mid-frame reads 'Save this hotel for your trip to Thailand...'. The first sound, at 0.08s, is the song vocal 'Just love me'. It stops the scroll for three reasons: the bubbling teal water against green jungle is instantly a 'private paradise' image, the text names a destination plus a direct action (save), and the ellipsis promises more to see. This is also the longest shot (1.53s), so the text can be read.

beats.what: Woman on edge of bubbling private jacuzzi on jungle deck; text 'Save this hotel for your trip to Thailand...' (1.53s)

Hotel title card 'LA LANNA / Chiang Mai, Thailand' appears. Shot: woman in white dress at the end of a corridor with a curved walkway over glowing green water, facing a glass waterfall window, framed by arched wooden doors
Bedroom with round rattan bed, woman lounging; a fully open sliding wall shows the deck jacuzzi and jungle
Villa exterior: sculpted stone-look wall, porthole window, round bed in the open doorway with woman, wooden deck, jacuzzi, tree canopy and blue sky
High drone angle of the same villa on stilts, with deck, jacuzzi and round bed tucked among trees
Second villa type: shallow turquoise private pool, glass water-wall feature, green sliding doors
Top-down drone of woman in hat lying on a round floating daybed in the shallow turquoise pool
Drone high angle of the white box villa wrapped in jungle, with pool and jacuzzi and woman in the water
Living area with walls fully open to a deck with a round jacuzzi and tall trees
Close medium of the jacuzzi bubbling hard, round window, lantern, jungle foliage
Bed with rolled towels facing a glass wall that opens onto the turquoise pool and round daybed
Pool steps beside the glass water wall, with big tropical leaves and dark jungle
Final wide: water cascading down the glass wall into the turquoise pool, bedroom and daybed visible, blue sky; ends at 13.0s

study.action_shots: There are no big action shots. The movement comes from ambient motion: jacuzzi jets bubbling (0-1.53s and 9.13-10.07s), the waterfall window (1.53-2.47s) and the glass water-wall cascade (12.0-13.0s). The woman barely moves, posing rather than doing anything. Within-shot motion stays low (1-8 out of 100) except the last half second (22.7), where the water wall pours and the camera drifts. Each shot plays at normal speed and starts on a music hit.
study.views: Three drone views carry the 'wow': a high angle of the stilted villa (4.4-5.33s), a top-down of the woman on the pool daybed (6.27-7.27s, the stillest shot at motion 1.9) and a high angle of the white villa in jungle (7.27-8.2s). Each is held about 0.93-1.0s with almost no camera movement, so the reveal comes from the cut itself rather than a pull-back. The room-to-view moments are built into framing: shots at 2.47s, 8.2s and 10.07s look from bed or living area through fully open glass walls to the jacuzzi, pool and jungle. The corridor-to-waterfall-window shot at 1.53s works as a 'door' reveal. The biggest views (the drone run) land in the middle (4.4-8.2s). The video closes on the water-wall pool wide at 12.0s.
study.how_place_is_shown: About 5 wides or aerials, 7 mediums of rooms and pools, and 1 detail-ish jacuzzi close. The creator is in roughly 7 of 13 shots, always as a small posed figure: back to camera, lounging, or seen from above. She makes the place feel lived-in without becoming the subject; there are no couples or families. Everything is filmed, not POV. All daytime in hard tropical sun with blue sky and dappled leaf shadows. The palette is consistent: white architecture, turquoise and teal water, deep green jungle. Footage is gimbal or tripod steady plus drone. The few details chosen (rolled towels on the bed, lanterns, round daybeds, bubbling jets) signal luxury and privacy rather than food or drink.
study.info_and_value: Minimal but exactly what's needed to act: the hotel name 'LA LANNA' and location 'Chiang Mai, Thailand' are on screen from 1.53s to the end. There is a location-pin icon, but no price, room type, booking tip or voiceover. The value is 'here's a specific, nameable hotel you can look up', paired with the explicit instruction to save it for a Thailand trip.
study.pacing: Very regular: the first shot is 1.53s, then 12 shots of 0.93-1.0s each (median 0.93s, 9.23 cuts per 10s). The rhythm is metronomic, one cut roughly every 0.93s. That matches a song beat (about 64 bpm, or every 2 beats at about 129). Cuts land on audio hits: 2.47 vs 2.53, 4.4 vs 4.43, 6.27 vs 6.34, 8.2 vs 8.25, 10.07 vs 10.15 and 12.0 vs 12.05, within roughly 0.03-0.08s. Only the hook is held longer, for text reading. No shot is held for a big view; the steady pulse itself is the energy.
study.on_screen_text: Two text states. From 0-1.53s: 'Save this hotel for your trip to Thailand...' in white sentence-case serif with a soft shadow, two lines, centered just above the middle (about 7 words per line). From 1.53-13.0s, a title card in the same spot stays through every cut. It has a thin location-pin icon on top and 'LA LANNA' in white uppercase, widely spaced serif. A thin horizontal rule sits under it, then 'Chiang Mai, Thailand' in white italic serif. No box or stroke, just a light shadow. It stays readable on bright shots but gets washed out on the white-wall shots (7.27s, 10.07s, 12.0s). No emoji.
study.audio: A trending pop song whose vocal ('would you still love me... love me') gives a romantic, dreamy mood. The first vocal at 0.0s means there is sound from frame one. There is no voiceover and no audible natural sound such as jets or water. Every cut is placed on a strong audio hit, so the slideshow feels rhythmic and 'edited to the beat'. The lyric 'love me' at 12.12-12.42 lands as the last shot plays, giving a soft emotional close.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only, all on the beat. Some cuts work as loose continuity: the jacuzzi villa is shown from the bedroom (2.47s), then outside (3.47s), then from the drone (4.4s), building one villa from inside to above. The same happens with the pool villa at 5.33s, 6.27s and 7.27s.
study.effects: A bright, airy grade. Teal and turquoise water and green foliage are boosted, whites are lifted, and there is a slight warm, soft haze, giving a cohesive 'aesthetic' look across shots. There are no zooms, shakes, freeze frames or graphics beyond the pin-icon title card.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 30fps, about 2 Mbps H.264. That is low resolution and bitrate (a re-upload or compressed export), so fine detail is soft. It still reads as a dream trip because the source footage is rock-steady (gimbal, tripod and drone), exposed for bright sun without blown water, and color-matched across all 13 shots. Strong composition with the subject small in a big frame, plus a consistent palette, carry it more than sharpness.
study.ending: There is no CTA beat at the end; the save instruction was front-loaded in the hook. It ends on a wide of the turquoise pool with the glass water wall pouring, on the lyric 'love me' (12.42s). The cut comes at 13.0s, about 1.0s after the last cut, on the final audio hit at 12.94s. Same-palette pool and jacuzzi shots at the start and end let it loop seamlessly into the jacuzzi hook, which encourages rewatches.
study.why_viral: 1) A save-bait hook ('Save this hotel for your trip to Thailand...') over a bubbling private jacuzzi in the jungle: it tells viewers what to do and why within the first second. 2) Unusual, highly photogenic architecture (water walls, a corridor over glowing water, stilted villas, round beds) that looks unreal, so people save it, tag a partner and comment 'where is this'. 3) A relentless one-shot-every-0.93s beat sync with 13 different 'wow' angles in 13 seconds, so there's no dead time and a rewatch loop. 4) A persistent name and location card, so the post doubles as an actionable bookmark.
lessons: Open with your single most enviable shot (moving water plus a person plus nature), hold it about 1.5s, and overlay a direct save instruction naming the destination, e.g. 'Save this hotel for your trip to [country]...'.

After the hook, swap the text for a persistent name and location card (hotel name in caps, city and country in italics, a pin icon) and keep it on until the end, so every screenshot or save carries the info.
For a pure montage, cut every 0.9-1.0s exactly on the song's beat hits (within about 0.05s); about 9 cuts per 10s keeps a 13s video moving without needing any action.
Order shots to build one space from inside to outside to above: room looking through open glass to the pool, then exterior, then drone. Put the drone run in the middle third.
Keep the person small and posed (back to camera, lounging, top-down) in about half the shots; it adds scale and aspiration without turning it into a vlog.
Pick shots with built-in motion (jacuzzi jets, waterfalls, water walls) so even 1s static gimbal or tripod shots don't feel frozen.
Grade everything to one palette (boost teal water and green foliage, lift whites) so footage from different cameras and drones reads as one dream place.
Export at full 1080x1920 with a high bitrate; this video's 576p and 2 Mbps softens the detail, and serif text on white walls needs a stronger shadow to stay readable.
End on a pool or water wide that matches the opening shot's colors, so the loop back to the hook is seamless and rewatches count.

study.format: 'Your sign to…' aesthetic resort montage: one persuasive price-hook sentence sits on screen the whole time over 6 fast b-roll clips (lobby view, pool loungers, ocean view, bathroom, restaurant, buffet, beach wildlife, friend group). There is no tour structure or narration. The text sells the deal and the clips act as proof of value.
study.place: An all-inclusive beach resort on what looks like a Pacific Mexico coastline, with palm trees, a mountain island offshore and high-rise hotels along a wide sand beach. Several things make it look special: a floor-to-ceiling glass lobby opening onto palms, pool and ocean; rows of lavender umbrellas over the pool loungers; an infinity-style pool looking at a misty headland; backlit-mirror marble bathrooms; a design-y restaurant; a pancake-and-strawberry buffet; an egret on the shoreline; and a golden-hour beach.
study.audience: Couples and friend groups in their 20s–30s looking for an affordable getaway. The '$100/night per person all-inclusive' line is built to make people tag their partner ('this is your sign'), save it for later and ask in the comments which resort it is. It reads as a traveler/creator account (camrietravels), not the resort's own marketing: the footage is handheld phone footage and ends on the creator's friend group.
study.hook: Frame 1 (0.0s) is a wide interior of a glossy marble lobby with a wall of glass framing palm trees, a turquoise pool, a kids' water park and blue ocean, with woven rattan pendant lamps overhead and a mirror-like floor reflection. The full sentence 'your sign to take a couples trip to an all inclusive resort for less than $100/night per person' is already on screen at 0.2s, centered in white serif. The first sound is the beat of a trending song (audio hit at 0.24s), and there are no vocals until 2.0s. It stops the scroll because a luxury-looking view is paired instantly with a surprisingly low price, and 'your sign' speaks directly to the viewer.

beats.what: Lobby wide through floor-to-ceiling glass: palms, pool, ocean, mirror floor. The price-hook text is already up. Slow handheld drift, held 1.4s.
Low-angle repeating line of pool loungers under closed lavender umbrellas, with the pool behind. Cut lands on the audio hit at 1.43s.
Through foreground leaves, an infinity-edge pool against the ocean surf and a misty mountain headland, shot past furled umbrellas.
Marble bathroom vanity with backlit LED mirrors in receding perspective. A luxury-detail flex.
Restaurant interior with round wood-framed mirrors, teal banquette, wood tables and wire chairs. Shown only briefly before the food.
Buffet close-up of a tray of pancakes topped with strawberries in front of scrambled eggs and bacon. Proves the 'all inclusive' value.
White egret with wind-blown plumes standing at the waterline, with a wave rolling in behind. A nature/charm moment.
Golden-hour beach group shot of six friends hugging and posing, with hotels and the offshore island behind. One woman playfully kicks her leg up while holding sandals. Held 1.44s to the end.

study.action_shots: There is no real action. The only movement shots are 4.13–5.0s, a wide static view of the egret with feathers blowing and a wave washing in, and 5.0–6.44s, a wide low-angle group pose where one woman slowly lifts her leg and swings her sandals. In that final shot motion drops to 2.0 and 1.3 by the end, which reads as slightly slowed or gentle movement. Energy comes from the cuts rather than from action, and the motion peak of 35.8–38.9 at 2.0–3.5s comes from handheld moves and scene changes.
study.views: The biggest view comes first: the lobby glass wall framing palms, pool and ocean at 0–1.4s, held for the longest opening shot with a slight handheld drift. It is revealed 'through a window', with the dark marble floor reflecting the scene to double the blue. The second view, around 2.0–2.33s, is the ocean and mountain headland seen past foreground leaves with a slight push and parallax, giving a peek-through reveal. The final view (5.0–6.44s) is the golden-hour beach with hotel towers and an island on the horizon under a soft peach sky, framed as a group shot. The video front-loads its best view instead of saving it, because the text needs the strongest image under it.
study.how_place_is_shown: Mostly wides and mediums of architecture and amenities (lobby, loungers, pool view, bathroom, restaurant), one food close-up (pancakes) and one nature close-ish shot (egret). People appear only in the last shot, a friend group rather than a single couple. Everything is filmed handheld on a phone with slight smooth drifts, not POV walk-throughs. There is no drone. The light runs from bright midday blue (lobby) to overcast pastel (pool and ocean) to warm indoor (bathroom, restaurant) to golden hour (beach). Details are chosen to prove 'cheap but nice': designer bathroom, stylish restaurant, abundant buffet. The repeated lavender and teal tones give it a cohesive pastel aesthetic.
study.info_and_value: The video gives one hard fact through on-screen text only: an all-inclusive resort for under $100 per night per person, framed as a couples trip. No resort name, location or booking info appears. Withholding the name drives comments ('where is this?') and saves, and the low price plus 'couples trip' drives partner tags and shares.
study.pacing: 6 shots in 6.44s (7.76 cuts per 10s). Shot lengths are 1.4, 0.93, 1.0, 0.8, 0.87 and 1.44s, with a median of 0.97s. The two longest shots are the opening view and the closing people shot; the middle four run under 1s each. Cuts land on audio hits: 1.4 to 1.43, 3.33 to 3.34, 4.13 to 4.06, 5.0 to 5.01. The beat grid runs about every 0.24–0.48s. Motion rises from 5–8 in the calm opening to 32–39 between 2.0 and 4.5s, then falls to 1–2 at the end, giving a calm, fast, calm shape.
study.speed: Mostly normal speed. The final group shot (5.0–6.44s) looks gently slowed, with the leg kick and sandal swing unfolding smoothly and motion falling to 1.3. The egret's plumes may also be slightly slowed. There are no ramps or timelapses.
study.on_screen_text: One static block runs the whole video (from 0.0s to the end): 'your sign to take a couples trip to an all inclusive resort for less than $100/night per person'. It is set in all-lowercase thin white serif (a Georgia/typewriter-like editorial look) with a very faint shadow and no box. It sits centered just below the middle of the frame (about 60% down) on 3 lines of roughly 8, 6 and 5 words. There are no emoji. It never changes, so the viewer reads it while the clips prove it.
study.audio: A trending pop song, with the lyric 'I'm going to crush on you' audible from 2.00–2.96s, which plays as a flirty couples cue. There is no voiceover and no natural sound. Strong beat hits fall at 0.24, 0.72, 0.97, 1.2, 1.43, 1.92, 2.15, 3.1, 3.34, 3.82, 4.06, 5.01, 5.25, 5.73 and 5.96s. Cuts are snapped to the hits at 1.43, 3.34, 4.06 and 5.01.
study.transitions: Hard cuts only, on the beat: lobby to loungers at 1.4, ocean view to bathroom at 2.33, restaurant to buffet at 3.33, buffet to egret at 4.13, egret to group at 5.0. The restaurant shot gives way to the pancakes almost instantly after 3.33, and the switch from loungers to the leafy ocean view around 2.0 happens inside what the detector counts as one shot, as a quick pan or second soft cut.
study.effects: A bright, saturated grade with boosted blue sky and water in the lobby, clean pastel lavender and teal at the pool, and warm amber on the bathroom and the golden-hour beach. There is mild sharpening/HDR-style clarity and gentle handheld push-ins. No graphics, maps, freeze frames or split screens.
study.quality: 576x1024 at 25fps, h264, about 1058 kbps. This is a low-bitrate upload, so fine textures soften, but the vertical framing is clean and the shots are stable handheld. Exposure is well controlled on the bright lobby windows despite the dark interior, and the colors are vivid and consistent. It looks like a polished phone vacation reel rather than a cinematic production, which suits the attainable '$100/night' message.
study.ending: It ends on the warm golden-hour friend-group shot, held 1.44s (the longest shot) with the woman mid-kick, then cuts about 0.5s after the last beat hit at 5.96s. The ending is a human moment, not a view, and there is no spoken or written CTA; the opening 'your sign' text does the CTA work. The short 6.4s runtime and the jump from calm beach back to the bright lobby make it rewatch and loop easily.
study.why_viral: 1) A price-shock hook ('all inclusive, less than $100/night per person') stays on screen the whole time over a luxury-looking lobby view. 2) The 'your sign to take a couples trip' framing is built to be sent to a partner, so it drives shares and tags. 3) It is extremely short (6.4s), with sub-1s beat-synced cuts that each prove a different value point (pool, view, bathroom, restaurant, buffet, beach), making it loop and boosting completion. 4) The resort name is withheld, which provokes 'where is this?' comments and saves.
lessons: Put the single most surprising value claim (price per night, all-inclusive) on screen from frame 1 and leave it up for the whole video; a 15–25 word sentence on 3 lines is readable over 6 seconds.
Open on your widest 'wow' view framed through a window or doorway and hold it about 1.4s, longer than the middle shots, so the viewer can read the text against it.
Keep middle shots at 0.8–1.0s and snap every cut to a beat hit (within about 0.05s), as here at 1.43, 3.34 and 5.01s.
Choose b-roll that proves the claim, one amenity per shot: pool, ocean view, bathroom, restaurant, food, beach. Each cut should answer 'is it really nice for that price?'
End on people (the couple or friends) at golden hour and hold the last shot about 1.4–1.5s, slightly slowed, so it lands emotionally and loops cleanly.
Use clean all-lowercase white serif text centered about 60% down, no box, so it reads as aesthetic rather than salesy and stays clear of platform UI.
Pick a trending song whose audible lyric matches the trip type (romantic for couples) and let the lyric hit around 2s, after the visual hook has landed.
Keep the total under 7–8s with 6 shots so viewers watch it 2–3 times; withhold the resort name to invite comments asking where it is.

study.format: Numbered 'don't make these mistakes' tips list: a 4-part 'Bali Airport Survival Guide'. It is built as a talking head with cutaways. The creator speaks to camera the whole way through. Each tip gets a numbered red title card, then B-roll that proves it: phone screen recordings of the official websites and apps, plus airport footage. A paid or affiliate integration (the Airalo eSIM with discount code A&G) sits inside tip #2 and is repeated in the closing CTA.
study.place: Bali, Indonesia, from arrival at Ngurah Rai/Denpasar airport to a tropical villa or resort. It is filmed by a turquoise pool with palm trees, frangipani, a white daybed cabana and a cream market umbrella over teal sun loungers. The 'special' look is the paradise backdrop behind practical airport advice. The tips cover the e-visa, the eSIM, the arrival card and the Grab Lounge pickup.
study.audience: First-time and upcoming Bali travelers, especially long-haul visitors nervous about immigration queues, data and taxis. The video is built to be saved ('Make sure you save this post for your next trip' at 10.24s, plus a 'SAVE THIS POST' graphic). It also invites comments ('Let me know if you've got any questions') and drives code redemptions. It reads as an experienced creator couple ('we', 'our sixth trip', code A&G) doing a monetized creator tip video, not as a brand or agent.
study.hook: First frame: a selfie medium shot of the creator under palm fronds next to a turquoise pool in bright sun. A red rounded box near the top reads 'Don't make these mistakes when you come to Bali', topped with ❌🇮🇩❌ emoji. She starts talking at 0.00s: 'Do not make these mistakes when you come to Bali.' The words 'Bali' and 'mistakes' land within 1.7s. Credibility follows at 3.36s ('our sixth trip here') over a cut to a crowded arrival hall queue at 3.0s. It stops the scroll through negative framing (fear of messing up), a dream-location backdrop and instant authority.

beats.what: Selfie by the pool under palms. Red-box title 'Don't make these mistakes when you come to Bali' with ❌🇮🇩❌. Spoken line matches the text.

Handheld walk through the airport arrival hall: crowded queue under the arched roof, a fast blurry pan around 5.3s, a backpacker walking toward the signs. The title text stays on at first. VO: 'sixth trip... people getting caught out of the airport.'
Back to the pool selfie. She holds up 4 fingers on 'four-part'. Title '4 Part Bali Airport Survival Guide' appears around 8.4s in red script-style type.
Early save CTA: 'SAVE THIS POST' white bold italic with a yellow check mark. VO: 'Make sure you save this post for your next trip.'

Location switch to the seated lounger under the umbrella. '1. Apply for your E-Visa 7 days before your flight' plus a URL-bar graphic 'https://evisa.imigrasi.go.id'. '(OR EARLIER IF YOU CAN)' is added around 14s.
Screen recording of the official Indonesian e-Visa website, held still.
Talking head explains the payoff: scan your passport at the e-gate, no immigration queue.
Tip 2: '2. Download an eSIM' title card. VO: 'sort your data before you land.'
Airalo logo pops in at upper left while she says they always use it.
B-roll of hands holding a phone with the Airalo app in the garden, then her on the phone by a bamboo hut. Red box 'CODE: A&G FOR $3 OFF' plus '➡️ YOUR FIRST ESIM'.
Talking head: 'All you need to do is download the Airalo app.'
Screen recording scrolls the Airalo country list with prices (£3.50–£7.50) over a blurred pool background. VO: '200 plus countries.'
Talking head: 'great if you're going somewhere else afterwards.'
Screen recordings: Indonesia packages (1GB £3.50, 3GB £7.00), then typing code 'A&G' into the discount field (38.87s).
Talking head: download it on good wi-fi, then switch it on when you arrive.
iOS settings screen recording: the 'Turn On This Line' toggle flips green, with a red hand-drawn arrow.
Tip 3: '3. Fill out your arrival form before your flight' plus URL graphic 'allindonesia.imigrasi.go.id'.
All Indonesia Arrival Card website with a red arrow pointing to 'Foreign Visitor'. VO: 'up to three days before.'
Talking head: show your QR code and it scans you in.
Punch-in to a tighter crop: 'no filling out forms in a long queue... much faster.'
Tip 4: '4. Order a grab taxi at the airport'. VO: 'Do not get stuck at the airport.'
Grab app screen recording: green splash, then the home screen.
Low-angle shot of the illuminated 'Grab Lounge' sign inside the airport.
Talking head gives directions: 'when you come out of the arrival section just go left.'
Closing CTA on a slightly tighter framing: 'Let me know if you've got any questions', then a repeat of 'download the Airalo app and use our code A&G for $3 off'.

study.action_shots: Very few, and none are timed to music. (1) 3.0–6.6s: handheld follow/POV walk through the arrival hall. It opens wide on the crowded queue, whips into a motion-blurred pan around 5.0–5.5s (motion about 36 at 2.0s, 38.7 at 6.5s), and ends behind a backpacker walking toward the departure boards. It plays at real speed and sells the 'arrival chaos' problem. (2) Around 27.3–30.6s: medium B-roll of hands tapping the phone in the garden, then the creator standing and talking on the phone by a bamboo hut with the pool behind. (3) Screen-recording scrolls (32.3–35.3s country list, around 37–38.9s package list, 43.4–46.6s toggle) act as the 'action' in the middle section. Everything else is a seated talking head with motion around 3–6.
study.views: No dedicated view shots or reveals. Beauty is carried by the backgrounds. The pool, palms and white cabana sit behind the walking selfie (0–3s, 6.6–12.07s), where the turquoise water fills the lower left. The umbrella-and-lounger set (12.07s onward) frames tropical garden, a thatched villa and the daybed. The airport arched roof is shown wide at 3.0s. The 'biggest view' is the opening pool selfie at 0s: the paradise look is front-loaded as the hook rather than saved for the end.
study.how_place_is_shown: Two looks. The first 12s are handheld selfie mediums, walking by the pool in harsh midday sun under a blue sky.
